Chapter page: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/chapter-928 — accessed 28 Oct 2026.

Section Summary Verbatim / key text Last amended
928.01 Definitions "Container" = innermost wrapping/packaging/vessel in direct contact with a final hemp-derived cannabinoid product for retail sale (not bulk shipping / outer wrapping). "Hemp" = Cannabis sativa L. + parts/derivatives/extracts/cannabinoids/isomers/acids/salts, with total THC incl. THCA ≤0.3% dry weight, EXCLUDING: (1) viable seeds from a plant over 0.3% total THC; (2) intermediate products with non-naturally-producible cannabinoids, or naturally-producible cannabinoids synthesised outside the plant, or >0.3% combined total THC + similar-effect cannabinoids per 928.031 lists; (3) intermediate products marketed/sold as final / direct to end consumer; (4) final products with non-naturally-producible cannabinoids, synthesised-outside-plant cannabinoids, or >0.4 mg combined total THC (incl. THCA) + similar-effect cannabinoids per container per 928.031 lists. "Hemp-derived cannabinoid product" = intermediate/final product derived from hemp (other than industrial hemp) containing cannabinoids, intended for human/animal use by any means (inhalation, ingestion, topical); excludes FDA-approved drugs (21 U.S.C. 355(c)/(j)). "Industrial hemp" = stalk/fibre, seed grain/oil/cake/nut/hull, microgreens/edible leaf from immature plants from compliant seeds, non-commerce research plants, viable seed for those materials. "Intermediate" = not yet final form, or powder/liquid/tablet/oil intended to be mixed/dissolved/formulated into another substance before use. "Marihuana" = ORC 3719.01 meaning. "(C) 'Hemp' means the plant Cannabis sativa L. and any part of that plant … with a total tetrahydrocannabinols concentration, including tetrahydrocannabinolic acid, of not more than three-tenths per cent on a dry weight basis. 'Hemp' does not include … (4)(c) Greater than four-tenths of a milligram combined total per container of total tetrahydrocannabinols, including tetrahydrocannabinolic acid, and any other cannabinoids that have similar effects, or are marketed to have similar effects, on humans or animals as a tetrahydrocannabinol as established by the superintendent of cannabis control in lists adopted under section 928.031" SB 56, eff. 20 Mar 2026 (definition rewritten; prior SB 57 definition was delta-9 THC ≤0.3% only)
928.02 Regulation/licensing Director of Agriculture may establish a cultivation programme and shall establish a processing programme; if cultivation programme exists and director intends to transfer it to USDA, director shall effectuate transfer; if cultivation programme implemented, director issues cultivation licences per 928.03 rules; Dept./university may cultivate/process for research without licence as authorised; licences valid 3 years unless suspended/revoked; Dept./university/any person may without licence possess/buy/sell hemp or hemp product; adding hemp/hemp product to another product does not adulterate it; out-of-state licence / work-experience / certification reciprocity under ORC Chapter 4796 for individuals. "(A)(1) The director of agriculture may establish a program to monitor and regulate hemp cultivation and shall establish a program to monitor and regulate hemp processing in this state." SB 56, eff. 20 Mar 2026 (cultivation "shall" → "may" is an SB 56 change; USDA-transfer language is new — see §1.5 / Run 2 Part 7)
928.03 Rules Director (with Governor + Attorney General, Ch. 119) shall adopt processing rules and, if a cultivation programme is implemented, cultivation rules: application forms/info, application + annual fees (cost-covering; one uniform cultivation fee), background investigations (ORC 4776.01–4776.04; no licence if non-compliant; 10-year felony-controlled-substance bar + revocation for 10 years on guilty plea/conviction), experience/equipment/facilities/land, processor financial responsibility, issuance/renewal/denial/suspension/revocation + Ch. 119 hearing, material falsification = ineligibility, land records (legal description, per federal law), no cultivating/processing marihuana, post-decarboxylation or similarly reliable THC testing, corrective action plans, annual inspections (random sample, cultivation + processing), federal enforcement compliance, disposal of violating plants/products, hemp byproducts (byproduct >0.3% THC counts as hemp product only if produced/stored/disposed per rules), USDA information-sharing, setback distance from marijuana cultivation (not applicable if marijuana cultivator moves in after hemp licensee starts), annual reporting, recordkeeping, lab-testing fees, testing/labelling/packaging standards, no processing in a personal residence or on residentially zoned land, production/manufacturing practices, transport/storage, "independent research institute" definition, other necessary requirements. "(L) A procedure for testing, using post-decarboxylation or other similarly reliable methods, tetrahydrocannabinol concentration levels of plants and products" SB 56, eff. 20 Mar 2026
928.031 Cannabinoid lists Superintendent of Cannabis Control, in consultation with Director of Agriculture, shall establish lists: (1) cannabinoids capable of being naturally produced by Cannabis sativa L.; (2) THC-class cannabinoids known to be naturally occurring; (3) all other known cannabinoids with similar / marketed-similar effects to THC-class; (4) any additional similar-effect / marketed-similar cannabinoids; plus additional "container" specificity. Federal (Congress / HHS / FDA under 7 U.S.C. 139o et seq.) additions/changes/removals are automatically effected, subject to superintendent amendment; superintendent may add/change/remove after reviewing federal determinations for Ohio-law accordance, current science, public-health risk; on initial publication or any change, superintendent + director shall adopt a Ch. 119 rule codifying the list, filed with JCARR within 6 months. Whether the lists have been published / codified as of 28 Oct 2026 was not confirmed in this run — [VERIFY; without the lists, the "similar effects" limb of 928.01 is not fully operable from the statute alone]. 928.04 Licences required Except research authorisations, no cultivation without a cultivation licence if the director implements a cultivation programme, and no processing without a processing licence; licensees must not violate Ch. 928/rules; corrective-action-plan subjects must comply; no transport of hemp/hemp product in violation of 928.03 rules. See chapter text. SB 56, eff. 20 Mar 2026
928.05 Corrective action plans Director shall issue a corrective action plan for negligent violation: reasonable correction date + 2-calendar-year compliance reporting; 3+ negligent violations in 5 years → revocation + 5-year refusal; culpable mental state greater than negligence → report to Attorney General, US Attorney General, county prosecutor. See chapter text. SB 57, eff. 30 July 2019 — not amended by SB 56

928.07 Entry / warrant / emergency / injunction Director may enter public/private property where hemp is cultivated/processed at reasonable times; may seek search warrant; emergency order without prior notice/hearing if immediate public-health/safety/environmental action needed (hearing within 30 days on application); director / AG / county prosecutor may seek common-pleas injunction. 928.99 Penalties Whoever recklessly violates 928.04: 1st offence minor misdemeanour; subsequent offences 4th-degree misdemeanour; court shall order 3rd/subsequent offender ineligible for cultivation/processing licence, notify director, director revokes + refuses. County prosecutor or AG may prosecute. Note: this is the only penalty section in Ch. 928 read; it does not by itself state the penalty for selling an intoxicating hemp product outside a dispensary — that exposure arises because the product is no longer "hemp" and is treated as marihuana under Ch. 2925/3796 (see §1.5). "(A) Whoever recklessly violates section 928.04 … is guilty of the following: (1) For a first offense, a minor misdemeanor; (2) For each subsequent offense, a misdemeanor of the fourth degree." 1.3 Possession, home grow, public consumption, vehicles, gifting, product types

Possession limits (adult-use)

Form Limit Cumulative? Source
Plant material 2.5 oz (70.9 g), excluding seeds, live plants, clones being cultivated/grown/possessed under 3796.04 Yes — cumulative homegrown + adult-use (3796.221(B)) https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.221
Extract 15 g Yes — cumulative (3796.221(B)(2)) Same
Other product forms (edibles, beverages, vapes, etc. as "extract" vs "other products") Ambiguity flagged: The statute caps "extract" at 15 g, but dispensary purchase rules (secondary, OAC 1301:18-8-09) are stated as 15,000 mg THC in other products per day. 15 g of extract ≠ 15,000 mg THC (a 15 g extract at 70% THC = 10,500 mg THC; at 90% = 13,500 mg). Possession vs purchase caps therefore do not map 1:1, and the 15,000 mg figure must not be quoted as the statutory possession limit. [VERIFY — read OAC 1301:18-8-09 and any DCC purchase-limit guidance to reconcile.] — Statute vs secondary: https://bloommarijuana.com/senate-bill-56

Home grow (detail)

  • 6 per adult-use consumer, 12 per single residence — 3796.04(A)(1)(a)–(b) (SB 56; unchanged numbers from Issue 2).
  • Location: primary residence only; within a secured closet, room, greenhouse or other enclosed area in/on the grounds of the residence, preventing under-21 access, not visible by normal unaided vision from a public space — 3796.04(A)(1)(c).
  • Prohibited locations: Type A/B family child care home (ORC 5104.01); halfway house / community transitional housing / community residential centre / similar facility licensed under ORC 2967.14; rental premises whose rental agreement prohibits the activities — 3796.04(A)(1)(d).
  • Allowed: process by manual/mechanical means (not hydrocarbon extraction — 3796.04(B)(3)); store homegrown + adult-use at primary residence; use homegrown grown/cultivated/processed at primary residence; possess paraphernalia/accessories — 3796.04(A)(2)–(5).
  • Not allowed: cultivate/grow/process except at primary residence; any use/cultivation/processing/transfer/transport before 21; hydrocarbon extraction; sale/profit; growing on behalf of another — 3796.04(B).
  • Penalty: knowing violation of 3796.04(C) (home-grow manner / public consumption / permitting) → illegal cultivation under ORC 2925.04 via 3796.99(E). Note: commentators state SB 56 lowered the criminal threshold vs Issue 2 (formerly criminal only at double the plant limit; now any excess) — that LSC-analysis claim is secondary and [VERIFY against the SB 56 final analysis].
  • Correction of a secondary error found in this run: one secondary article stated the household limit "was reduced from 12 plants" / "Ohioans are already prohibited from growing more than six plants in a household" (Focal News, 6 Oct 2026, on package rules). That contradicts the primary text read (3796.04: 6 per adult, 12 per residence). The 6-per-package limit in OAC 1301:18-4-06 is a package limit for clones/live plants/seeds sold, not the household grow limit. Do not repeat the "6 per household" claim.

Public consumption / vehicles / gifting — see §1.1 table; operative texts

  • Public consumption: 3796.04(C)(2)–(3) (knowing consumption in a public place prohibited; operator must not knowingly permit); 3796.06(C)(2) (smoking/combustion/vaporisation only on privately owned residential/agricultural property); 3796.06(C)(3) (also banned in child-care homes, halfway-house-type facilities, lease-prohibited rentals, public places / places of employment as defined in ORC 3794.01).
  • Vehicles: 3796.062 (transport, above) + 3796.99(A) (penalties, above). Edibles in a vehicle: the original-packaging storage rule (3796.06(H)) applies "at all times when the products are not actively in use" — it is not limited to the home in the text read.
  • Gifting: 3796.221(A)(4) + (C) (above). No "gifting" of unlimited homegrown surplus is authorised; the daily transfer cap applies to the recipient, and the giver's own possession cap still applies.

Allowed product types and limits (adult-use vs medical)

Statutory forms: §1.2, 3796.06(A)–(B). Statutory potency: 35% plant, 70% extracts (both), DCC may increase extracts by rule (3796.06(E)(3)) — exercised to 90% in OAC 1301:18-4-06 (Oct 2026). Package/serving limits: OAC 1301:18-4-06 (Oct 2026) — see §1.2 table; adult-use edibles 10 mg/serving, 100 mg/package and adult-use beverages 10 mg/container are the widely reported figures, flagged [VERIFY] for full-text quotation. Medical edibles/beverages higher (55 mg) per secondary summaries, flagged [VERIFY].

Changes since Issue 2 (summary): Issue 2 allowed the same broad forms list but set no statutory THC % caps, no 1-oz package cap, no 2-g vape cap, no per-serving/per-package edible caps in statute, no edible original-packaging rule, no private-property-only smoking rule in its final form, and no source restriction. All of those restrictions are SB 56 and/or 2026 DCC rules. The 90% extract figure in Oct 2026 rules is higher than SB 56's 70% statutory cap — lawful only because SB 56 itself authorises DCC to increase it by rule; it is not a return to Issue 2 (which had no cap to exceed).

1.4 Medical programme

Qualifying conditions (ORC 3796.01(A)(6) — SB 56 text, list originates HB 523)

Statutory list (21 limbs + Medical Board additions): (a) acquired immune deficiency syndrome; (b) Alzheimer's disease; (c) amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; (d) cancer; (e) chronic traumatic encephalopathy; (f) Crohn's disease; (g) epilepsy or another seizure disorder; (h) fibromyalgia; (i) glaucoma; (j) hepatitis C; (k) inflammatory bowel disease; (l) multiple sclerosis; (m) pain that is chronic and severe or intractable; (n) Parkinson's disease; (o) positive status for HIV; (p) post-traumatic stress disorder; (q) sickle cell anemia; (r) spinal cord disease or injury; (s) Tourette's syndrome; (t) traumatic brain injury; (u) ulcerative colitis; (v) any other disease/condition added by the State Medical Board under ORC 4731.302.

Medical Board additions (secondary, consistent across sources — [VERIFY against Medical Board orders]): cachexia, Huntington's disease, irritable bowel syndrome, spasticity, terminal illness. Secondary sources also describe Board determinations that arthritis, chronic migraines, complex regional pain syndrome, degenerative disc disease and lupus with pain present are covered under the existing chronic-pain qualifier — not as standalone additions. Not qualifying on the evidence found: anxiety alone, autism spectrum disorder alone (petitions under OAC 4731-32-05 not approved on the reporting found). Opioid use disorder was proposed in SB 9 (2023, not enacted) — not a qualifying condition.

Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/chapter-3796 (§3796.01); additions: https://www.mmj.com/ohio-medical-marijuana-card/qualifying-conditions/ and https://leafwell.com/medical-card/ohio — accessed 28 Oct 2026.

Physician certification (Certificate to Recommend, CTR)

  • Physician = individual authorised under ORC Chapter 4731 to practise medicine/surgery or osteopathic medicine/surgery (3796.01(A)(5)).
  • Must hold a Certificate to Recommend (CTR) issued by the State Medical Board under ORC 4731.30; dispensary may dispense medical marijuana only on a written recommendation from a CTR physician (3796.20(B)(1)).
  • CTR eligibility (State Medical Board, OAC 4731-32-02; Board annual report): active unrestricted MD/DO licence; unprohibited OARRS access; active DEA registration; no DEA/state licence denial/restriction for inappropriate prescribing of a controlled substance/dangerous drug; no disciplinary action for inappropriate prescribing; 2 hours CME certified by the Ohio State Medical Association or Ohio Osteopathic Association on qualifying conditions + treating them with medical marijuana incl. drug interactions; no financial relationship with a marijuana entity (per JD Supra summary of OAC 4731-32-02). No separate CTR fee (renewed with medical licence; physician may renew licence without renewing CTR since June 2020).
  • Standard of care (OAC 4731-32-03): bona fide physician-patient relationship established by in-person or telehealth examination with expectation of ongoing care; medical record (visits, conditions, history incl. prescription + substance-use history, diagnostics, prior treatment/response, standard treatment attempted/considered, drug screen if indicated, relevant physical exam, diagnosis/confirmation); on recommendation: treatment plan, 12-month OARRS review + abuse/diversion discussion, risks/benefits explanation + opinion benefits outweigh risks, patient consent (parent/legal representative if minor), caregiver name if needed; check for existing active registration/recommendation in OARRS; annual report to the Medical Board on effectiveness observations (no patient identification) under ORC 4731.30 / OAC 4731-32-03.
  • Count (secondary, Board document): 504 active CTR physicians as of 30 June 2026 (2026 CTR Physician Annual Report). Source: https://dam.assets.ohio.gov/image/upload/med.ohio.gov/for-the-public/medical-marijuana/CTR_Physician_Annual_Report_2026.pdf — accessed 28 Oct 2026.
  • Petition for new condition: OAC 4731-32-05 (evidence incl. peer-reviewed studies, physician support letters; Board decision). [VERIFY current petition window / 2026 decisions.]

Patient and caregiver registration and fees

  • Process: physician (or delegate) submits application to DCC on patient's/caregiver's behalf (3796.08(A)(1)); certification must state bona fide relationship, qualifying-condition diagnosis, 12-month drug-database report requested, risks/benefits informed; application names caregiver(s)/patient(s); if complete, DCC registers + issues ID card; registration expires per 3796.03 rules, renewable (3796.08(C)).
  • Fee: $0 state registration fee on current secondary reporting (former $50 annual patient fee removed — Leafwell/MMJ summaries, 2026). The statute read does not state a fee amount (fees are in rules under 3796.03(B)(1)); [VERIFY fee = $0 against OAC 1301:18-10 / DCC fee schedule before Run 2 repeats it as fact.] Physician evaluation fees are private (e.g. $99 telehealth example in secondary source) — not a state fee, do not present as one.
  • Validity: 1 year, expiring last day of month of issue; renewal submission up to 30 days before expiry; DCC email 45 days before expiry (secondary summary of OAC 1301:18-10-01(H)) — [VERIFY].
  • Caregiver limits in older rules (secondary, pre-2026): patient ≤2 caregivers; caregiver ≤2 patients — [VERIFY whether retained in OAC 1301:18-10; not in the statute text read].
  • Confidentiality: registration information confidential, not a public record; shareable with a licensed dispensary only to confirm valid registration (3796.08(B)).

Purchase limits and the 90-day supply

  • Statute: patient possession ≤90-day supply as specified in rules under 3796.03 (3796.22(B)); caregiver possession ≤90-day supply per patient, separate inventories (3796.23(B)).
  • Old system (pre-Mar 2026): "whole day units" / days'-supply by form (e.g. former OAC 3796:8-2-04: 90-day supply by form, terminal-illness variant 10 oz plant / 29.5 g THC topical / 11 g THC oral / 59 g THC vaporisation — historic rule text via Cornell LII, eff. 14 Feb 2022). Do not quote the old whole-day-unit figures as current.
  • Current system (from 24 Mar 2026, secondary/DCC guidance): daily 2.5 oz plant + 15,000 mg THC in other products; patients may buy up to 4 days at once (10 oz / 60,000 mg); caregivers daily limit only, no stacking; 90-day cap = 90 × daily (14.06 lb plant / 1,350 g THC). Physician recommendation still caps the patient (cannot exceed authorised 90-day supply; must follow recommendation). [VERIFY against OAC 1301:18-8-09.]
  • Dispensary duties on medical sale: ID + CTR recommendation, OARRS/drug-database reporting (ORC 4729.771), labelling (processor/dispensary, patient/caregiver, physician, directions, date, quantity/strength/kind/form), adequate medical supply (3796.20(B)).

Out-of-state patients

  • No reciprocity right exists unless DCC has entered an agreement under 3796.16 (substantially comparable eligibility + mutual recognition). No such agreement was located in this run. An out-of-state cardholder therefore cannot rely on 3796.22/3796.23 in Ohio on the evidence found; they may still purchase as an adult-use consumer (21+) subject to adult-use caps and taxes, but that is not medical recognition. [VERIFY — DCC reciprocity list, Part 10.] Note: a non-resident can become an Ohio patient only if they meet Ohio registration requirements (Ohio residency is stated in secondary patient guides — [VERIFY residency requirement in OAC 1301:18-10; the statute text read does not state it expressly]).

Transfer from Board of Pharmacy / Commerce to Division of Cannabis Control

  • Original split (HB 523): Commerce licensed cultivators/processors/labs; Board of Pharmacy licensed dispensaries + registered patients/caregivers + approved forms; State Medical Board certified physicians + added conditions.
  • HB 33 (2023): created the Division of Marijuana Control in Commerce (now Division of Cannabis Control, ORC 3796.01(B) name-deeming provision), transferred all medical-programme assets/liabilities/obligations and personnel from Commerce + Board of Pharmacy to the Division by 31 Dec 2023; Board continued patient/caregiver applications until 180 days after 3 Oct 2023 (3796.08(A)(1)); Medical Board role retained.
  • SB 56 (2026): completed the consolidation in statute — the Division now licenses all types, registers patients/caregivers, and administers both medical and adult-use under one chapter; former Chapter 3780 licences are deemed equivalent Chapter 3796 licences and merged where same person + location (3796.33).
  • Current regulator for historic records: Board of Pharmacy and State Medical Board retain historic/physician records (CTR, condition petitions); operational licensing/registration is DCC. Do not direct a current patient to the Board of Pharmacy for registration.

1.5 Hemp and intoxicating hemp

THC limits and how THC is measured

  • Plant / hemp threshold: total THC including THCA ≤0.3% on a dry-weight basis (ORC 928.01(C)). Measurement: post-decarboxylation or other similarly reliable methods (ORC 928.03(L)). This is a total-THC standard, not delta-9-only — Ohio adopted total-THC in SB 56 (Mar 2026), ahead of the federal total-THC definition's full effect (11 Dec 2026).
  • Intermediate product threshold: >0.3% combined total THC (incl. THCA) + similar-effect cannabinoids (per 928.031 lists) → excluded from hemp (928.01(C)(2)(c)).
  • Final product threshold: >0.4 mg combined total THC (incl. THCA) + similar-effect cannabinoids per container → excluded from hemp (928.01(C)(4)(c)). "Container" = innermost retail wrapping/vessel in direct contact with the final product (jar, bottle, bag, box, packet, can, carton, cartridge); bulk shipping containers and non-essential outer wrappings excluded (928.01(A)).
  • Synthetic / non-natural cannabinoids: any cannabinoid not capable of being naturally produced by Cannabis sativa L., or capable of being naturally produced but synthesised/manufactured outside the plant, in an intermediate or final product → excluded from hemp (928.01(C)(2)(a)–(b), (4)(a)–(b)). This limb catches delta-8, delta-10 and similar converted cannabinoids as a category, regardless of mg, when synthesised outside the plant. Naturally occurring trace amounts in compliant hemp are not the same thing — but the statute's lists (928.031) determine which cannabinoids count as "similar effects" — [VERIFY lists publication].
  • Industrial hemp (stalk/fibre, seed products, microgreens/edible leaf from immature compliant-seed plants, non-commerce research plants, viable seed for those uses) is hemp under 928.01(G) and is not a "hemp-derived cannabinoid product" (928.01(E) excludes industrial hemp from that definition).

Rules for hemp-derived intoxicating products (delta-8, delta-9, THCA, others)

There is no Ohio "intoxicating hemp licence" or general-retail intoxicating-hemp regime in the current statute read. The mechanism is definitional + channel:

  1. A product over 0.4 mg/container total THC, or containing a synthetic/non-natural or synthesised-outside-plant cannabinoid, or an intermediate product sold as final/direct-to-consumer, is not hemp (928.01).
  2. What is not hemp is marihuana (928.01(J) → 3719.01).
  3. Marihuana may lawfully be possessed/used only as medical marijuana (registered patient/caregiver, dispensary), adult-use marijuana (21+, dispensary or homegrown), or homegrown marijuana — i.e. through the licensed dispensary channel or lawful home grow (3796.221, 3796.04, 3796.22–3796.23).
  4. Sale outside a licensed dispensary therefore has no lawful channel in the statute read. Secondary sources phrase this as "sale limited to licensed dispensaries, 21+" — that phrasing should be read as "the only lawful retail channel for a >0.4 mg / synthetic product as marijuana is a licensed dispensary (and then only if the product itself complies with Chapter 3796 product rules, testing, packaging and potency caps — a hemp-derived product does not automatically become a lawful dispensary product by being carried into a dispensary)". [VERIFY — DCC guidance on whether / how hemp-derived products may enter dispensary inventory; Part 11.]
  5. THCA specifically: THCA counts toward total THC (928.01(C) expressly includes THCA). High-THCA flower that exceeds 0.3% total THC (incl. THCA) is not hemp, even if its delta-9 THC alone is ≤0.3%. This is the core THCA change vs the pre-SB 56 delta-9-only definition.
  6. Delta-9 in compliant hemp: delta-9 THC within the 0.3% total-THC plant limit and within the 0.4 mg/container final-product limit remains hemp. A "delta-9" gummy or beverage over 0.4 mg/container does not.
  7. CBD / non-intoxicating hemp: products within the hemp definition (≤0.3% total THC plant; ≤0.4 mg/container final; no synthetic/similar-effect excess) remain hemp; possession/buying/selling without a hemp licence is expressly allowed (928.02(C)). No minimum age, testing or labelling regime for general-retail hemp is stated in Chapter 928 itself — testing/labelling/packaging standards are to be in Agriculture rules under 928.03(X) [VERIFY current 901:14 rules]; the EO 2025-05D complaints (no age verification, no child-resistant packaging, no mandatory testing for intoxicating products) describe the pre-SB 56 general-retail market, not a current statutory permission for intoxicating products.

Order Date / scope / expiry Current status

DeWine urged legislative action from Jan 2024 (secondary: Ohio Capital Journal / Postindustrial, Dec 2025), but no separate 2024 hemp EO was found. [VERIFY — Governor's EO index search for 2024–2025 before Run 2 asserts "only EO 2025-05D".] —

Law banning/restricting intoxicating hemp or limiting sales to dispensaries

  • SB 56, ORC 928.01 (eff. 20 Mar 2026) — the operative ban/restriction, by definition (above). No standalone "intoxicating hemp ban" section number exists in Chapter 928; the ban is the definitional exclusion + marihuana treatment.
  • Enrolled SB 56 Chapter 3779 (drinkable cannabinoid products) — vetoed in relevant part. As passed, SB 56 would have allowed hemp beverages up to 5 mg THC to be made/shipped/sold in Ohio until 31 Dec 2026 (and manufacture of stronger beverages for out-of-state sale), "operative notwithstanding any other provision of the Revised Code to the contrary" (former 3779.211). Governor DeWine line-item vetoed that carve-out on signing (19 Dec 2025), citing the new federal hemp ban and consumer confusion. The Ohio Supreme Court case 2026-0264 (Fifty West Brewing et al.) challenges the veto as "lawless executive overreach" (Ohio Constitution permits line-item veto only in appropriations bills, per relators) and seeks recognition of the enrolled version + regulations by 20 Mar 2026. Outcome [VERIFY — 2026-0264 disposition not found in this run; do not state the veto was upheld or struck down]. Until a court orders otherwise, the vetoed (no-grace-period) version is the operative law.
  • Federal alignment note: The Senate summary of SB 56 states the bill "follows recent federal actions closing the intoxicating hemp loophole by reclassifying any product with more than 0.4mg of THC as marijuana" — that is a political summary, not a legal citation; the federal reclassification's full effect is 11 Dec 2026 per the baseline, while Ohio's is 20 Mar 2026. Ohio is ahead of federal enforcement, not following it in time.

Minimum age, THC beverages, testing and labelling (hemp)

  • Minimum age for hemp: No age limit is stated in Chapter 928 for compliant (non-intoxicating) hemp products. For products that are marihuana (over-threshold / synthetic), the Chapter 3796 age rule applies: 21+ for adult-use, registered patient/caregiver for medical (3796.06(F)–(G), 3796.20). There is no separate "hemp beverage 21+" statute in force after the veto — the vetoed Chapter 3779 would have created a drinkable-cannabinoid regime; it is not law as vetoed.
  • THC beverages: Any beverage over 0.4 mg total THC per container is not hemp (928.01(C)(4)(c)). A beverage within 0.4 mg/container remains hemp. No lawful general-retail THC-beverage category above 0.4 mg exists after the veto. Dispensary-sold cannabis beverages are governed by Chapter 3796 + OAC 1301:18-4-06 (adult-use 10 mg/container per secondary summary — [VERIFY]).
  • Testing: Hemp plant/product THC testing by post-decarboxylation or similarly reliable methods (928.03(L)); Agriculture rules to set testing/labelling/packaging standards (928.03(X)) and lab-testing fees (928.03(W)). No hemp testing panel (pesticides, solvents, etc.) is stated in the statute read — [VERIFY 901:14].
  • Labelling: Same — standards in Agriculture rules (928.03(X)), not in the statute. Do not import Chapter 3796 dispensary labelling (3796.19(B), 3796.20(B)–(C)) into hemp: those apply to licensed marijuana, not to hemp products.
  • State response to the new federal hemp definition and the 12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026 dates: No separate Ohio statute, EO or Agriculture rule responding to PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019 was located in this run. Ohio's response, in substance, pre-dates the federal dates: SB 56 (Dec 2025 / Mar 2026) adopted the same 0.4 mg/container + total-THC + synthetic-exclusion architecture, and the Governor's veto message expressly invoked the federal ban as a reason to end the beverage grace period immediately rather than "going until the date in November set by federal law" (secondary paraphrase of veto message — [VERIFY veto message text]). After 11 Dec 2026, Ohio law and federal law will be aligned on threshold, but Ohio's channel restriction (dispensary-or-homegrown only for over-threshold product) is a state-law consequence that federal law alone does not impose. The USDA DEA-lab testing delay to 31 Dec 2026 and the federal appropriations rider to 11 Dec 2026 have no stated Ohio implementing provision in the sources read — [VERIFY ODA/USDA Ohio plan correspondence in Part 7].

Hemp cultivation transfer to USDA — flag for Part 7

ORC 928.02(A)(1)–(2) as amended by SB 56 makes the cultivation programme discretionary ("may establish") and provides for transfer to USDA if the director establishes then intends to transfer it. Secondary sources state: "From January 1, 2026, persons wishing to cultivate hemp in Ohio will have to apply for a hemp producer license through the USDA's Domestic Hemp Production Program" and, as of June 2026, 44 registered hemp processors in Ohio and 26 growers per the USDA search tool. These secondary claims were not verified against an ODA notice or USDA plan approval in this run and must be verified in Part 7 before stating that Ohio cultivation is now USDA-only. The statute alone does not prove a transfer has occurred — it only authorises one.

1.6 Packaging, labelling, advertising, delivery, zoning and buffer rules

Packaging and labelling (marijuana)

  • Statute: Processor must package to child-resistant standard 16 C.F.R. 1700.15(b) (as of 8 Sept 2016), label THC + CBD content, comply with DCC rules under 3796.03 + 3796.32 (3796.19(B)). Dispensary medical label: processor + dispensary name/address, patient (+ caregiver) name, physician name, directions if any, date dispensed, quantity/strength/kind/form (3796.20(B)(3)). Dispensary adult-use label: processor + dispensary name/address, under-21 harmful-and-illegal statement, quantity/strength/kind/form per DCC rules (3796.20(C)(3)). Dispensary must prominently display under-21 statement + addiction/health-consequences information (3796.20(D)(3)).
  • Child-attractive ban (statute + rule): No form/method attractive to children per DCC rules (3796.06(D)(1)); no human/animal/fruit likeness incl. artistic/caricature/cartoon (3796.06(D)(2)); no packaging/advertising/marketing with cartoon / fictional / pop-culture child-targeted figure (3796.32(D)); OAC 1301:18-4-08 adds: false/misleading, obscene/indecent, candy-resembling, health-statement, endorsement-suggesting, trademark/copyright-violating, off-registered-name (incl. slang); no characterising flavours in smoking/combustion/vaporisation products except strain-mimicking.
  • Rules (Oct 2026 package): OAC 1301:18-4-04 (universal THC symbol), -4-06 (package limits, see §1.2), -4-07 (strain names), -4-19 (pre-approval for packaging/labelling for direct sale), -4-20 (packaging/labelling for direct sale), -4-21 (additional limitations), -4-23 (single serving units). DCC Packaging and Labelling Guidance (Aug 2026) adds: flower/bud/shake/trim/raw single servings — no packaging/labelling/advertising with THC content other than approved range, sum total terpenes/cannabinoids, delta-9 THC, delta-8 THC, or THCA; processed products — no sum total terpenes/cannabinoids; seeds/clones/live plants (untested) — no purported THC/terpene/cannabinoid content at all; QR codes may carry COA / extra info but may not replace required label info and must comply with -4-21/-4-22 + DCC approval. Source: https://dam.assets.ohio.gov/image/upload/com.ohio.gov/DCC/Guidance/Packaging_and_Labeling_Guidance_-_August-2026.pdf — accessed 28 Oct 2026.
  • Edible storage (consumer): 3796.06(H) — store edible adult-use and medical products in original packaging at all times when not actively in use (SB 56).

Advertising

  • Statute: 3796.32 (above). Rule: OAC 1301:18-4-22 (above): prior submission + written approval before any use; DCC may approve / deny / deny-with-10-business-day resubmission / approve with conditions; bans on false/misleading, obscene/indecent, child-attractive, cartoon/fictional/pop-culture-child-targeted ads; statutory 500-ft ad buffer (except facility signage) and health-benefit ban for adult-use ads; names/logos/signs/materials approval with 21-business-day deemed approval under 3796.32(G) — see Research Note R-5 on how (G) deemed approval interacts with the rule's "no use until written approval" for advertisements generally.
  • Adult-use ad rules must be at least as stringent as the most stringent federal/state tobacco/alcohol ad rules (3796.32(B)) — a statutory floor, not a description of any specific tobacco/alcohol rule.

Delivery

  • Medical only, by statute: 3796.20(A)(1)(e) + 3796.03(B)(15)(b). Adult-use delivery: no statutory authority. Online/mobile ordering is authorised for both (3796.03(B)(15)(a)) — ordering ≠ delivery; online orders are fulfilled by in-person pickup on the secondary reporting found. Whether DCC medical-delivery rules are in force and whether any dispensary actually delivers is [VERIFY — DCC delivery rule / licensee list, Parts 4/11]. Older rules (former OAC 3796:6-3-22(K)) prohibited dispensary delivery to residences — that rule is superseded in structure by Chapter 1301:18, but its replacement must be read before stating medical delivery is operational.

Zoning and buffer distances (state level; local detail is Part 3)

  • 500-ft buffer (state): No licensed cultivator/processor/dispensary/lab within 500 ft of a parcel boundary with a school, church, public library, public playground or public park (3796.30(A); also an eligibility condition in 3796.09(C)(4)/3796.10(C)(4)); relocation into the buffer denied (3796.30(B)); grandfathered if certificate of operation predates the protected facility's arrival (3796.30(C)); OAC 1301:18-3-01 measures linearly, shortest parcel-line-to-structure distance, with same-premises certificate-of-operation exception.
  • 1-mile dispensary separation (state, SB 56): No new/relocated dispensary within 1 mile of another licensed dispensary (3796.05(B)(4)(a), 3796.10(C)(5)(a)).
  • Liquor-permit bar (state, SB 56): No new/relocated dispensary at a Chapter 4303 beer/intoxicating-liquor permit premises (3796.05(B)(4)(b), 3796.10(C)(5)(b)).
  • Advertising buffer: 500 ft from school/church/library/playground/park parcel, except facility signage (3796.32(F)).
  • Local power: Municipalities (ordinance) and townships (resolution, unincorporated territory only) may prohibit or limit the number of licensed cultivators/processors/dispensaries (3796.29(A)), subject to the pre-SB 56 provisional-licence/certificate grandfather clause (3796.29(B)(1)) — i.e. a jurisdiction that prohibited adult-use after a medical business was already provisionally licensed / certificated cannot use a post-SB 56 ordinance to shut that existing holder, unless the ordinance predates SB 56's effective date. This answers the Part 3 "existing medical businesses" question at state-law level; jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction application is Part 3. Counties have no 3796.29 power. Localities may not levy cannabis-specific gross-receipts or discriminatory taxes/fees (3796.31).
  • Hemp setback: Agriculture rules must include a setback distance for hemp cultivation from marijuana cultivation (928.03(T)), inapplicable if the marijuana cultivator moves in after the hemp licensee starts. Distance value is in rules, not statute — [VERIFY 901:14].
  • Hemp processing location: Rules must prohibit processing in a personal residence or on residentially zoned land (928.03(Y)).

1.7 Seed-to-sale tracking system

  • Statutory system: ORC 3796.07 — DCC electronic database, seed source through cultivation, processing, testing and dispensing; instantaneous updates; licensee submits information DCC determines necessary; data confidential, not a public record (ORC 149.43), no identification of a specific consumer/patient, aggregate release allowed. DCC may contract with a separate entity to establish/maintain all or part of it.
  • Vendor: Metrc is the system used in Ohio, per multiple secondary sources (IndicaOnline Ohio market page; OhioStateCannabis banking page; CannBus Q3 2026 report noting "Metrc is the system and updated its Ohio product categories on July 13, 2026"). The vendor name does not appear in ORC 3796.07 and was not confirmed on a DCC page opened in this run — [VERIFY against a DCC Metrc page / licensee guidance before Run 2 states it as an official fact.] Medical sales are additionally reported to the drug database (OARRS) under ORC 4729.771 (3796.20(B)(2)).
  • Hemp tracking: No seed-to-sale system for hemp is stated in Chapter 928; hemp licensees are subject to land records, annual reporting and recordkeeping under Agriculture rules (928.03(J), (U), (V)), and USDA reporting if under a USDA plan — [VERIFY Part 7].

1.8 Employment and drug testing protections (including zero-tolerance rights)

Ohio provides no employment protection for marijuana use. It expressly preserves employer action.

Verbatim — ORC 3796.28 (SB 56, eff. 20 Mar 2026; extends the former medical-only rule to all marijuana):

"(A) Nothing in this chapter does any of the following: (1) Requires an employer to permit or accommodate an employee's use, possession, or distribution of marijuana; (2) Prohibits an employer from refusing to hire, discharging, disciplining, or otherwise taking an adverse employment action against a person with respect to hire, tenure, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment because of that person's use, possession, or distribution of marijuana; (3) Prohibits an employer from establishing and enforcing a drug testing policy, drug-free workplace policy, or zero-tolerance drug policy; (4) Interferes with any federal restrictions on employment, including the regulations adopted by the United States department of transportation in Title 49 of the Code of Federal Regulations, as amended; (5) Permits a person to commence a cause of action against an employer for refusing to hire, discharging, disciplining, discriminating, retaliating, or otherwise taking an adverse employment action against a person with respect to hire, tenure, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment related to marijuana; (6) Affects the authority of the administrator of workers' compensation to grant rebates or discounts on premium rates to employers that participate in a drug-free workplace program established in accordance with rules adopted by the administrator under Chapter 4123. of the Revised Code."

"(B) A person who is discharged from employment because of that person's use of marijuana shall be considered to have been discharged for just cause for purposes of division (D) of section 4141.29 of the Revised Code and shall be ineligible to serve a waiting period or to be paid benefits for the duration of the individual's unemployment as described in division (D)(2) of that section if the person's use of marijuana was in violation of an employer's drug-free workplace policy, zero-tolerance policy, or other formal program or policy regulating the use of marijuana."

"(C) It is not a violation of division (A), (D), or (E) of section 4112.02 of the Revised Code if an employer discharges, refuses to hire, or otherwise discriminates against a person because of that person's use of marijuana if the person's use of marijuana is in violation of the employer's drug-free workplace policy, zero-tolerance policy, or other formal program or policy regulating the use of marijuana."

Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.28/3-20-2026 — accessed 28 Oct 2026.

Consequences, plainly: - An employer may maintain and enforce drug-testing, drug-free-workplace and zero-tolerance policies, and may refuse to hire / discharge / discipline for marijuana use, possession or distribution — medical card or not, adult-use or not. - No cause of action lies against the employer for such action under Chapter 3796. - Discharge for use in violation of such a policy = discharge for just cause for unemployment-compensation purposes; ineligible for waiting period / benefits for the duration of unemployment as described in ORC 4141.29(D)(2). - No violation of Ohio civil-rights law (ORC 4112.02(A), (D), (E)) if the action is for use in violation of such a policy. - Federal restrictions preserved, including US DOT Title 49 CFR rules. - Workers' compensation drug-free-workplace premium rebates/discounts unaffected. - Limits of the section: It does not authorise an employer to act on a basis other than marijuana use/possession/distribution in violation of a formal policy (e.g. disability discrimination unrelated to marijuana use is not addressed here). It does not address off-duty conduct testing procedures, confirmation testing, or safety-sensitive definitions — those live in employer policy, DOT rules, and general Ohio drug-testing law (e.g. ORC Chapter 4123 context), not in 3796.28. Licensee-employee background checks are a separate regime (3796.13; ORC 4776.01–4776.04).

Federal baseline applied (fixed, not re-researched): state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); all adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I; IRS §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity and remains fully applicable to adult-use; hemp PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026 but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026, after which the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per-container cap apply; USDA DEA-registered-lab testing enforcement is delayed to 31 December 2026; the federal medical appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026; there is no federal cannabis banking law. No Ohio source found in this research contradicts that baseline. For Ohio dual licensees the consequence, stated here only as the federal-baseline consequence, is that medical and adult-use activity must be split for federal purposes: the medical slice follows the Schedule III / §280E-lifted treatment, the adult-use slice remains Schedule I / fully §280E-subject. How the IRS or Ohio Department of Taxation will administer that split for a single dual-use dispensary's books is Verify — no Ohio-specific allocation guidance was located in this research.
