2.2 Adult-use excise tax — rate, history, and verbatim operative text

Rate: 10%, unchanged by SB 56. The only thing SB 56 changed about the excise tax itself was its codification and its distribution (see §2.4); it did not raise it to 15% or 20%, although a 15% proposal was debated during SB 56's passage and a doubling proposal appeared in the Governor's budget proposal. Those proposals were not enacted and must not be quoted as law.

Original Issue 2 text: former ORC §3780.22 levied "a ten percent adult use tax" on adult-use sales, in addition to sales tax, with quarterly distribution. Source: Ohio Auditor of State Bulletin 2025-003 (describing former §§3780.22–3780.23) — https://ohioauditor.gov/publications/bulletins/2025/2025-003.pdf — accessed 28 Oct 2026; and the Moritz College of Law comparison of Issue 2 and SB 56 (updated 26 March 2026) — https://dev-moritz-college-of-law-v2.pantheonsite.io/sites/default/files/2026-07/Ohio%20reforms_SB56%20and%20Issue%202_January%208%202026_final.pdf — accessed 28 Oct 2026.

Current text (later amendment — SB 56, effective 20 March 2026): ORC §3796.40, "Excise tax on sale of adult-use marijuana", last updated on codes.ohio.gov 3 February 2026, latest legislation Senate Bill 56, 136th General Assembly. Verbatim operative provisions, quoted exactly as they appear on the official page (emphasis added only in the headings):

"(B) For the purpose of funding the needs of the state and local governments that host adult-use marijuana dispensaries, an excise tax is levied on the retail sale of adult-use marijuana. The rate of the tax shall equal ten per cent of the price of adult-use marijuana and is in addition to taxes levied under Chapters 5739. and 5741. of the Revised Code."

"(C) The tax shall be paid by the consumer to the vendor at the time of the sale, and the vendor shall report and remit the tax to the state in the same manner and at the same time the vendor reports and remits the tax levied under Chapter 5739. of the Revised Code. The return required by this division shall be filed on a form prescribed by the tax commissioner, which shall be separate from the return required to be filed under section 5739.12 of the Revised Code. The tax levied under this section shall be collected consistent with Chapters 5703. and 5739. of the Revised Code."

"(D) For the same purpose as the tax levied under division (B) of this section, a tax is levied on a vendor that sells any marijuana other than adult-use marijuana or medical marijuana to a consumer. That tax equals ten per cent of the price of such marijuana, and the consumer and vendor are liable for any amounts, including tax, interest, and penalties, imposed under this section and chapter in the same manner as vendors subject to the tax imposed under division (B) of this section."

"(E) All amounts collected from a tax levied under this section shall be deposited into the adult use tax fund, which is created in the state treasury."

Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.40 — accessed 28 Oct 2026. The same page states division (A) (terms have the same meanings as in ORC §5739.01) and division (G) (the tax commissioner may prescribe forms and adopt rules).

Administration notes (secondary, to be confirmed against a Department of Taxation page before filing): dispensaries file and pay through the Department's OH|TAX / Ohio Business Gateway system by the 23rd of the month following the sale, on a return separate from the sales-tax return. Source: GreenGrowth CPAs page above — accessed 28 Oct 2026. Verify: no Department of Taxation adult-use tax instruction page was successfully opened in this research window, so the filing portal and due-date detail are secondary-only. The Department of Taxation's general site is tax.ohio.gov; a dedicated adult-use tax page URL was not verified here and is listed as a follow-up in the research notes.

What the excise tax is NOT: it is not a wholesale or cultivation tax; it is levied at retail, on the price paid by the consumer. No per-gram, per-milligram-THC, potency-tier or weight-based excise tax on cannabis exists in current Ohio law as read here. Verify for any future potency-based proposal — none was located as enacted.

2.3 State and local sales tax

  • State base rate 5.75%. This is ORC §5739.02's statewide rate, unchanged since 1 September 2013 (HB 59). It applies to retail sales of tangible personal property, which includes cannabis sold at retail. Sources: multiple secondary guides all citing ORC §5739.02 and the Department of Taxation — e.g. https://www.commenda.io/usa/ohio/sales-tax-rates and https://legalclarity.org/what-is-the-sales-tax-in-ohio-rates-and-exemptions/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026. Caveat: the §5739.02 page itself was not opened in this window, so the 5.75% figure rests on convergent secondary sources citing the statute, not on a direct read of the statute page. That is the honest grading for this one figure.
  • Local add-ons are county and transit-authority taxes, not city sales taxes. No Ohio city levies its own general sales tax. The combined rate is therefore state + county permissive tax + any regional transit authority tax in the district. The Department of Taxation's official lookup is "The Finder" (address-based rate lookup on tax.ohio.gov). Any county rate below must be checked there for the exact street address, because a single ZIP code or city can straddle counties and transit districts (Columbus, for example, spans Franklin, Delaware, Fairfield and Union counties, and the COTA district does not cover every part of every surrounding county).
  • Combined-rate range and conflicts — read this before using any single county figure. Secondary sources agree on the broad range but disagree on individual counties and on the top of the range, and the disagreement is material:
  • Most sources give 6.50%–8.00% combined, with Cuyahoga (Cleveland) and Franklin (Columbus) at 8.00%, Hamilton (Cincinnati) at 7.80%, Lucas (Toledo) at 7.75%, Montgomery (Dayton) and Mahoning (Youngstown) at 7.50%, Summit (Akron) at 6.75%, and Butler, Lorain, Stark and Wayne at 6.50% as the floor.
  • Other secondary tables give different figures for the same counties: e.g. Franklin at 7.50% in one table (pre-April 2025 COTA increase) versus 8.00% after the COTA increase effective 1 April 2025 (0.50% → 1.00%); Lorain at 6.50% versus 6.75%; Stark at 6.50% versus 7.50%; Clark (Springfield) at 7.25% versus 7.50%; Richland (Mansfield) at 7.00% versus 7.25%; Athens at 7.00% versus 7.25%; Erie (Sandusky) at 6.75% versus 7.25%; Portage (Kent) at 7.00% versus 7.50%; and one table reporting 8.25% for Franklin/Licking COTA-overlay areas while others cap the state at 8.00%.
  • Treatment in this report: no single-county combined rate is asserted as settled official fact. The table in §3.5 gives the most commonly repeated figure for each required city/county marked Verify where sources conflict, and the safe statement for any consumer or business calculation is the range plus the Finder check. The COTA increase (Franklin County transit portion 0.50% → 1.00% effective 1 April 2025, taking most of Columbus to 8.00%) is the best-evidenced of the moving parts, because it is tied to a dated Department of Taxation rate-change notice cited in secondary coverage — https://legalclarity.org/what-is-the-sales-tax-in-columbus-ohio-rates-exemptions/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026 — but even that notice itself was not opened directly here.
  • Sales-tax treatment of medical vs adult-use is the same for sales tax purposes; the difference is only the excise tax (see §2.4 below). Both are retail sales of tangible personal property subject to Ch. 5739/5741 sales/use tax. No medical sales-tax exemption for cannabis was located in Ohio law. (Contrast: some other states exempt medical cannabis from sales tax; Ohio does not, on the sources found.)

2.4 Medical cannabis tax treatment

  • Medical purchases are exempt from the 10% adult-use excise tax. That is the whole of the medical tax advantage at the register. The excise tax by its terms (§3796.40(B)) is levied "on the retail sale of adult-use marijuana"; medical marijuana is outside that levy. Sources: ORC §3796.40 (above); Moritz adult-use page (medical programme: "No special tax levied on medical marijuana purchases") — https://moritzlaw.osu.edu/research/adult-use-marijuana-ohio-what-you-need-know — accessed 28 Oct 2026.
  • Medical purchases still pay state + local sales tax at the combined rate of the dispensary's county/transit district (see §2.3). Sources: Moritz page (patients "subjected to regular state … and local sales tax"); Dimov Tax, "Ohio Cannabis Taxes" (22 November 2025) — https://dimovtax.com/ohio-cannabis-tax/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026; GreenGrowth CPAs page above — accessed 28 Oct 2026.
  • No patient registration fee interacts with tax: Ohio eliminated its former $50 patient registration fee in 2024 (secondary sources; physician evaluation fees are separate and are not a tax). This is noted only to prevent confusion between a fee and a tax; it is not a Part 2 tax finding and is Verify against DCC patient pages.
  • Interaction with the federal Schedule III change (baseline, not Ohio law): because medical activity is now Schedule III federally, a medical-only or medical-slice business is generally outside federal §280E after 28 April 2026, while its adult-use slice is not. Ohio's own tax treatment does not change the excise/sales-tax position: the excise exemption follows the medical/adult-use character of the sale, not the federal schedule. No Ohio statute was found that redefines "medical marijuana" for tax purposes by reference to the federal schedule — Verify if a future Ohio conformity bill appears.

2.5 Distribution of excise revenue — Issue 2 vs SB 56 (the central change)

2.5.1 Original Issue 2 distribution (7 December 2023 – 19 March 2026)

Former ORC §3780.23, verbatim in substance from the Auditor of State bulletin and the archived §3780.23 text:

All monies collected from the tax "shall be deposited into the adult use tax fund" and distributed quarterly as follows: "(1) Thirty-six per cent to the cannabis social equity and jobs fund to be used to implement the requirements of 3780.19 …; (2) Thirty-six per cent to the host community cannabis fund for the benefit of municipal corporations or townships that have adult use dispensaries, and the municipal corporations or townships may use such funds for any approved purpose. Distributions … shall be based on the percentage of adult use tax attributable to each municipal corporation or township; (3) Twenty-five per cent to the substance abuse and addiction fund to support the efforts of the department of mental health and addiction services … under section 3780.30 …; and (4) Three per cent to the division of cannabis control and tax commissioner fund …"

Sources: https://ohioauditor.gov/publications/bulletins/2025/2025-003.pdf (Bulletin 2025-003, "Cannabis Revenue", which also states host payments were to be made "by the end of the month following the end of each calendar quarter" by the Department of Taxation) and https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/ohio/oh-code/ohio_code_3780-23 (archived §3780.23) — both accessed 28 Oct 2026. Note: the Auditor bulletin is dated 2025 and describes the Issue 2 scheme as then in force; it does not reflect SB 56 and must not be used as a statement of current law.

The appropriation gap (why host money sat undistributed for ~17 months): the voter-passed law created the funds and the percentages but contained no appropriation mechanism authorising disbursement, so excise revenue accumulated in a state account from the start of adult-use sales (6 August 2024) without reaching host communities until SB 56 supplied the appropriation and the distribution machinery. This account is given in secondary reporting (Ohio Cannabis Report, March 2026, analysing the 2024–2025 distributions) — https://ohiocannabisreport.substack.com/p/ohio-cannabis-tax-revenue-distribution?r=5h4ufi&triedRedirect=true — accessed 28 Oct 2026 — and is consistent with the fact that the first distributions are dated January–February 2026 (see §2.9). The legal mechanism (lack of appropriation) is Verify against the SB 56 fiscal note / LSC analysis, which was not opened in full here.

2.5.2 Current distribution (SB 56, effective 20 March 2026) — verbatim

ORC §3796.40(F), quoted exactly from the official page:

"(F) After making any transfers required under division (E) of this section, the director of budget and management shall transfer amounts remaining in the adult use tax fund as follows: (1) Sixty-four per cent to the general revenue fund; (2) Thirty-six per cent to the host community cannabis fund, which is created in the state treasury, for the benefit of municipal corporations or townships that have at least one licensed dispensary. Distributions to such municipal corporations and townships shall be based on the portion of the tax levied under division (B) of this section attributable to each municipal corporation or township. Municipal corporations and townships receiving funds under this division may use such funds for any lawful purpose. The tax commissioner shall make distributions under this division by the end of each month based on tax collections from the preceding month."

Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.40 — accessed 28 Oct 2026.

What SB 56 therefore did to the Issue 2 funds, in one table:

Fund (Issue 2) Issue 2 share SB 56 share Status after SB 56
Cannabis Social Equity and Jobs Fund (§3780.19 programme) 36% 0% — programme and dedicated fund eliminated The 36% that would have gone here now goes to the General Revenue Fund. Secondary sources are unanimous on the elimination; the Moritz comparison table states it as "64% General Revenue Fund" with only the host share surviving.
Host Community Cannabis Fund 36% 36% — retained, unchanged in percentage Now the only earmarked share. In price terms: 36% of the 10% excise = 3.6% of the retail price flows to the host city/township. This 3.6% figure is stated expressly in the City of Lakewood Ordinance 15-2026 recitals (see §3.4).
Substance Abuse and Addiction Fund (25%) 25% 0% dedicated share Absorbed into the General Revenue Fund. Note: SB 56 separately requires the Division to contract for drug-misuse prevention/education/public-awareness initiatives (former §3780.37, now §3796.34), but that is a programme duty, not a dedicated 25% revenue stream — do not conflate the two.
Division of Cannabis Control and Tax Commissioner Fund 3% 0% dedicated share Absorbed into the General Revenue Fund; DCC and Taxation operations are instead funded through the operating appropriations in SB 56 (appropriations effective 19 Dec 2025).
General Revenue Fund 0% (Issue 2 had no GRF share) 64% The residual.
Distribution timing Quarterly (Auditor bulletin: by end of month following quarter-end) Monthly (by end of each month, on preceding month's collections) §3796.40(F), last sentence.

Appropriations for the host fund in SB 56 itself: SB 56 §12 appropriated $47,500,000 for fiscal year 2026 and $49,000,000 for fiscal year 2027 for the host community cannabis fund. Source: Ohio Supreme Court filing in Case No. 2026-0264 (breweries' challenge to the SB 56 line-item vetoes), summarising SB 56 §12 — https://www.supremecourt.ohio.gov/pdf_viewer/pdf_viewer.aspx?pdf=999501.pdf&subdirectory=2026-0264%5CDocketItems&source=DL_Clerk — accessed 28 Oct 2026; corroborated by CannBus Q3 2026 market report ("$47.5M (FY 2026) · $49.0M (FY 2027)") — https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/oh_cannmir.html — accessed 28 Oct 2026. Verify against the enrolled SB 56 appropriations section itself, which was not opened directly here.

Sales-tax revenue is NOT part of this distribution. State sales tax goes to the state general revenue fund and local (county/transit) sales tax goes to the levying county/transit authority under the ordinary sales-tax distribution rules. The Moritz page states this expressly for the Issue 2 scheme ("The state sales tax and the local sales tax would be deposited in respective general funds") and SB 56 did not change that structure. Do not add sales tax into the 36%/64% split.

Pending change that would cut the host share — NOT law: H.B. 160 (136th GA, Rep. Stewart) would keep the 10% rate but dedicate only 20% of excise receipts to host municipalities/townships for a temporary period (described in House materials as the first four years; in other summaries as five years beginning in fiscal 2026), with the remainder to the General Revenue Fund, and would eliminate the social equity fund/programme. Status: pending / consolidated into the SB 56 conference process in November 2025 according to the Ohio Council / OBC legislative update (January 2026) — https://obc.memberclicks.net/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=7387:ohio-general-assembly-update-january-2026&catid=29:insight&Itemid=252 — accessed 28 Oct 2026 — and described as "remains pending before the House Judiciary Committee" in April 2026 secondary coverage — https://www.ohio.news/stories/the-wacky-tobaccy-waltz-ohio-lawmakers-dance-fine-line-between-marijuana-revenue-and-regulation/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026. H.B. 160's 20% figure must not be quoted as current law. Its final status on legislature.ohio.gov was not re-confirmed in this window and is a follow-up item. The House sponsor's own summary is at http://ohiohouse.gov/members/brian-stewart/news/rep-stewart-introduces-bill-updating-ohios-marijuana-laws-128585 — accessed 28 Oct 2026.

2.6 IRS §280E and Ohio decoupling — the contested point

Federal position (baseline, fixed): adult-use activity remains Schedule I and fully subject to IRC §280E (no deduction for ordinary business expenses; cost of goods sold remains deductible). Medical activity, as Schedule III from 28 April 2026, is generally outside §280E. Dual licensees must allocate between the two slices. This report does not re-litigate the federal rule.

Ohio state position — what is established: - Ohio has no general corporate income tax (it was replaced by the CAT). The state income tax that matters for cannabis operators is therefore the individual income tax (ORC Ch. 5747) for sole proprietors, partners and S-corporation shareholders, and the CAT (a gross-receipts tax, on which §280E — an income-tax deduction rule — has no direct application). - ORC §5747.01(A) defines "Ohio adjusted gross income" as federal adjusted gross income, as defined in the Internal Revenue Code, adjusted as provided in §5747.01. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-5747.01/3-20-2025 — accessed 28 Oct 2026. No §280E add-back or add-back-reversal appears in the §5747.01 adjustments located here. - The logical consequence, stated by a specialist Ohio cannabis tax source, is: "Ohio conforms to the Internal Revenue Code. The starting point is Federal Adjusted Gross Income. There is no provision that states Section 280E does not apply" (for state individual income tax). Source: AndreTaxCo, "Cannabis Ohio" — https://www.andretaxco.com/ohio-cannabis-280e — accessed 28 Oct 2026. GreenGrowth CPAs (October 2026 check) states the same conclusion in short form: "Ohio has no state 280E decoupling." Source: https://greengrowthcpas.com/industries/cannabis/ohio-cannabis-accounting/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026.

Ohio decoupling — CONFLICT, flagged, not resolved: - One secondary roundup ("280E Deductions by State: 2026 Update") claims that "[b]y early 2026, the list of decoupled jurisdictions has grown to include … Ohio …" and that 28 states + DC have decoupled. Source: https://cannabusinessplans.com/280e-deductions/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026. - That claim is inconsistent with the two Ohio-specific sources above, with the CannBus Q3 2026 report ("state tax relief for 280E could not be confirmed"), and with the absence of any Ohio decoupling statute in the ORC sections read here. No Ohio bill enacting a §280E decoupling was located in this research. - Treatment: this report records Ohio as not shown to have decoupled, with the contrary secondary claim listed as a conflict in the research notes. Do not advise a taxpayer that Ohio has decoupled on the basis of the roundup alone. The practical consequence if the no-decoupling reading is right: before 28 April 2026, a §280E disallowance at federal level flowed into Ohio AGI (because Ohio starts from federal AGI); after 28 April 2026, the medical slice's federal deductibility should likewise flow into Ohio AGI, while the adult-use slice's federal disallowance continues to flow through. Whether Ohio will issue conformity guidance for the mid-year Schedule III change is Verify / Unavailable — no Department of Taxation guidance on the 2026 Schedule III transition was located.

CAT and §280E: because CAT is levied on gross receipts above $6,000,000 (see §2.7), §280E's expense-disallowance rule does not reduce CAT liability; if anything, a business that cannot deduct expenses for income tax still pays CAT on its receipts. No CAT exemption or credit for cannabis businesses was located.

2.7 Other state-level taxes that apply to cannabis businesses (not cannabis-specific)

  • Commercial Activity Tax (CAT), ORC Ch. 5751: 0.26% on Ohio taxable gross receipts above the exclusion; exclusion $3,000,000 for 2024, $6,000,000 for 2025 onward; annual minimum tax eliminated from 1 January 2024; annual filing eliminated (last annual return was for 2023, due 10 May 2024); all CAT taxpayers file quarterly, due 10 May, 10 August, 10 November and 10 February. Registration within 30 days after taxable gross receipts first exceed the exclusion. Sources: secondary CAT guides citing ORC §§5751.01, 5751.03, 5751.051 and Dept. of Taxation Information Release CAT 2023-01 — e.g. https://rkubeservices.com/blog/ohio-cat-tax-threshold-2026 and https://nacatpros.org/midwest/ohio/ohio-cannabis-accounting-280e-2025 — accessed 28 Oct 2026. Verify against current ORC Ch. 5751 / Dept. of Taxation CAT page before filing; the CAT page itself was not opened here.
  • Municipal income tax (ORC Ch. 718): cities and villages may tax business net profits and employee earnings at locally set rates (commonly around 1%–2.5%, but the rate is entirely local). No cannabis-specific municipal income-tax rate or exemption was located. A dispensary's municipal liability therefore depends on its host city's ordinance and on where its employees work, and must be checked city by city. Verify for any specific host city.
  • Employer withholding, unemployment compensation, workers' compensation, property tax: apply to cannabis businesses like any other Ohio employer/property owner on the sources found; no cannabis-specific rate or exemption was located for any of them. Property-tax abatement for a specific facility (e.g. the Gibsonburg, Sandusky County, enterprise-zone abatement reported for a medical marijuana facility) is a local economic-development agreement, not a statewide cannabis tax rule, and is not generalised here.
  • No Ohio tax was located on: wholesale transfers between licensees as such (tax is at retail), home-grown cannabis (no sale, no tax), or hemp biomass/cultivation as such (see §2.8 for hemp products).

2.8 Hemp product tax — and how the federal hemp dates interact with Ohio's own rules

Current Ohio position (enacted SB 56, effective 20 March 2026): - No standalone hemp excise tax survived into the enacted bill. Earlier House-passed versions of SB 56 (and the related SB 86 drafts) would have levied a 10% tax on a dispensary's intoxicating-hemp-product receipts (credited to the General Revenue Fund) and a per-gallon excise on drinkable cannabinoid products (figures in drafts ranged from $1.20/gallon to $3.50/gallon, and one draft stated 15% on hemp receipts). The conference committee removed those intoxicating-hemp-product provisions, including the tax, and replaced them with narrowed, federally compliant hemp definitions. Source: LSC Synopsis of Conference Committee Amendments for SB 56 — https://trackbill.com/s3/bills/OH/136/SB/56/analyses/synopsis-of-conference-committee-amendments.pdf — accessed 28 Oct 2026; and the Ohio Supreme Court filing in Case No. 2026-0264, which states: "The bill imposes a ten percent excise tax on the sale of marijuana (but not hemp). Id. §3796.40(B), (D)." — https://www.supremecourt.ohio.gov/pdf_viewer/pdf_viewer.aspx?pdf=999501.pdf&subdirectory=2026-0264%5CDocketItems&source=DL_Clerk — accessed 28 Oct 2026. - What that means in practice: a product that meets Ohio's (narrowed) hemp definition is not subject to the §3796.40 10% excise tax; a product that falls outside that definition is treated as marijuana, may be sold only in a licensed marijuana dispensary, and when sold as adult-use (or as other non-medical marijuana under §3796.40(D)) it is subject to the 10% excise tax plus sales tax. The conference synopsis states the reclassification consequence expressly ("requires products that fall outside the scope of the new narrowed hemp definition to be considered marijuana and sold exclusively in marijuana dispensaries"). The narrowed definition includes, in part, that hemp does not include any final hemp-derived cannabinoid product that exceeds 0.4 mg of total THC per container, includes non-naturally-producible cannabinoids, or includes naturally-producible cannabinoids synthesised/manufactured outside the plant. Source: same conference synopsis — accessed 28 Oct 2026. - Ordinary sales tax on hemp products: no hemp-specific sales-tax exemption or hemp sales-tax rate was located. The default position recorded here is that retail sales of hemp products that are tangible personal property are subject to ordinary state + local sales tax under Ch. 5739/5741, like other retail goods. Verify — no Department of Taxation ruling on hemp-product sales-taxability (e.g. for CBD ingestibles vs topicals vs smokables) was located, and food/drug exemption analysis for specific hemp product types was not undertaken in this Part 2/3 research. - Governor's veto and the drinkable-product chapter: as enrolled, SB 56 created a Chapter 3779 drinkable-cannabinoid-product regime with a 31 December 2026 sunset; the Governor's line-item vetoes struck the beverage grace period (which would have allowed hemp beverages up to 5 mg THC through 31 December 2026). The Ohio Supreme Court ruled against the brewery plaintiffs on 20 March 2026 and declined to delay SB 56. Sources: Moritz adult-use page — https://moritzlaw.osu.edu/research/adult-use-marijuana-ohio-what-you-need-know — accessed 28 Oct 2026; Supreme Court filing above — accessed 28 Oct 2026. The vetoed Chapter 3779 tax provisions therefore never became operative tax law and must not be quoted as current hemp taxes.

Interaction with the federal hemp dates (baseline dates: 12 November 2026 / 11 December 2026): - Ohio's 0.4 mg per-container threshold (effective 20 March 2026) pre-dates and anticipates the federal 0.4 mg per-container cap that applies after 11 December 2026 under the baseline. In other words, Ohio already imposes, at state level, a cap numerically identical to the coming federal cap, but Ohio's cap has applied since March 2026 and is tied to Ohio's own narrowed hemp definition (including the naturally-produced / synthesised-outside-the-plant tests), whereas the federal cap after 11 December 2026 is tied to the federal total-THC hemp definition. - No Ohio official response to PL 119-37 §781 or PL 119-103 §2019 was located — no Ohio Department of Agriculture, Division of Cannabis Control or Governor's statement addressing the 12 November / 11 December 2026 federal dates was found in this research. That absence is recorded as Unavailable, not as Ohio silence having a legal meaning. In particular, whether Ohio will conform its ORC Chapter 928 hemp definition to the post-11-December federal total-THC definition, or will keep its own definition, is Verify and is the single most important hemp-tax follow-up: if Ohio conforms, the state/federal definitions converge; if it does not, a product could be hemp federally but marijuana in Ohio (or vice versa) with different tax consequences. - USDA DEA-lab testing delay to 31 December 2026 (baseline): no Ohio-specific tax consequence follows from the testing delay; it is a compliance-cost matter for hemp licensees, not a tax rate matter, and is noted here only so it is not mistaken for a tax holiday.

2.9 Revenue figures — official data first, secondary figures labelled

A note on fiscal years and why two "FY 2025" excise figures differ. Ohio's state fiscal year runs 1 July–30 June. Adult-use sales began 6 August 2024, so FY 2025 (1 July 2024–30 June 2025) contains roughly 11 months of adult-use sales. Two different FY 2025 excise totals circulate, and they cannot both be the same measure:

Figure Amount Period / measure as stated by its source Source + accessed
Sales tax (medical + adult-use) + adult-use excise, first fiscal year of adult-use operations $115,531,644 sales tax (both programmes) and $61,978,042 excise tax (adult-use only), Aug 2024–June 2025 Moritz DEPC, "Adult-Use Marijuana in Ohio: What You Need to Know", Tax and Revenue section https://moritzlaw.osu.edu/research/adult-use-marijuana-ohio-what-you-need-know — accessed 28 Oct 2026 (the page text as opened in this research; the figures appear in the search-indexed version of the page)
Adult-use excise tax, FY 2025 $55,600,000, described as "first FY with substantial collections" Tax Foundation 2026 analysis / Ohio Common Ground white paper (RL-2026-013), citing Dept. of Taxation collections https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6a2c66b245187259ecb5e52b/6a6349b7ac6fc29903ba8958_FOR%20RELEASE%20Replacing_Ohio_Property_Tax_Revenue_FINAL(1).pdf — accessed 28 Oct 2026; and Motley Fool state revenue table citing DCC (2026) — https://www.fool.com/research/marijuana-tax-revenue-by-state/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026
Treatment Conflict — do not average. The $61.98m figure is adopted here as the headline for Aug 2024–June 2025 because it is paired with a sales-tax figure and a defined period on a university research page; the $55.6m figure is retained as the conflicting FY 2025 figure, possibly reflecting a different collections-vs-distributions or fiscal-year cut-off. The Department of Taxation's own monthly/annual adult-use tax table would resolve it and is a follow-up item (see research notes).

Other revenue/sales figures (all secondary unless stated, with dates):

  • Adult-use sales topped $836 million in calendar 2025 (secondary summary of DCC data, via a February 2026 advocacy summary) — https://lobbyistsforcitizens.com/2026/02/06/marijuana-may-be-ohios-new-state-flower/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026. Verify against DCC sales data; a different secondary source (CannBus, modelled) gives $1.07B combined adult-use + medical for 2025, which is not directly comparable.
  • Total tax proceeds Aug 2024–Nov 2025 approx. $103 million (10% excise + state/local sales tax combined), per the same February 2026 summary — accessed 28 Oct 2026. Secondary estimate; Verify.
  • Combined medical + adult-use sales passed $4.4 billion through 16 October 2026 ($1,987,109,580 adult-use + $2,438,844,126 medical = $4,425,955,615), per Ohio Cannabis Report (updated 16 October 2026, citing DCC figures) — https://ohiocannabisreport.substack.com/p/ohio-cannabis-sales-top-44-billion — accessed 28 Oct 2026. Secondary compilation of (stated) DCC data; Verify against the DCC dashboard itself.
  • Host Community Fund appropriations: $47.5m FY 2026, $49.0m FY 2027 (SB 56 §12) — see §2.5.2.
  • No monthly excise-revenue series is reproduced here, because no Department of Taxation monthly table was opened in this window. Monthly figures circulating in secondary coverage (e.g. early-2026 monthly distributions after SB 56 took effect) are not reproduced as a series, to avoid presenting a partial series as complete. This is a gap, not a finding of no data.

PART 3 — LOCAL RULES

3.1 Who can do what: municipalities, townships, counties

The statute that answers this question is ORC §3796.29 (current, SB 56, effective 20 March 2026), "Limitations on number of cultivators, processors, or retail dispensaries by localities." Verbatim:

"(A) Except as otherwise provided in division (B) of this section, the legislative authority of a municipal corporation or a board of township trustees may adopt an ordinance or a resolution, to prohibit, or limit the number of, licensed cultivators, licensed processors, or licensed dispensaries within the municipal corporation or within the unincorporated territory of the township, respectively."

"(B) The legislative authority of a municipal corporation or a board of township trustees shall not adopt or enforce an ordinance or a resolution that does any of the following: (1) Prohibits or limits the operations of a license holder that received a provisional license or certificate of operation before the effective date of this amendment, except that a municipal corporation or township may enforce such an ordinance or such a resolution if it was adopted before the effective date of this amendment; (2) Prohibits or limits any activity authorized under this chapter, except as expressly permitted under division (A) of this section; (3) Prohibits or limits research related to marijuana conducted at a state university, academic medical center, or private research and development organization as part of a research protocol approved by an institutional review board or equivalent entity."

Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.29/3-20-2026 — accessed 28 Oct 2026 (page last updated 14 January 2026; versions listed: 8 September 2016 HB 523, and 20 March 2026 SB 56).

What each level can and cannot do, on that text:

Level Power over cannabis businesses Limits / notes
Municipal corporation (city or village) — legislative authority (council) by ordinance, majority vote Prohibit, or limit the number of, licensed cultivators, processors or dispensaries within the municipal corporation (§3796.29(A)). Also exercises ordinary home-rule zoning, building, and business-regulation powers (Ohio Constitution Art. XVIII, §3) within the general laws — e.g. confining dispensaries to commercial/industrial districts, conditional-use review, hours and design conditions that are not a disguised prohibition of a state-authorised activity. Cannot prohibit/limit a pre-amendment provisional licensee / certificate holder, except by enforcing an ordinance adopted before 20 March 2026 (§3796.29(B)(1)). Cannot prohibit/limit any other activity authorised under Ch. 3796 except as §3796.29(A) expressly permits (§3796.29(B)(2)). Cannot prohibit/limit approved university/academic-medical-centre/private research (§3796.29(B)(3)). Cannot ban home grow or other state-authorised personal activity by this section — that was express in the Issue 2 text and remains the structure of (B)(2); the Moritz moratorium page states the same limit for the Issue 2 scheme.
Township — board of township trustees by resolution Prohibit, or limit the number of, licensed cultivators, processors or dispensaries within the unincorporated territory of the township (§3796.29(A)). Separately, township zoning power expressly preserves this: ORC §519.21(D) provides "Nothing in this section prohibits a township zoning commission, board of township trustees, or board of zoning appeals from regulating the location of marijuana cultivators, processors, or retail dispensaries or from prohibiting such cultivators, processors, or dispensaries from being located in the unincorporated territory of the township." (As amended by SB 56, effective 20 March 2026; the section page is https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-section-519.21 — accessed 28 Oct 2026; note the pre-SB 56 text said "medical marijuana" and SB 56 conformed it to "marijuana".) Same §3796.29(B) limits as municipalities. A township resolution has no effect inside an incorporated city or village located within the township's geographic area — only in unincorporated territory. This is why township names in the Moritz table are given with counties and why, e.g., a ban by "Springfield Township" (county not stated in the Moritz row) must not be confused with the City of Springfield, Clark County.
County (board of county commissioners) No §3796.29 opt-out power. The statute names only municipal corporations and townships. A county cannot by resolution prohibit dispensaries countywide. Counties act indirectly: (a) county sales tax / transit tax (see Part 2) applies regardless of opt-out; (b) a county may zone only where it has statutory zoning authority, which in Ohio is limited (principally for unincorporated areas in counties that have adopted county zoning, and even then subject to §519.21-type township powers — Verify for any specific county, because county zoning in Ohio is the exception, not the rule, and no county-wide cannabis zoning ordinance was located); (c) county agencies (health, building, sheriff) enforce state law and local building/health codes. Do not attribute a "county ban" to a board of commissioners without checking whether the instrument was in fact a city/village ordinance or township resolution within that county.
State (Division of Cannabis Control) Licensing, the 500-foot state buffer (see §3.5), and a licensing gate: under OAC Rule 1301:18-2-07(A)(6) (effective 28 August 2025), a provisional licence may issue only if the proposed premises are "(a) Not subject to a local moratorium or other action that would prohibit operation; (b) Compliant with all applicable local ordinances, rules, and regulations … including … (ii) Local approval to operate as a cannabis business." Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-2-07 — accessed 28 Oct 2026. A local moratorium in effect at application is therefore grounds for denial of a provisional licence — the state does not override a valid local prohibition by licensing through it.

What localities cannot tax: under the Issue 2 text as described by Moritz, localities could not "levy a tax, fee, or charge on adult-use operators that are not being levied on other businesses within the municipal corporation or township." That sentence does not appear in the §3796.29(B) text quoted above as currently codified. Verify: whether a discriminatory-fee ban survives elsewhere in current Ch. 3796 (e.g. in a licensing or fee section not read here) or was dropped by SB 56. Until that is checked, do not assert either that a city may impose a cannabis-only local fee or that it may not. Ordinary generally-applicable fees (zoning, building, business-licence fees charged to all businesses) are not in issue.

How existing medical businesses were treated when a jurisdiction prohibited adult-use — Issue 2 vs SB 56

This is the point on which the two versions differ most, and the difference must not be blurred:

Under original Issue 2 (former §3780.25(B), effective 7 December 2023): 1. Existing medical operators were protected outright: "Existing cultivators, processors, or dispensaries who have a certificate of operation may not be prohibited or limited by a municipal corporation or township from operating under Chapter 3796 … unless there is a revocation of the certificate of operation." 2. Co-located adult-use operators were protected: an adult-use cultivator/processor/dispensary co-located on the same or contiguous parcels with a medical operator, whose owners held a certificate of operation at the same location on the effective date, could not be prohibited/limited "because of the significant capital investment in the facilities." 3. Standalone medical dispensaries got a 120-day window rule: a medical dispensary (or its owner) not co-located with a cultivator/processor was authorised to operate as an adult-use dispensary once licensed by the Division, unless a majority of the municipal legislative authority / township trustees affirmatively passed an ordinance/resolution after the licence issued and within 120 days of licence issuance prohibiting it. If such a prohibition passed, the dispensary had to stop adult-use operation within 60 days unless it filed a valid petition with the board of elections to put to voters whether the dispensary should remain open (and whether the jurisdiction should receive host-community funding); if valid, the issue went to the next general election ballot, no sooner than 90 days after filing.

Sources: Justia archive of former §3780.25 (2024) — https://law.justia.com/codes/ohio/2024/title-37/chapter-3780/section-3780-25/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026; Moritz moratorium page (120-day / 60-day / petition summary) — https://moritzlaw.osu.edu/research/local-moratoriums-ohio-adult-use-marijuana-operators — accessed 28 Oct 2026.

Under current law (SB 56, §3796.29, effective 20 March 2026): - The three-part Issue 2 protection is replaced by the single grandfathering rule in §3796.29(B)(1) quoted above: a locality "shall not adopt or enforce" an ordinance/resolution that "[p]rohibits or limits the operations of a license holder that received a provisional license or certificate of operation before the effective date of this amendment, except that a municipal corporation or township may enforce such an ordinance or such a resolution if it was adopted before the effective date of this amendment." - Reading (with the caution that this is a textual reading, not a court holding): a business that was already provisionally licensed / certificated before 20 March 2026 is protected against a new local prohibition adopted after that date, but a locality that had already adopted a prohibition before 20 March 2026 may enforce it against that business. The 120-day post-licence prohibition window and the voter-petition-to-remain-open mechanism that existed in former §3780.25(B)(3) do not appear in the current §3796.29 text read here. Whether they survive in another current section, or were deliberately repealed by SB 56, is Verify — the absence was checked only against §3796.29 itself. - Practical consequence for "existing medical" businesses: a medical dispensary that had converted to dual-use before 20 March 2026 and sits in a jurisdiction that had not prohibited adult-use before that date is, on the current text, protected against a later prohibition. A medical dispensary in a jurisdiction that had prohibited adult-use before 20 March 2026 is not protected by §3796.29(B)(1) against enforcement of that pre-existing prohibition — which is why the Moritz table can show jurisdictions marked "Yes" (moratorium active) that nevertheless show "Dual Use Dispensary" as present (e.g. Beavercreek, Dublin, Euclid, Struthers): the table records the moratorium and the operator side by side without resolving whether the operator predates, is exempt from, or is in tension with the moratorium. Do not infer from the Moritz "Has An Active Marijuana Operator?" column alone that a moratorium is ineffective or that an operator is unlawful; the ordinance text and the licence dates must be checked for that jurisdiction.

3.2 Local prohibitions, moratoriums, caps and zoning — statewide picture

Headline counts (Moritz DEPC tracker — the best available statewide compilation, but NOT a state source; see §3.3 for its limits): - 196 active local moratoriums as of 1 October 2026 (tracker introduction), 224 municipal corporations or townships having passed moratoriums at some point as of the same date (tracker body text), of which the tracker collected the ordinance language for 170. Of the 170 collected, 157 enacted full moratoriums for all types of adult-use operators; 133 left the length undefined ("indeterminate"/"indefinite"); the rest averaged ~17 months; 159 are a full year or longer; 8 are six months or shorter. - The 196 active jurisdictions represent around 19% of Ohio's population, averaging ~11,000 residents; by size: 124 in localities of 0–10,000, 54 in 10,001–20,000, 39 in 20,001–50,000, 7 in 50,000+ (tracker Figure 2 — note these size bands sum to 224, not 196, which is part of the internal inconsistency flagged in §3.3). - Earlier counts for trend (same tracker, earlier editions): 111 jurisdictions as of 23 September 2024; 137 active / 163 ever as of 1 May 2026 (as reported by CannBus summarising the tracker); 163 as of 1 May 2026 (Budpedia summary of the tracker). The direction is upward, driven in part by an August 2026 comprehensive review that added 60+ moratoriums not previously counted — i.e. part of the jump from ~163 to 196/224 is better counting, not necessarily 60+ new bans in one month. Do not present the increase as pure new-ban growth without that qualification. - Sources: https://moritzlaw.osu.edu/research/local-moratoriums-ohio-adult-use-marijuana-operators — accessed 28 Oct 2026; https://www.cannbus.org/lsum/oh_lsum.html (May 2026 summary) — accessed 28 Oct 2026; https://budpedia.com/articles/ohio-163-local-cannabis-moratoriums-may-2026 — accessed 28 Oct 2026.

Stated purposes (tracker Table 2, of the ordinances collected): preserve public health 124; waiting for full state rules 52; council actively studying/drafting recommendations 55; council can shorten/extend the moratorium 35. (Categories overlap; they do not sum to 170.)

Typical moratorium form: a brief ordinance/resolution, often citing "public peace, health, safety, and welfare", the need to review ordinances for conflicts with state law, and/or waiting for the General Assembly to revise Issue 2. Many were adopted in the window November 2023–mid-2024, immediately after Issue 2 passed and before adult-use sales began. A moratorium is temporary in form even when marked "indeterminate" — it is a pause pending zoning, not necessarily a permanent ban — but an "indeterminate"/"indefinite" moratorium that is never revisited functions as a ban in practice. The tracker itself warns: "jurisdictions that have a moratorium ending date in the past will remain marked as active until we are able to confirm whether or not they have been extended."

Caps (as distinct from bans): caps are exercised under the same §3796.29(A) "limit the number" power and appear in the tracker as qualified entries, e.g.: - Berea (Cuyahoga County): cultivators/processors/retailers limited to 1, enacted 13 May 2024, dual-use dispensary present. - Englewood (Montgomery County): cultivators/processors/retailers limited to 1, enacted 24 September 2024, dual-use dispensary present. - Huron (Erie County — the city of Huron, not Huron County generally): cultivators/processors allowed, retail dispensaries limited to 1, enacted 23 July 2024, dual-use dispensary + cultivator + processor present. - Oxford (Butler County): limited to 2 non-medical dispensaries, enacted 16 January 2024, dual-use dispensary present. - West Carrollton (Montgomery County): cultivators/processors prohibited, retail dispensaries limited to 2, enacted 12 December 2023, ending 30 September 2026. - Elyria (Lorain County) planning commission (April 2025) recommended capping local adult-use permits at 2 and co-location with medical conditional-use approval — a recommendation, not yet shown as an enacted cap in the tracker (see §3.5). - Mansfield (Richland County): council voted 5–3 to allow up to 3 recreational and/or medical dispensaries (see §3.5). - Parma Heights (Cuyahoga County): proposed (not shown as enacted in the tracker row) no more than 1 dispensary per multi-use district, spaced at least 1 mile apart (see §3.5).

Local voter initiatives on cannabis businesses: - Under former §3780.25(B)(3), a dispensary facing a 120-day prohibition could petition to put its continued operation to voters at the next general election (see §3.1). That was a business-initiated voter mechanism, not a citizen ban initiative. - General local-option / referendum practice: Ohio municipalities and townships also have general initiative/referendum powers under the Ohio Constitution and ORC Ch. 731 / §519.12-type procedures, and a local prohibition ordinance is itself subject to referendum in a municipality unless it is an emergency measure. No specific local ballot measure banning or allowing a dispensary was verified in this research for any of the §3.5 cities, and none is asserted. The one statewide referendum effort located — Ohioans for Cannabis Choice's attempt to refer parts of SB 56 itself (filed 29 December 2025, initial summary rejected 13 January 2026, refiled 20 January 2026, certified 3 February 2026, needing 248,092 valid signatures before 20 March 2026, suspended 18 March 2026) — is a state-level referendum against SB 56, not a local voter initiative, and it did not stay SB 56. Source: Moritz adult-use page — https://moritzlaw.osu.edu/research/adult-use-marijuana-ohio-what-you-need-know — accessed 28 Oct 2026. - Decriminalisation ordinances are a different thing and are not counted here: many Ohio cities (including several in §3.5) adopted local ordinances reducing penalties for small-amount possession (e.g. Cleveland, January 2020, up to 200 grams). Those ordinances concern possession penalties, not whether a dispensary may operate, and are not treated as "prohibitions" or "permissions" for Part 3 purposes.

3.3 Official list or map of jurisdictions that prohibit or allow adult-use businesses

Finding: no official (state) list or map was located.

  • What was searched for: a Division of Cannabis Control (DCC) list, map or dataset of jurisdictions that have prohibited or limited adult-use operators, and a DCC "opt-out" page. Searches of the DCC site (com.ohio.gov/cannabis) and general web searches returned no DCC opt-out list or map. The DCC does publish an interactive dispensary locator/map (licensed dispensary locations), which shows where dispensaries are, not where they are prohibited — absence from that map is not proof of a prohibition, because a jurisdiction may simply have no applicant.
  • Exact URLs / locations tried or identified (so a follow-up researcher can re-check without re-guessing):
  • Ohio Department of Commerce, Division of Cannabis Control home: https://com.ohio.gov/cannabis — no opt-out list found on this portal in this research (the portal's dispensary locator is the only location-based tool identified).
  • Moritz DEPC tracker (the substitute used throughout Part 3): https://moritzlaw.osu.edu/research/local-moratoriums-ohio-adult-use-marijuana-operators — this is a university research tracker, not an official state list, and it says so itself ("may not be comprehensive").
  • Ohio Secretary of State / county boards of elections: no statewide compilation of local cannabis ordinances was located there either.
  • If an official list exists, it was not retrievable by the searches above — that negative result is itself the finding, and it must be reported as such, not papered over with the Moritz tracker presented as official.
  • Internal inconsistency in the substitute tracker (flagged, not smoothed over): the tracker introduction says "196 active local moratoriums … as of October 1, 2026"; the body text says "224 Ohio municipal corporations or townships have passed moratoriums" as of the same date and "The 196 jurisdictions with active moratoriums represent around 19% of Ohio's population"; the population-size chart bands sum to 224 (124+54+39+7). The most coherent reading is 224 ever-passed, 196 still active — but the tracker does not state that reconciliation expressly, and the earlier search-indexed version of the same page said "196 active" while a May 2026 summary said 137 active / 163 ever. Use 196 active / 224 ever only with the date (1 Oct 2026) and the caveat that the tracker warns it is not comprehensive and that past-end-date moratoriums remain marked active until confirmed extended.
  • What would resolve it: a DCC or Department of Commerce publication, or a statutory requirement that localities file prohibitions with the Division (no such filing requirement was located in §3796.29 or in the DCC rules read here — Verify). Until then, any "allow" list must be built jurisdiction by jurisdiction from council minutes and codes, which is why §3.5 is organised as a checked-city table with gaps marked, not as a statewide allow/ban map.

3.4 Host community revenue — which jurisdictions receive it, how much, and where it is officially reported

Who receives it (law): only municipal corporations or townships that have at least one licensed dispensary (§3796.40(F)(2)). Counties do not receive host-community distributions as counties — the statute distributes to the host city/village/township, "based on the portion of the tax … attributable to each municipal corporation or township." A dispensary in unincorporated township territory therefore generates host money for that township, not for the county; a dispensary inside a city generates it for that city, even if the city spans multiple counties. Funds "may [be used] for any lawful purpose" (§3796.40(F)(2)) — the earlier Issue 2 phrase "any approved purpose" is substantively the same latitude. How a city actually spends it is a local appropriation decision (see Cleveland and Cincinnati examples below).

Where it is officially reported (and the gap): distributions are made by the Tax Commissioner (monthly, by end of each month on preceding month's collections, under current §3796.40(F); quarterly under Issue 2). No Department of Taxation published table of jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction host payments was opened in this research. The Department is therefore the official reporting source in law, but its jurisdiction-level table, if published, was not retrieved — that is a follow-up item, not a claim that it does not exist. What exists in the open sources is: (a) the statutory formula, (b) the SB 56 appropriation totals, and (c) city-reported receipts and secondary compilations, set out below with their status clearly marked.

Totals (official/appropriation level): - First bulk distribution: more than $35 million (reported as $35.9 million in one analysis) to approximately 100 communities, covering collections from August 2024 through 30 November 2025, with distributions beginning 7 January 2026 and continuing in February 2026. Sources: Ohio Cannabis Report (March 2026) — https://ohiocannabisreport.substack.com/p/ohio-cannabis-tax-revenue-distribution?r=5h4ufi&triedRedirect=true — accessed 28 Oct 2026; Scioto Post (Circleville) summary of Dept. of Taxation distributions — https://www.sciotopost.com/circlevilles-marijuana-moratorium-may-be-costing-city-thousands-in-tax-revenue/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026. Secondary; the Department's own total was not opened. - Appropriations: $47.5m FY 2026 / $49.0m FY 2027 (see §2.5.2).

Notes on the conflicts: Columbus $4.2m vs $4.7m and Cleveland $740k vs $803k are not necessarily errors — they may reflect different cut-off dates (e.g. November 2024 start vs August 2024 start, or a partial vs full first distribution). Because the underlying Department table was not opened, this report does not choose between them; both are recorded with their stated periods. Any Part 6 market-data use of these figures must carry the same caveat.

What host money may be spent on, in practice (local examples, not state mandates): Cleveland Ordinance 460-2026 allocates 50% of the City's marijuana legalisation initiative revenues to Council's Neighborhood Equity Fund; Cincinnati's October 2026 Budget Committee proposal (not yet shown as enacted) would split future revenue among home repairs, lead prevention, homeownership, children's savings and youth employment; Tallmadge deposits its allocation in the General Fund for annual appropriation; Lakewood created a dedicated Host Community Cannabis Fund section in its code. These are local appropriation choices under the "any lawful purpose" rule, not state earmarks.

Jurisdictions that prohibit adult-use operators forgo host money by definition (no licensed dispensary = no host distribution for that jurisdiction), though they still collect ordinary local sales tax on other retail activity. The Moritz tracker and the Ohio Cannabis Report both make this incentive point, and it is cited as a reason some early moratoriums have been repealed.

3.5 Local zoning / buffer rules that differ from the state — checked cities

State baseline that every city below sits on top of (so a "difference" can be recognised): - ORC §3796.30 (SB 56, effective 20 March 2026): "Except as provided in divisions (C) and (D) … no licensed cultivator, licensed processor, licensed dispensary, or licensed laboratory shall be located within five hundred feet of the boundaries of a parcel of real estate having situated on it a school, church, public library, public playground, or public park." Relocation into such a buffer must be denied. A facility already certificated when a protected facility later locates/establishes within 500 feet need not relocate or close (division (C)). Research at a state university / academic medical centre / private R&D organisation under an IRB-approved protocol is exempt (division (D)). Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.30/3-20-2026 — accessed 28 Oct 2026. - OAC Rule 1301:18-3-01 (effective 31 October 2024): no cultivator, processor, testing laboratory or dispensary within 500 feet of the boundaries of a parcel with a "prohibited facility" (as defined in OAC 1301:8-1-01); distance measured linearly at the shortest distance between the prohibited facility's parcel line and the physical structure under the cannabis facility's control; pre-existing certificate holders and IRB research exempt; a later-established prohibited facility does not force relocation if the licensee notifies the Division and submits security modifications. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/chapter-1301:18-3 — accessed 28 Oct 2026. - What counts as "different from the state": a local rule is listed below as differing only if it adds a buffer, a spacing rule, a district restriction, a cap, hours or a permit type beyond the 500-foot state buffer. A local ordinance that merely repeats the 500-foot rule is recorded as "mirrors state" and is not a difference.

Checked-city table. "Verify" in this table means the local code section was not opened directly in this window and the entry rests on secondary reporting of that code.

3.6 Business concentration — only what official sources say

What can be said without estimating or ranking: - The Division of Cannabis Control's dispensary locator/map (com.ohio.gov/cannabis) is the official location source, but it is an interactive map/directory, not a downloadable county table, and no official county-by-county licensee count table was opened in this research. Any county ranking derived by counting locator pins would be this report's own estimate, which the task forbids — so no ranking is given. - The only location counts found are secondary and dated: as of September 2024, Moritz/Ganjapreneur reporting of DCC data put Columbus at 13, Cincinnati at 10, Dayton at 6, Cleveland at 5 dispensaries, with 124 dual-use dispensaries statewide and 111 moratorium jurisdictions at that date — https://ganjapreneur.com/ohio-adult-use-cannabis-sales-exceed-76-2m-in-under-two-months/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026. Those are September 2024 figures, not current counts, and the statewide dual-use count has since risen (secondary reports put it around 190–228 by early-to-mid 2026, with a 400 statutory cap under SB 56 — Verify against the DCC for a current count; Part 4, not Part 3, owns licence counts). - What the host-payment evidence shows, without ranking: approximately 100 municipalities/townships received host distributions for Aug 2024–Nov 2025 (see §3.4). That is evidence that licensed dispensaries are present in roughly 100 host jurisdictions, spread across the state (examples in §3.4 span Franklin, Hamilton, Cuyahoga, Montgomery, Stark, Summit, Butler, Clark, Ross and other counties). It is not evidence of concentration, because the payment amounts are proportional to sales in each jurisdiction, not to a count of stores, and the full jurisdiction list was not published in the sources opened. - What the moratorium evidence shows, without ranking: moratoriums are concentrated in smaller jurisdictions (124 of the tracker's bands are in places under 10,000 people; only 7 are in places over 50,000), while the largest cities in §3.5 (Columbus, Cleveland, Cincinnati, Toledo, Akron, Dayton, Canton, Youngstown) are not shown as moratorium-active in the tracker excerpts. That is a statement about the tracker's composition, not a claim that large cities have the most stores — store counts per city were not verified for the current date. - No official statement was located that any particular city or county is a "cluster", "hub" or saturated/undersaturated market. Do not add such a characterisation on the basis of host-payment size alone: a large host payment can reflect high sales per store, many stores, or both, and the data to separate those causes was not opened.

Ohio Cannabis and Hemp — Run 1, Parts 4–6 ONLY

Scope: Licence types (Part 4), licence data sources (Part 5), and market data (Part 6) only. Parts 0–3 and 7–12 are not covered here and are left to the other runs. Date accessed for all facts in this file: 28 October 2026, unless a source itself is dated otherwise. Federal baseline applied (fixed, not re-researched): State-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); all adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. IRS 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to 280E. Ohio licensees are therefore overwhelmingly dual licensees who must split medical from adult-use activity for federal tax and scheduling purposes — a single Ohio licence does not make adult-use activity Schedule III or 280E-exempt. Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 effective 12 November 2026, limited by PL 119-103 §2019 until 11 December 2026; after 11 December 2026 the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. USDA DEA-registered-lab enforcement is delayed to 31 December 2026. No federal cannabis banking law exists. Reading note on Ohio law after SB 56: The adult-use chapter created by Issue 2 (former ORC Chapter 3780) was repealed and its substance merged into ORC Chapter 3796 by Senate Bill 56, 136th General Assembly, signed 19 December 2025 and effective 20 March 2026. Every current licence citation below is therefore to Chapter 3796 as amended by SB 56, read directly on codes.ohio.gov on 28 October 2026. Where an earlier SB 56 version, an LSC fiscal note, or a secondary source states a different cap, canopy, or fee, that is flagged as a conflict rather than silently overwritten. Former Chapter 3780 sections are shown as "[Repealed effective 3/20/2026 by S.B. 56]" on codes.ohio.gov — e.g. former §§3780.13 (Level III cultivator), 3780.14 (adult-use processor), 3780.15 (adult-use dispensary), 3780.16 (adult-use testing laboratory). No personal phone numbers or emails of individuals are reproduced in this file. Official public agency contact routes are given only where the source itself publishes them.

PART 4 — LICENCE TYPES

4.1 The current licence architecture (post-SB 56)

Ohio now has one merged licence system, not two parallel systems. ORC §3796.02 (effective 20 March 2026, SB 56) provides:

"There is hereby established a division of cannabis control in the department of commerce under the supervision and direction of the superintendent of marijuana control… The division shall provide for the licensure of marijuana cultivators, processors, retail dispensaries, and laboratories that test marijuana. The division shall also provide for the registration of patients and their caregivers."

  • Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/chapter-3796 — accessed 28 Oct 2026.
  • ORC §3796.01(A)(18)–(23) defines the two-step licence: a provisional licence (temporary, setting conditions to be met) followed by a certificate of operation (authorising actual operation) for cultivators, processors, retail dispensaries and laboratories. A provisional licence does not permit sales.
  • Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/chapter-3796 — accessed 28 Oct 2026.
  • ORC §3796.33 (effective 20 March 2026, SB 56) — "Equivalent licenses": a licence issued under former Chapter 3780 "shall be treated, for all purposes, as the equivalent license under this chapter." The equivalents are: adult-use cultivator → cultivator licence of the same level under §3796.09/§3796.18; adult-use processor → processor licence (§3796.19); adult-use dispensary → retail dispensary licence (§3796.20); adult-use testing laboratory → laboratory licence (§3796.21).
  • Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/chapter-3796 — accessed 28 Oct 2026 (search-result summary of §3796.33 corroborates the same text).

There is no separate wholesale, distributor, transporter, delivery-only, microbusiness, or consumption-lounge licence in Chapter 3796. Transport and wholesale movement occur between the four licence types themselves; delivery is an activity a licensed dispensary may perform for medical marijuana only, and only under rules adopted under §3796.03 — see §4.6. This "no separate licence" point is corroborated by secondary summaries but is stated here on the basis that §§3796.18–3796.21 exhaustively list the licensed activities; [Verify] — a full OAC Division 1301:18 rule-by-rule check for any niche licence (e.g. a standalone transport or research licence) was not completed in this run and should be confirmed against the current OAC chapter list before publication.

4.2 Licence types in detail

4.2.1 Cultivator — Level I and Level II (ORC §3796.18)

What it allows — verbatim operative text, §3796.18(A)(1) (effective 20 March 2026, SB 56):

"(a) Cultivate medical marijuana and adult-use marijuana; (b) Deliver, transfer, or sell medical marijuana and adult-use marijuana to other license holders; (c) Purchase or otherwise obtain medical marijuana and adult-use marijuana from other license holders; (d) Acquire seeds, clones, plants, and other genetic material."

"(2) A licensed cultivator engaging in the activities authorized by this chapter shall do so respecting both medical marijuana and adult-use marijuana."

"(B) A licensed cultivator shall not cultivate medical marijuana or adult-use marijuana for personal, family, or household use or on any public land, including a state park…"

"(C) A licensed cultivator shall identify, package, and label all medical marijuana and adult-use marijuana products in accordance with this chapter and any rules adopted thereunder before delivering or selling the products to a licensed processor or licensed dispensary."

  • Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/chapter-3796 — accessed 28 Oct 2026.

Canopy limits — current law, §3796.18(D) (effective 20 March 2026, SB 56):

"(D) The division of cannabis control shall issue the following types of cultivation licenses: (1) A level I cultivator license that authorizes the license holder to operate a cultivation area specified by the division, not to exceed one hundred thousand square feet; (2) A level II cultivator license that authorizes the license holder to operate a cultivation area specified by the division, not to exceed fifteen thousand square feet."

"(E) A licensed cultivator may request and receive one or more expansions to the cultivator's cultivation area, subject to the approval of the division, so long as the resulting total cultivation area, including all expansions, does not exceed the applicable maximum cultivation area prescribed by division (D) of this section."

  • Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/chapter-3796 — accessed 28 Oct 2026.

Canopy history — read this before quoting any secondary figure: - Original medical programme (HB 523 era, OAC): Level I initial area 25,000 sq ft, Level II initial area 3,000 sq ft, with discretionary expansions (Level I to 50,000 then 75,000 sq ft; Level II to 6,000 then 9,000 sq ft). Source: Register of Ohio rule-history document for former OAC 3796:5-6-01, https://www.registerofohio.state.oh.us/servlet/RooBusinessPDF?ruleActionId=519283&docTypeId=14 — accessed 28 Oct 2026 (via search result). - Original Issue 2 text: Level I adult-use cultivator "up to one hundred thousand square footage" and Level II "up to fifteen thousand square footage," each increasable on approved expansion. Source: Issue 2 full text as reproduced at http://frontlinesohio.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/issue-2-full-text-of-the-law.pdf — accessed 28 Oct 2026 (via search result). - Conflict / version trap [Verify]: An LSC fiscal note for SB 56 as introduced / Senate-passed describes a proposal to cut Level I to 25,000 sq ft (expandable to 75,000) and Level II to 3,000 sq ft (expandable to 9,000), and an LSC analysis dated October 2025 still tables "Level 1 (up to 25,000 sq. ft. capacity under current law) and Level II (up to 3,000 sq. ft. capacity under current law)" for the then-37 cultivator certificates. Those figures describe the pre-SB 56 medical initial-area practice and/or an earlier SB 56 draft — they do not match the enacted §3796.18(D) text (100,000 / 15,000) read on codes.ohio.gov on 28 Oct 2026. Do not quote 25,000/3,000 as the current statutory maxima without noting this. Secondary pages that still say "Level I up to 25,000" (e.g. CannBus Q3 2026 summary table, https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/oh_cannmir.html) are stale on this point. - Practical consequence: a cultivator's actual authorised area is the area "specified by the division" in its licence, up to the statutory maximum — the statute does not itself grant every Level I holder 100,000 sq ft.

4.2.2 Processor (ORC §3796.19)

What it allows — verbatim, §3796.19(A)(1) (effective 20 March 2026, SB 56):

"(a) Purchase or otherwise obtain medical marijuana and adult-use marijuana from other license holders; (b) Subject to division (B) of this section, process medical marijuana and adult-use marijuana into a form described in section 3796.06 of the Revised Code; (c) Deliver, transfer, or sell processed medical marijuana and adult-use marijuana to other license holders."

"(2) A licensed processor engaging in the activities authorized by this chapter shall do so respecting both medical marijuana and adult-use marijuana."

Before delivery/sale to a dispensary the processor must: (1) package to child-resistant effectiveness standards in 16 C.F.R. 1700.15(b) (as of 8 September 2016); (2) label with THC and CBD content; (3) comply with DCC packaging/labelling rules under §§3796.03 and 3796.32 (§3796.19(B)).

  • Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/chapter-3796 — accessed 28 Oct 2026.
  • There is no statutory sub-type (standalone vs plant-only vs vertically integrated) in §3796.19 itself; secondary descriptions of three processor facility types are not adopted as statutory categories here [Verify] against current OAC 1301:18 processor rules.

4.2.3 Retail dispensary (ORC §3796.20)

What it allows — verbatim, §3796.20(A)(1) (effective 20 March 2026, SB 56):

"(a) Purchase or otherwise obtain medical marijuana and adult-use marijuana from other license holders; (b) Dispense or sell medical marijuana in accordance with division (B) of this section; (c) Dispense or sell adult-use marijuana in accordance with division (C) of this section; (d) Sell paraphernalia that may be used in the administration of adult-use marijuana or medical marijuana as specified in rules adopted under section 3796.03 of the Revised Code; (e) Provide delivery of medical marijuana in accordance with the rules adopted under section 3796.03 of the Revised Code; (f) Deliver, transfer, or sell medical marijuana and adult-use marijuana to other license holders."

"(2) A licensed dispensary engaged in the activities authorized by this chapter shall do so respecting both medical marijuana and adult-use marijuana."

Medical sales require a current valid government-issued ID and a physician recommendation from a physician holding a certificate to recommend under ORC §4731.30, plus reporting to the drug database (OARRS) under §4729.771 and specified package labelling (§3796.20(B)). Adult-use sales require a government-issued ID proving age 21+, and a dispensary "shall not knowingly dispense or sell more than the amount of adult-use marijuana that may be legally possessed by an adult-use consumer under section 3796.221" to the same consumer in the same day (§3796.20(C)). Dispensaries must maintain an adequate supply for typical patient demand (§3796.20(B)(4)), use only employees meeting DCC training rules, not disclose patient/consumer-identifying information, and prominently display the under-21 harm/illegality statement and addiction/health information (§3796.20(D)).

  • Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/chapter-3796 — accessed 28 Oct 2026.
  • Delivery note: §3796.20(A)(1)(e) authorises medical delivery only, under DCC rules. Adult-use delivery is not authorised by this section. Secondary reporting (CannBus Q3 2026, https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/oh_cannmir.html, accessed 28 Oct 2026) states DCC planned formal rulemaking in fall 2026 for medical delivery — [Verify] whether those rules have been adopted; no adopted delivery rule text was located in this run.

4.2.4 Testing laboratory (ORC §3796.21)

What it does — verbatim, §3796.21 (effective 20 March 2026, SB 56):

"(A) …a licensed laboratory … shall do both of the following: (1) Obtain medical marijuana and adult-use marijuana from one or more licensed cultivators, licensed processors, and licensed dispensaries; (2) Conduct testing in the manner specified in rules adopted under section 3796.03 of the Revised Code. (B) When testing medical marijuana or adult-use marijuana, a licensed laboratory shall do both of the following: (1) Test for potency, homogeneity, and contamination; (2) Prepare a report of the test results."

  • Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/chapter-3796 — accessed 28 Oct 2026.
  • Independence rule: Under §3796.09(C)(2), a cultivator or processor applicant must demonstrate that none of its owners, officers, board members, administrators, employees, agents, or affiliates who may significantly influence or control it has an ownership/investment interest in, or compensation arrangement with, a licensed laboratory or laboratory applicant. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.09 — accessed 28 Oct 2026.
  • Secondary detail [Verify, non-official]: ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation within two calendar years of a provisional licence and a scientific director holding a doctorate + 2 years' experience or a master's + 4 years (CannBus summary, https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/oh_cannmir.html). This was not verified against current OAC text in this run and must not be quoted as statute.

4.2.5 Level III cultivator — abolished, never issued

  • Original Issue 2 created up to 40 Level III adult-use cultivator licences (up to 5,000 sq ft, expandable on DCC approval) with preference for certified Cannabis Social Equity and Jobs Program participants, under former ORC §3780.13.
  • LSC analysis of SB 56 (House Finance version): "No level III adult-use cultivator licenses have been issued as of June 18, 2025." Source: https://www.legislature.ohio.gov//download?key=26235 — accessed 28 Oct 2026 (via search result).
  • SB 56 repealed former §3780.13 effective 20 March 2026; codes.ohio.gov now shows §3780.13 as "[Repealed effective 3/20/2026 by S.B. 56, 136th General Assembly]". Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/search — accessed 28 Oct 2026 (via search result).
  • There is therefore no Level III licence to apply for, and no Level III holder to count. Any source still listing Level III as a live Ohio licence type is stale.

4.2.6 Employee / badge licences — changed by SB 56

  • Formerly, DCC issued employee badges (responsible party / owner-officer / employee, $100 each at initial application and renewal, per the OAC 1301:18-2-09 schedule reproduced in search results). Secondary reporting states SB 56 "eliminates employment licenses for cannabis workers and requires background checks for all employees" (CannBus, https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/oh_cannmir.html). ORC §3796.13 now provides that a person seeking employment with a licence holder must comply with ORC §§4776.01–4776.04 (criminal records checks) and must not be employed if the report shows a disqualifying offence, with a provisional-employment regime (max 3 months, renewable once for 3 months) for exigent circumstances. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/chapter-3796 — accessed 28 Oct 2026.
  • [Verify]: Whether any badge fee survives in current OAC 1301:18-2-09 after SB 56, or whether the $100 badge line is repealed/superseded, was not resolved from the rule text in this run. Do not quote a current employee-badge fee as settled.

4.3 How many licences exist or may be issued — caps and counts

Statutory caps (current, SB 56): - Dispensaries: "Not more than four hundred licensed dispensaries shall be permitted to operate in this state at any one time." — ORC §3796.05(B)(1) (effective 20 March 2026, SB 56). Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.05/3-20-2026 — accessed 28 Oct 2026. - [Conflict resolved in favour of the statute]: Early SB 56 versions and an LSC fiscal note (January 2025) described a 350-dispensary cap. The enacted §3796.05(B)(1) says 400. The 350 figure must not be used for current law. - Geographic-distribution guardrail: §3796.05(B)(3) requires DCC, when issuing retail dispensary licences, to "ensure that the geographic distribution of dispensary sites does not result in the oversaturation of any geographic area." - New-dispensary spacing (post-SB 56): §3796.05(B)(4) — DCC shall not, on or after 20 March 2026, issue a retail dispensary licence for, or approve relocation to, a location (a) within one mile of another licensed dispensary, or (b) for which a Chapter 4303 permit to sell beer/intoxicating liquor has been issued. Source: same §3796.05 page. - Provisional-licence clock: §3796.05(B)(2) — DCC may revoke a dispensary licence for failure to secure a certificate of operation within 18 months after issuance of a provisional licence; the holder may apply for not more than two 6-month extensions on a good-faith-effort showing. - Cultivators: no fixed statutory number. §3796.05(A) requires DCC, when establishing the number of cultivator licences permitted at any one time, to consider (1) state population, (2) number of patients seeking medical marijuana, (3) number of adult-use consumers seeking adult-use marijuana. No processor or laboratory number cap is stated in §§3796.18–3796.21. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.05/3-20-2026 — accessed 28 Oct 2026. - Ownership caps — verbatim, §3796.05(C): "No person shall own or operate more than eight licensed dispensaries, more than one licensed cultivator, or more than one licensed processor license at any time." Source: same page. Note the earlier medical-programme "5 dispensaries per owner" figure in older secondary material is superseded for current law; the 8-dispensary figure is also stated in LSC's SB 56 analysis ("limits the number of dispensaries owned by a permit holder to eight," https://www.legislature.ohio.gov/download?key=26231 — accessed 28 Oct 2026).
