4.5 How medical licensees converted to dual licences; lotteries and application windows; whether new applications are open

Dual-use conversion (2024): - DCC formally began accepting dual-use applications 7 June 2024 from existing medical licensees. Source: secondary contemporaneous reporting, https://cannabisriskmanager.com/wp-content/themes/cannabis/generate-pdf.php?post_id=24919 — accessed 28 Oct 2026; and DCC Dual-Use Application Instructions, https://dam.assets.ohio.gov/image/upload/com.ohio.gov/DCC/Dual-Use_Application_Instructions.pdf — accessed 28 Oct 2026. - Mechanics (from those instructions): one application per licence/location; packet = application form + dual-use attestation + tax authorisation form; submission by email to the DCC applications mailbox (file size limit 150 MB in the instructions) or via the State of Ohio File Drop with a notifying email; a provisional licence issues via the DCC eLicense portal and does not permit non-medical sales until a certificate of operation issues. First dual-use dispensary certificates of operation — and therefore first adult-use sales — issued 6 August 2024. Source for the 6 August 2024 date: Ohio House news release summarising DCC, https://ohiohouse.gov/members/jamie-callender/news/adult-use-cannabis-continues-its-successful-rollout-in-ohio-122045 — accessed 28 Oct 2026; DCC reported 120 dual-use dispensary licences, 36 dual-use cultivator licences and 41 dual-use processor licences approved as of 14 August 2024 (same source). - Legal effect after SB 56: conversion is now moot as a distinct status — §3796.33 treats former Chapter 3780 adult-use licences as equivalent Chapter 3796 licences, and §§3796.18–3796.20 require every licence holder to act "respecting both medical marijuana and adult-use marijuana." In practice, "dual-use" is now simply what an Ohio cannabis licence is. The few licences described in October 2025 as not dual-use ("all but two" of the then-certificates were dual-use, LSC October 2025) are the exception, not a separate licence class — [Verify] which two, and whether any medical-only licence survives after SB 56.

10(B) dispensary licences (former ORC §3780.10(B), now merged into Chapter 3796 practice): - Eligibility (as described in DCC 10(B) materials and secondary summaries, and consistent with former §3780.10(B)): Level I cultivators could apply for up to 3 additional dispensary licences; Level II cultivators for 1; a medical dispensary without common ownership/control with a cultivator or processor could apply for 1 additional dispensary licence. Source: https://www.cannabisindustrylawyer.com/how-to-open-a-dispensary-in-ohio/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026; DCC 10(B) Phase Two Instructions, https://dam.assets.ohio.gov/image/upload/com.ohio.gov/DCC/DCC_10_B_Phase_Two_Instructions.pdf — accessed 28 Oct 2026. - Process: application packet (fillable PDF application + 10(B) applicant attestation + tax authorisation form) + $5,000 fee; completed applications entered into an Ohio Lottery Commission drawing using a random number generator to assign rankings; results posted on the DCC website; then a two-phase site-selection process — Phase One: facility site location application naming three preferred sites, checked against a one-mile buffer from existing dispensaries/other proposed sites; Phase Two: regional districts and a preference ranking. Source: DCC 10(B) materials via https://dam.assets.ohio.gov/image/upload/com.ohio.gov/DCC/DCC_10_B_Phase_Two_Instructions.pdf and https://thdwholesale.com/blogs/how-to-open-a-recreational-dispensary-in-ohio-online/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026. - Drawing results page (official): https://com.ohio.gov/divisionsandprograms/cannabiscontrol/licenseeresources/applications/10Bdispensarydrawing — cited in DCC 10(B) instructions; [Verify] — this URL was not directly opened in this run, so its current content and update date are unverified. - Status in late 2026: secondary reporting (CannBus Q3 2026) describes DCC as still "process[ing] pending RFA II and 10(B) provisional license applications toward the 400-dispensary cap." Source: https://www.cannbus.org/lsum/oh_lsum.html — accessed 28 Oct 2026. That is processing of an existing pipeline, not a new open window.

RFA II (medical dispensary Request for Applications, second round): - The medical programme held RFA rounds in 2017 and 2021; RFA II (2021) offered up to 73 provisional dispensary licences by lottery across 31 geographic dispensary districts, site-specific, with a 5-dispensary-per-owner limit under the then-rules. Source: secondary summaries, https://ohiostatecannabis.org/licensing/dispensary and https://miraclekerop.blogg.se/2022/may/how-to-get-a-business-license-for-ohio.html — accessed 28 Oct 2026. [Verify] — the RFA II district map, lottery results, and how many RFA II provisionals remain unconverted/unbuilt in 2026 were not located as a single official source in this run; the April 2026 snapshot's "11 RFA II provisional dispensary licenses" pending (CannBus, above) is the latest located figure.

Is a new, general application window open? No — not as a general open round. - No DCC announcement of a new general adult-use cultivator, processor, laboratory, or dispensary application window was located for 2026. Secondary guides state only that DCC "is expected to open additional application windows … as the program expands toward the 400-dispensary cap" and to "watch the DCC website closely" (https://www.cannabisindustrylawyer.com/how-to-open-a-dispensary-in-ohio/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026). That is expectation, not an open window, and must not be reported as one. - For cultivators/processors/laboratories specifically: applications are by DCC-noticed application period under OAC 1301:18 and §3796.09 ("The division shall evaluate and prioritize applications … according to the applicant's eligibility, suitability, and ability to operate," §3796.09(B)). No open period was located. Status: capped/closed except for the RFA II + 10(B) pipeline and any future DCC-noticed round [Verify against the DCC applications page on the day of publication].

General eligibility and requirements (statutory core): - One application per location (§3796.09(A), §3796.10(A) analogue for dispensaries): "An entity that seeks to cultivate, process, or conduct laboratory testing … shall file an application for licensure with the division of cannabis control. The entity shall file an application for each location from which it seeks to operate." Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.09 — accessed 28 Oct 2026. - Criminal records checks: §3796.12 requires checks for administrators/daily operators, owners/prospective owners, officers/prospective officers, and board members/prospective board members, via the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation and, where the 5-year Ohio residency proof is not shown, the FBI; DCC must deny a licence if a subject person fails to complete/forward the check or instruct BCI to submit the report to DCC. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/chapter-3796 — accessed 28 Oct 2026. - Employment checks: §3796.13 (see §4.2.6). - Tax compliance: DCC may obtain tax-compliance information from the Department of Taxation (§3796.11); provisional-licence issuance requires compliance with Ohio tax laws and accurate disclosure, site ownership/valid lease, 500-foot separation from a prohibited facility (OAC 1301:18-2-07(A)), no local moratorium/prohibition on operation, and compliance with local ordinances/building standards/local approval to operate as a cannabis business (OAC 1301:18-2-07(A)(6)–(7)). Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-2-07 (effective 28 August 2025) — accessed 28 Oct 2026. - Lab-independence bar: §3796.09(C)(2) (see §4.2.4). - Age: secondary sources state 21+ for owners/officers/board members/administrators; the statute's disqualifying-offence and suitability framework is in §3796.03(B)(2) and §3796.09(C)(1). [Verify] the precise age rule in current OAC text before quoting it as statute. - Financial responsibility / surety and insurance: former medical rules required surety bonds/escrow (Level I reduced from $2,000,000 to $750,000; Level II from $200,000 to $75,000, with performance-trigger reductions) plus general/product liability insurance (Register of Ohio history for former OAC 3796:5-6-01, above). [Verify] current OAC 1301:18 financial-responsibility amounts — they were not confirmed for the post-SB 56 rules in this run and older figures must not be carried forward as current. - Secondary-only requirement claim [flagged, not adopted]: a "$250,000 minimum liquid assets" figure and a "registered with the Ohio Secretary of State with a current certificate of good standing + proof of site ownership/lease" requirement appear in CannBus's summary (https://www.cannbus.org/lsum/oh_lsum.html). The Secretary of State registration and site-control elements are consistent with DCC application materials; the $250,000 figure is not traced to a statute or rule text in this run and is marked secondary/unverified.

4.6 Other licence-adjacent authorisations

  • Medical delivery: dispensary activity only, under DCC rules (§3796.20(A)(1)(e)); no standalone delivery licence; rulemaking status [Verify] (see §4.2.3).
  • Research: ORC §3796.032 (effective 20 March 2026, SB 56) provides Chapter 3796 "does not authorize the division of cannabis control to oversee or limit research conducted at a state university, academic medical center, or private research and development organization" that is approved by a listed federal agency/body (AHRQ, NIH, National Academy of Sciences, CMS, DoD, CDC, VA, DEA, FDA, or an NIH-recognised board). That is a carve-out from DCC oversight, not a DCC research licence. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/chapter-3796 — accessed 28 Oct 2026. University hemp research licences (ODA, pre-2026) are covered in Part 7 of the full research, not here.
  • Hemp licences are not cannabis licences and are not counted in any figure in Part 4. Since 1 January 2026 Ohio hemp cultivation is licensed by USDA, not ODA, while ODA continues to regulate hemp processors (see Part 5, §5.9). Any source that blends hemp processor counts into cannabis processor counts is wrong.

4.7 Cannabis Social Equity and Jobs Programme — created by Issue 2, repealed by SB 56

What Issue 2 created (original text, now repealed): - A Cannabis Social Equity and Jobs Program administered by the Ohio Department of Development, which was to certify applicants and provide financial assistance, loans, grants, and technical assistance from the Cannabis Social Equity and Jobs Fund (funded by 36% of adult-use excise revenue under Issue 2's distribution). - Eligibility (Issue 2, former ORC §3780.19 and related provisions, as summarised in Ohio State University Moritz College / Drug Enforcement and Policy Center analysis): certification based on social and economic disadvantage — membership in a racial or ethnic minority group; demonstrated personal disadvantage due to colour, ethnic origin, gender, or physical disability; demonstrated disadvantage due to long-term residence in an area of high unemployment; or having been arrested, convicted, or adjudicated delinquent for a marijuana offence, or being the spouse, child, or parent of such a person — plus a wealth test left to Department of Development discretion. Source: https://moritzlaw.osu.edu/faculty-and-research/drug-enforcement-and-policy-center/research-and-grants/policy-and-data-analyses/cannabis-social-equity — accessed 28 Oct 2026. - Licence preference: DCC was to issue up to 40 Level III adult-use cultivator licences and up to 50 additional adult-use dispensary licences with preference for certified programme participants, and to waive at least 50% of licence/application fees for certified participants. Sources: same Moritz page; JD Supra summary of Issue 2, https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/another-domino-falls-ohio-voters-1510520/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026. - Department of Development duties also included encouraging employment of minorities, women, veterans, and persons with disabilities, studying/funding judicial reforms, and direct investment in disproportionately impacted communities (same sources).

What SB 56 did (current law): - SB 56 repealed the Cannabis Social Equity and Jobs Program and eliminated both the Level III cultivator licence and the 50 additional social-equity dispensary licences, and redirected the 36% excise share to host communities (see Part 2 of the full research for revenue distribution; the host-community share is noted here only to explain where the equity money went). LSC's SB 56 analysis states this expressly: "The bill eliminates DCC's authority to issue up to 50 additional adult-use dispensary licenses, and up to 40 level III cultivator licenses, with preference given to certified Cannabis Social Equity and Jobs Program participants. The Cannabis Social Equity and Jobs Program is repealed by the bill." Source: https://www.legislature.ohio.gov//download?key=26235 — accessed 28 Oct 2026. Corroborated by CannBus Q3 2026: "SB 56, effective March 20, 2026, repealed the Cannabis Social Equity and Jobs Program… and eliminated the Level III cultivator license." Source: https://www.cannbus.org/lsum/oh_lsum.html — accessed 28 Oct 2026. - No Level III licence was ever issued (see §4.2.5), so the repeal extinguished an unexercised preference, not an operating licence class. - What, if anything, replaced the preference: secondary reporting states DCC licence ranking "may consider plans to hire and educate Ohio residents, veterans, disabled persons, women or minorities" (CannBus, https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/oh_cannmir.html). [Verify] — this is not traced to a current statutory text in this run and must not be presented as a surviving equity set-aside.

Certification and litigation — gaps: - Social equity certification list: [Unavailable]. No Department of Development certification list, certified-applicant count, or certification rule was located in this run. Given the programme was repealed before any Level III licence issued, it is unclear whether any certification ever issued. Do not invent a certified count. - Litigation over the programme or its repeal: [Unavailable in this run]. No case, docket, or judgment concerning the Cannabis Social Equity and Jobs Program was located. Separately, note — do not conflate — that Attorney General Dave Yost sued nine multistate operators on 5–6 February 2026 under Ohio's Valentine Act alleging shelf-space deals disadvantaging smaller Ohio cultivators/processors (allegations, not findings). Source: CannBus summary citing the Attorney General, https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/oh_cannmir.html — accessed 28 Oct 2026. That antitrust suit is not a social-equity-programme case. - Referendum effort against SB 56: secondary reporting states the effort to put a referendum on SB 56 on the ballot failed on 18 March 2026 (signature deadline 19 March 2026 in another summary) — the programme repeal therefore stands. Source: https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/oh_cannmir.html and https://drugpolicywatch.info/states/ohio.html — accessed 28 Oct 2026. [Verify] against the Secretary of State's referendum-petition record before stating the failure mechanism in detail (Part 9 of the full research owns this).

PART 5 — LICENCE DATA SOURCES

Instruction applied: No holder-by-holder list is given. This is an inventory of sources, with access mechanics. Where a source could not be directly opened in this run, that is stated; search-result evidence is not presented as a direct read.

General limitation that applies to almost every Ohio source below: DCC publishes licence information across (a) a dispensary map/list, (b) "By the Numbers" PDFs, (c) a weekly historical sales workbook, and (d) application-specific spreadsheets/PDFs — not as a single open-data licence register with a stable API or a single downloadable CSV of all licence types. Anyone needing a reconciled, current census must join those sources and date-stamp the join. There is no evidence in this run of a DCC bulk-download CSV/XLSX covering all cultivators, processors, laboratories and dispensaries in one file.

5.1 Division of Cannabis Control — dispensary map / dispensary list

  • What it is: Interactive map + directory/list of licensed medical and dual-use dispensaries. Described in multiple secondary sources as "the Ohio DCC provides an interactive map and full directory of licensed medical and dual-use cannabis dispensaries across Ohio" and as a map with a "click to download the spreadsheet" function in older Medical Marijuana Control Program material.
  • URL: No single canonical map URL was returned verbatim by a tool result in this run. The DCC hub is https://com.ohio.gov/cannabis (task-brief URL) and the applications hub is https://com.ohio.gov/divisionsandprograms/cannabiscontrol/licenseeresources/applications (verbatim from DCC instructions). The exact map URL is [Unavailable] from tool results in this run — do not guess it; navigate from the DCC hub on the day of use and record the URL then.
  • Holder type: Retail dispensaries (medical / dual-use) only — not cultivators, processors, or laboratories.
  • Format: Interactive map/search page. Older programme material describes a downloadable spreadsheet from the map; whether the current map retains a download/export button is [Verify] — no current export button was confirmed in this run.
  • How to access: Via the DCC website (no login described in any source located). The State Medical Board's physician newsletter (January 2026) states: "Click the map to view the dispensary locations or to download a complete list of Ohio-licensed dispensaries." Source: https://myemail.constantcontact.com/CTR-Physician-Newsletter---January-2026.html?aid=4l67bAQXm8g&soid=1142211591979 — accessed 28 Oct 2026.
  • Update frequency as stated: Not stated in any source located — [Unavailable].
  • Latest data date: The underlying counts move with DCC's periodic updates; the latest count derived from DCC reporting is 233 operating + 47 provisional dispensaries through 10 October 2026 (see §4.3), but that is not the same as the map's own "last updated" stamp, which was not located.
  • Fields available (expected, [Verify] against the live map): Business name, address, city, licence type/status (certificate of operation vs provisional), dual-use status. Phone/website fields, if any, are business public contacts.
  • Limitations: Dispensary-only; provisional vs operating status must be checked per record (a provisional listing is not an open store — DCC itself stresses this, e.g. for the Canton Curaleaf provisional site: "a provisional license does not permit the entity to sell cannabis," via https://www.cantonrep.com/story/business/2026/08/13/curaleaf-dispensary-is-being-built-in-canton-ohio-exclusive/91078423007/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026); no bulk file confirmed; local moratorium status is not shown on the state map (local rules are Part 3 of the full research).

5.3 Division of Cannabis Control — historical sales data workbook (weekly sales)

  • What it is: The canonical DCC sales time series: weekly medical and adult-use (non-medical) sales, plant-material pounds, manufactured-product units, receipts, and average prices, from January 2019 onward.
  • Format: XLSX workbook (one sheet, 16 columns, 398 weekly rows from 19 January 2019 to 29 August 2026 in the copy examined by an independent tracker on 16 August 2026 — the tracker notes the workbook ships its whole history on every download, so revisions are absorbed by rebuilding, not by incremental append). A retired PDF version also existed. Source: https://www.districtcannametrics.com/ohio.html — accessed 28 Oct 2026 (independent tracker describing the DCC workbook; the DCC workbook's own direct URL was not returned verbatim in this run).
  • Direct download link and file name: [Unavailable] from tool results in this run. The tracker describes the file as "DCC Historical Sales Data (Excel)" / "Rev. 5/1/2026" in CannBus's source list (https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/oh_cannmir.html — accessed 28 Oct 2026), but neither source printed the dam.assets.ohio.gov URL in the text returned. Do not guess the URL; locate it from the DCC sales/statistics page on the day of use. This is the single most important download gap in Part 5 — the file plainly exists and is publicly downloadable (multiple independent trackers rebuild from it), but its exact current URL/file name could not be verified here.
  • Holder type: N/A — sales aggregates, not licence holders. Licence counts are sometimes printed on the same DCC updates that accompany the workbook (see §4.3 snapshots).
  • How to access: Unauthenticated download (per the tracker: "Unauthenticated, no key, no referer check, Access-Control-Allow-Origin *").
  • Update frequency as stated: Weekly (DCC publishes weekly sales; weeks end on Saturdays). The tracker warns Ohio weeks do not nest inside calendar months, so "monthly" sums built from weekly rows are sums of weeks ending in that month, not calendar months — a material caveat for Part 6 monthly tables.
  • Latest data date: DCC reporting through 10 October 2026 is the latest located (Marijuana Herald summary of the 16 October 2026 DCC release — see §6.1). The workbook copy examined by the tracker ran to 29 August 2026.
  • Fields available (per tracker and DCC summaries): Week-ending date, total sales, non-medical sales, medical sales, plant-material pounds (by channel), manufactured-product units (by channel), receipts/transactions (by channel), average price per 1/10 oz and per gram (plant material), average manufactured-product price. Pre-August 2024 non-medical cells print "-" (no channel), not zero.
  • Limitations: (1) The tracker flags that July–August 2026 weekly rows fail the source's own Total = Non-Medical + Medical identity in at least one week, and it withholds the channel split for those weeks — channel-split figures for mid-2026 must be treated as [Verify]; (2) weekly, not daily, granularity; (3) no product-category split (flower vs vape vs edible dollars) in the workbook as described — category dollars in §6.3 come from secondary reporting of state data, not from this workbook; (4) no county or store-level breakdown as described.

5.9 Ohio Department of Agriculture — hemp licence lists (and the 2026 transfer)

  • Regulatory break that governs every hemp source: ODA regulated hemp cultivation and processing from spring 2020 under a USDA-approved state plan (ORC Chapter 928, OAC Chapter 901:14). The state operating budget, HB 96 (passed June 2025), authorised ODA to transfer hemp cultivation regulation to USDA; ODA began the transfer 25 July 2025; as of 1 January 2026, Ohio hemp growers must be licensed through USDA and all ODA cultivation licences are void; ODA continues to regulate hemp processors. Sources: Ohio State University Farm Office, 26 March 2026, https://farmoffice.osu.edu/blog/thu-03262026-931am/interested-growing-hemp-ohio-there-are-some-regulatory-and-statutory-changes and https://farmoffice.osu.edu/blog-tags/hemp — accessed 28 Oct 2026; corroborated by https://www.mmjdaily.com/article/9824231/us-oh-examining-regulatory-changes-to-hemp-cultivation-in-state/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026.
  • ODA hemp programme pages (URLs as printed in OSU Farm Office material): https://agri.ohio.gov/divisions/hemp-program/cultivation and https://agri.ohio.gov/divisions/hemp-program/faqs, plus ODA Food Safety hemp-products resources at https://agri.ohio.gov/divisions/food-safety/resources/Hemp-Products. These URLs appear in OSU material (https://farmoffice.osu.edu/blog-tags/hemp — accessed 28 Oct 2026) but were not directly opened in this run — [Verify] live status, since the cultivation pages may now redirect to a USDA-transition notice.
  • ODA hemp processor list: ODA historically published a "Hemp Processor List" (listed among ODA hemp-programme resources in secondary material, e.g. https://www.cbdseedco.com/where-we-grow/ohio/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026). No current direct URL or file name for the processor list was returned verbatim in this run — [Unavailable] as a verified link. Do not cite a processor-list URL without opening it.
  • ODA hemp licence counts from secondary/ODA-via-testimony sources (not a live list): 2024 — 36 registered farmers, of whom 24 grew; 33 registered and active processors (7 raw-flower, 4 extraction, 30 wholesale, 18 retail — categories overlap, so they do not sum to 33). Source: OSU Drug Enforcement and Policy Center testimony citing ODA information, https://search-prod.lis.state.oh.us/api/v2/general_assembly_135/committees/cmte_s_gen_govt_1/meetings/cmte_s_gen_govt_1_2024-12-03-0330_1496/testimony/14192/douglasberman_sb326_iptestimony.pdf — accessed 28 Oct 2026.
  • Format / update / fields for ODA lists: [Unavailable] beyond the above — no format, update frequency, or field list for a current ODA processor list was confirmed. Historical ODA hemp fees (for context, pre-transfer; Part 7 owns hemp licensing detail): cultivation application $100 + $500 per growing location per year + $250 site-modification + $150 per additional pre-harvest sample; processor application $100 + per-site annual fees $500 (raw grain), $500 (raw fibre), $3,000 (raw floral incl. extraction/smokable), $500 (wholesale cannabinoid food/supplement/cosmetic), $250 (retail in the same categories) — secondary summary at https://OhioStateCannabis.org/cannabis-business — accessed 28 Oct 2026. [Verify] against OAC 901:14 before reuse; cultivation fees are moot after 1 January 2026 in any case.
  • ODA hemp rules in transition: OAC 901:14-1-12 (reporting/records) was filed 25 August 2026 as "TO BE RESCINDED" (Register of Ohio, https://registerofohio.state.oh.us/pdfs/901/14/1/901$14-1-12_PH_OF_R_RU_20260825_1350.pdf — accessed 28 Oct 2026), consistent with the cultivation transfer. Processor rules in OAC 901:14-2 (e.g. 901:14-2-10, sources) were also in proposed-rule filings in August 2026. Anyone citing OAC 901:14 must check the current rule status on the day of use.

5.10 USDA hemp records for Ohio (post-1 January 2026 cultivation authority)

  • USDA plan status: USDA's "List of USDA-approved Hemp Plans" (updated 17 February 2026) lists Ohio as "USDA Hemp Producer License" — i.e. Ohio has no approved state plan; USDA issues the producer licence directly. Source: https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review — accessed 28 Oct 2026.
  • How to find Ohio producers: USDA Hemp Public Search Tool / HeMP (Hemp eManagement Platform) Search Tool — USDA's FAQ states: "Information on licensees in your area can be obtained through the Hemp Public Search Tool." Source: https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/frequently-asked-questions-faq — accessed 28 Oct 2026. Application route: create a HeMP account and submit a USDA Hemp Application; applications accepted on a rolling basis; a felony controlled-substance conviction in the last 10 years bars licensure. Source: https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/information-for-hemp-growers — accessed 28 Oct 2026.
  • Format: Interactive search tool. No bulk download/CSV of Ohio USDA producers was confirmed; no export button was confirmed — [Verify] against the live HeMP tool. FOIA-released records are also available via the AMS FOIA page, and a formal FOIA request is the documented route to a bulk record (same FAQ).
  • Latest count located (secondary, via USDA search tool): As of June 2026, 26 growers and 44 registered hemp processors in Ohio "according to the USDA search tool" — but processors are ODA-regulated, so the "44 processors" figure's attribution to the USDA tool is internally suspect (see §6.5). Source: https://hempcbdbusinessplans.com/ohio-hemp-industry/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026. [Verify] — treat the 26-grower figure as secondary and the 44-processor attribution as unreliable until checked against the live tools.
  • Fields available (expected, [Verify]): Producer name, licence number, location/county, status, licence period (USDA licences run to 31 December of the third year after the year of issue, per 7 CFR 990.21, as summarised in secondary material). No field list was confirmed from the live tool in this run.

5.11 Ohio Secretary of State — business entity search

  • What it is: The Secretary of State's business-entity search (corporations, LLCs, partnerships, etc.) — the only way to verify an Ohio cannabis company's legal entity, formation date, standing, statutory agent, and officers as filed, independent of its DCC licence.
  • URL: [Unavailable] as a verbatim tool result in this run. The Secretary of State's business search is a well-known public service, but no URL was returned by a search result here and none is guessed. Navigate from the Ohio Secretary of State's official site on the day of use.
  • Holder type: All business entities (not cannabis-specific). A DCC licensee's entity can be looked up by exact legal name; a search for "cannabis" will not return a licence-holder list.
  • Format: Interactive search page (entity detail pages; no bulk cannabis download).
  • How to access: Free public search (no login described in sources located). DCC application materials require proof of Secretary of State registration and a certificate of good standing (see §4.5) — which is why this source matters for licence diligence even though it is not a licence register.
  • Update frequency / latest data date / fields: [Unavailable] from tool results — the search is live/transactional; fields typically include entity name, entity number, type, status (active/cancelled), formation date, agent, and incorporators/organisers, but the field list was not confirmed from the live search in this run.
  • Limitations: Entity existence ≠ licence existence. An entity may be in good standing with the Secretary of State while holding no DCC licence, a provisional licence only, or a revoked licence. Always join to a DCC source.

5.12 Local (county / city / village / township) permit and zoning records

  • No statewide local-permit register exists. Local records are held by each jurisdiction and, where published at all, appear as:
  • Local licensing chapters (example located: Beavercreek, Ohio, Code §115.02, "Licensing of Medical Marijuana Dispensaries" — local operating licence + local provisional licence, building-permit/occupancy gating, Secretary of State registration and good-standing proof). Source: https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/beavercreek/latest/beavercreek_oh/0-0-0-28566 — accessed 28 Oct 2026. This is an example of the form local records take, not a claim about Beavercreek's current licensees.
  • County recorder / auditor records (e.g. a Stark County Recorder notice of commencement for a Canton dispensary build-out, reported at https://www.cantonrep.com/story/business/2026/08/13/curaleaf-dispensary-is-being-built-in-canton-ohio-exclusive/91078423007/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026) — useful for site-level verification, not a licence list.
  • Municipal code libraries (American Legal Publishing / Municode / Qcode) for zoning and moratorium ordinances — Part 3 of the full research owns the jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction inventory.
  • Format / access / update / fields: [Unavailable] as a general statement — each jurisdiction differs; most small villages/townships publish no machine-readable permit list. Do not claim a local permit database exists for any named jurisdiction without opening that jurisdiction's code/records page.
  • What DCC requires locally (so local records matter): OAC 1301:18-2-07(A)(6) requires a provisional-licence site to be free of a local moratorium/prohibition and compliant with local ordinances, building standards, and local approval to operate as a cannabis business (see §4.5). A DCC licence therefore implies a local clearance at the time of issuance, but local moratoriums adopted later, and SB 56's grandfathering for pre-20 March 2026 licensees, complicate any "currently permitted locally" inference — Part 3 owns this.

5.13 Total licence counts by type (summary — official figures only)

See §4.3 for the dated table. In one line, latest located official-via-DCC snapshot (through 10 October 2026): 233 operating dual-use dispensaries + 47 provisional dispensaries; 37 cultivators; 45 processors; 6 testing laboratories; 9,916 active industry employee licences. Source: https://themarijuanaherald.com/2026/10/ohio-marijuana-sales-top-1-billion-in-2026-4-43-billion-since-launch/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026. Earlier snapshots in §4.3 show the trajectory and the testing-lab count discrepancy (9 → 6) that remains unresolved.

PART 6 — MARKET DATA

Method note: Ohio's official sales series is weekly (weeks ending Saturdays). Calendar-year totals below are either (a) DCC cumulative anchors quoted exactly as reported, from which a year total is arithmetic, or (b) secondary annual totals explicitly marked as such. "Monthly" figures in secondary sources are usually sums of weeks ending in that month, not calendar months (see §5.3) — this file therefore gives weekly anchors and annual totals, and flags any monthly figure as approximate. All dollar figures are retail sales value as reported by DCC, not tax collections (taxes are Part 2).

6.3 Active licence and dispensary counts; patient counts (market context)

  • Licence/dispensary counts: see §4.3 (latest: 233 operating + 47 provisional dispensaries; 37 cultivators; 45 processors; 6 labs; 9,916 employee licences — through 10 Oct 2026).
  • Patient counts: see §5.8. Headline for market sizing: 476,589 registered patients as of 31 August 2026, but only 73,396 with both an active registration and an active recommendation; 440,441 unique patients had purchased medical marijuana as reported to OARRS as of 31 August 2026; 42,922 registered caregivers; 484 certificates to recommend as of 14 October 2026. Source: DCC By the Numbers PDF, https://dam.assets.ohio.gov/image/upload/com.ohio.gov/DCC/DCC%20Stats/DCC_Update_By_The_Numbers.pdf — accessed 28 Oct 2026 (via search result).
  • Trajectory: registered patients rose from 456,921 (June 2025) to 465,854 (31 Dec 2025) to 476,589 (31 Aug 2026), while the active-registration-plus-recommendation count fell from 95,439 (June 2025) to 79,731 (Dec 2025) to 73,396 (Aug 2026) — i.e. the registered base grows while the currently-active patient base shrinks, consistent with patients migrating to adult-use purchasing (which requires no registration). That interpretation is this file's analysis of the two DCC series, not a DCC statement. Unique purchasers (OARRS) rose over the same span (435,713 → 445,994 → 440,441 — the August 2026 figure is lower than January 2026's, which may reflect the different "as of" dates or a reporting change; [Verify] before charting a trend).
  • Physician counts: 506 certificates to recommend as of 31 March 2026 (secondary summary, https://themarijuanaherald.com/2026/04/ohio-marijuana-sales-top-331-million-in-2026-all-time-purchases-pass-3-7-billion-across-40-8-million-transactions/ — accessed 28 Oct 2026) vs 484 as of 14 October 2026 (By the Numbers PDF) — see §5.8 caveat.

6.5 Market saturation — only what official sources say

  • Statutory saturation guardrail: ORC §3796.05(B)(3) requires DCC to ensure geographic distribution "does not result in the oversaturation of any geographic area" when issuing dispensary licences, and §3796.05(B)(4) bars new/relocated dispensaries within one mile of another licensed dispensary (post-20 March 2026). Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.05/3-20-2026 — accessed 28 Oct 2026.
  • Headroom under the cap (arithmetic from §4.3): 233 operating + 47 provisional = 280 dispensaries accounted for against a 400 cap — i.e. 120 slots of headroom before counting any further pipeline, on the latest snapshot. This is arithmetic, not a DCC saturation assessment.
  • Local constraint (official-adjacent, owned in detail by Part 3): More than 130–137 municipalities/townships with adult-use moratoriums or bans are reported across 2025–2026 secondary coverage citing DCC/Capital Journal counts (e.g. "more than 130 Ohio municipalities and townships currently have moratoriums," MJBizDaily Jan 2026, https://mjbizdaily.com/news/ohio-cannabis-sales-top-1-billion-in-first-full-year-of-adult-use/613984/; "137 jurisdictions had adult-use moratoriums as of July 2026," CannBus, https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/oh_cannmir.html). No official DCC moratorium list/map URL was verified in this run — Part 3 must confirm it; saturation analysis that ignores local bans will overstate addressable geography.
  • No official DCC saturation metric (stores per capita, sales per store, or a saturation index) was located. No cluster ranking is given in this file, per the task instruction: official sources state where licensees are only through the dispensary map/list (§5.1) and the 10(B) district materials (§5.4), not as a ranked concentration analysis. Any "most saturated city/county" claim would be this file's own estimate and is therefore omitted.
  • Per-store arithmetic (derived, for scale only): 2025 total sales ~$1,069m across an average of roughly 190–210 operating dispensaries implies roughly $5–5.6m per operating store per year — a crude average that mixes medical and adult-use, ignores provisional stores opening mid-year, and ignores the wide store-to-store spread. It is given only to show the order of magnitude and must not be quoted as a DCC figure.

Federal baseline applied (fixed, not re-researched)

  • State-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). All adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. The broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is not final.
  • IRS 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to 280E.
  • Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026. After 11 December 2026, the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply.
  • USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026.
  • The federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026.
  • There is no federal cannabis banking law.
  • No contradiction to this baseline was found in Parts 7–8. Two alignments are worth stating, because they are easy to misread: (1) Ohio's own 0.4 mg/container rule (ORC 928.01, SB 56, eff. 20 March 2026) already matches the post-11 December 2026 federal cap, so 11 December 2026 does not create a new Ohio threshold — see Run 1 §1.5; (2) the USDA hemp page returned in search in this run repeats the DEA-lab enforcement delay to 31 December 2026, consistent with the baseline — source: https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index].

PART 7: HEMP LICENCES

7.1 The answer in one paragraph — and the resolution of the Run 1 tension

Ohio does NOT run its own USDA-approved state hemp plan in 2026. It did from spring 2020 to 31 December 2025. It now uses the USDA programme (the federal plan under 7 CFR Part 990, USDA Domestic Hemp Production Program, DHPP) for cultivation, and it retains a single Ohio state licence for processing through the Ohio Department of Agriculture (ODA). There is no Ohio hemp retailer licence and no standalone Ohio hemp-derived-product registration located (see §7.6).

Resolution of the Run 1 tension — CONFLICT RESOLVED, Part 5/6 adopted, Part 0–1 flag superseded:

Run 1 position What Run 2 found Disposition
Part 0–1 §1.5, "Hemp cultivation transfer to USDA — flag for Part 7": statute only authorises a transfer; secondary claim (USDA licences from 1 Jan 2026) "not verified against an ODA notice or USDA plan approval in this run" Register of Ohio RSFA for OAC 901:14-1-03, filed 25 August 2026, states in terms: "Effective September 30, 2025, House Bill 96 … modified Ohio Revised Code Chapter 928 which made the state hemp cultivation regulatory program discretionary (it was previously mandatory). On December 31, 2025, the Ohio Department of Agriculture (ODA) withdrew its Approved State Plan and transferred regulatory authority over hemp cultivation to the USDA Domestic Hemp Production Program. Persons interested in growing hemp in Ohio must receive a production license through USDA DHPP." The same wording appears in the RSFAs for 901:14-1-13 and 901:14-1-14. Adopted. The transfer is confirmed, not merely authorised.
Part 5 §§5.9–5.10 and Part 6 §6.6: HB 96 (June 2025) authorised transfer; ODA began transfer 25 July 2025; as of 1 Jan 2026 growers must be USDA-licensed and all ODA cultivation licences are void; ODA retains processors; USDA plan list (updated 17 Feb 2026) lists Ohio as "USDA Hemp Producer License" OSU Farm Office, 26 March 2026, opened directly in this run, states identically: "On July 25, 2025, ODA started the process of transferring the regulation of hemp cultivation to the USDA. As of January 1, 2026, if you are growing hemp in Ohio, you must be licensed through USDA, and all ODA cultivation licenses are now void. ODA continues to regulate hemp processors." USDA plan list returned by search in this run (updated 17 February 2026) again lists "Ohio USDA Hemp Producer License".
Part 0–1: HB 96's role vs SB 56's role was unclear HB 96 (136th GA, eff. 30 September 2025 for the Chapter 928 changes) made cultivation discretionary ("may" instead of "shall") and permitted the transfer; SB 56 (eff. 20 March 2026) then rewrote ORC 928.02 in the same discretionary terms and added the express transfer language. Both bills point the same way; HB 96 is the transfer authority, SB 56 is the current codification. Adopted, with the sequence stated.

Register of Ohio RSFA, OAC 901:14-1-03, filed 25 August 2026: https://registerofohio.state.oh.us/pdfs/901/14/1/901$14-1-03_PH_OF_R_RS_20260825_1350.pdf — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index / RSFA]. Register of Ohio RSFA, OAC 901:14-1-13: https://registerofohio.state.oh.us/pdfs/901/14/1/901$14-1-13_PH_OF_R_RS_20260825_1350.pdf — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index / RSFA]. HB 96 LSC comparison document (AGRCD17, "Permits the AGR Director to transfer jurisdiction to implement Ohio's hemp cultivation licensure program to the USDA"): https://www.lsc.ohio.gov/assets/legislation/136/hb96/phc/files/hb96-agr-comparison-document-as-pending-in-house-committee-136th-general-assembly.pdf — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index].

What this means in practice, and what it does not mean: - A person who wants to grow hemp in Ohio in 2026 must hold a USDA Hemp Producer License. An ODA cultivation licence, even if unexpired on its face, is void after 1 January 2026. Growing hemp for personal use without a licence remains prohibited — the transfer changed the licensor, not the licence requirement. - A person who wants to process hemp in Ohio must still hold an ODA hemp processing licence. USDA does not license Ohio processors. - A person who only buys, sells or possesses compliant hemp or a compliant hemp product needs no hemp licence at all — see ORC 928.02(C) as summarised in Run 1 §1.2 and §7.6 below. That is a possession/sale rule, not a retailer licence. - The transfer does NOT change the Ohio product thresholds: plant total THC (incl. THCA) ≤0.3% dry weight, and final-product >0.4 mg combined total THC (incl. THCA) per container is not hemp (ORC 928.01, SB 56). USDA's own sampling/testing regime (7 CFR Part 990) applies to the crop; Ohio's Chapter 928 definition applies to the product in Ohio commerce. Where the two use different measurement language, the stricter Ohio product rule governs sale in Ohio — do not cite a USDA crop pass as proof that a finished product complies with ORC 928.01.

7.2 Statutory framework (current text, verbatim operative provisions)

All citations are to ORC Chapter 928 as amended by SB 56, effective 20 March 2026, unless stated otherwise. Run 1 read the chapter directly; this run did not re-open the chapter page (direct-open failed in this window), so quotations below are carried from Run 1's direct read and flagged [Carried from Run 1 direct read] — re-open codes.ohio.gov before quoting them in a filing.

Section Plain-English summary Verbatim operative text (excerpt) Last amended / origin
928.01 Definitions "Hemp" = Cannabis sativa L. and parts/derivatives/extracts/cannabinoids/isomers/acids/salts with total THC incl. THCA ≤0.3% dry weight, EXCLUDING viable seeds from an over-threshold plant, intermediate products with non-naturally-producible cannabinoids / synthesised-outside-plant cannabinoids / >0.3% combined total THC + similar-effect cannabinoids, intermediate products marketed/sold as final or direct to end consumer, and final products with non-naturally-producible or synthesised-outside-plant cannabinoids or >0.4 mg combined total THC (incl. THCA) + similar-effect cannabinoids per container. "Container" = innermost retail wrapping/vessel in direct contact with the final product. "Industrial hemp" = stalk/fibre, seed grain/oil/cake/nut/hull, microgreens/edible leaf from immature compliant-seed plants, non-commerce research plants, viable seed for those uses. "Hemp-derived cannabinoid product" excludes industrial hemp and FDA-approved drugs. "(C) 'Hemp' means the plant Cannabis sativa L. and any part of that plant … with a total tetrahydrocannabinols concentration, including tetrahydrocannabinolic acid, of not more than three-tenths per cent on a dry weight basis. 'Hemp' does not include … (4)(c) Greater than four-tenths of a milligram combined total per container of total tetrahydrocannabinols, including tetrahydrocannabinolic acid, and any other cannabinoids that have similar effects, or are marketed to have similar effects, on humans or animals as a tetrahydrocannabinol as established by the superintendent of cannabis control in lists adopted under section 928.031" SB 56, eff. 20 Mar 2026 (rewrote the pre-SB 56 delta-9-only definition) [Carried from Run 1 direct read]
928.02 Regulation / licensing Director of Agriculture may establish a cultivation programme and shall establish a processing programme; if a cultivation programme exists and the director intends to transfer it to USDA, the director shall effectuate the transfer; if a cultivation programme is implemented, the director issues cultivation licences per 928.03 rules; Dept./university may cultivate/process for research without licence as authorised; licences valid 3 years unless suspended/revoked; Dept./university/any person may without licence possess/buy/sell hemp or hemp product; adding hemp/hemp product to another product does not adulterate it; out-of-state licence / work-experience / certification reciprocity under ORC Chapter 4796 for individuals. "(A)(1) The director of agriculture may establish a program to monitor and regulate hemp cultivation and shall establish a program to monitor and regulate hemp processing in this state." HB 96 (discretionary cultivation, eff. 30 Sep 2025) then SB 56 (current text, eff. 20 Mar 2026) [Carried from Run 1 direct read]
928.03 Rules Director (with Governor + Attorney General, Ch. 119) shall adopt processing rules and, if a cultivation programme is implemented, cultivation rules covering: application forms/info, application + annual fees (cost-covering; one uniform cultivation fee — now moot for Ohio cultivation), background investigations (ORC 4776.01–4776.04; 10-year felony-controlled-substance bar), experience/equipment/facilities/land, processor financial responsibility, issuance/renewal/denial/suspension/revocation + Ch. 119 hearing, material falsification = ineligibility, land records (legal description, per federal law), no cultivating/processing marihuana, post-decarboxylation or similarly reliable THC testing, corrective action plans, annual inspections (random sample), federal enforcement compliance, disposal of violating plants/products, hemp byproducts, USDA information-sharing, setback distance from marijuana cultivation (not applicable if the marijuana cultivator moves in after the hemp licensee starts), annual reporting, recordkeeping, lab-testing fees, testing/labelling/packaging standards, no processing in a personal residence or on residentially zoned land, production/manufacturing practices, transport/storage, "independent research institute" definition, other necessary requirements. "(L) A procedure for testing, using post-decarboxylation or other similarly reliable methods, tetrahydrocannabinol concentration levels of plants and products" SB 56, eff. 20 Mar 2026 [Carried from Run 1 direct read]
928.031 Cannabinoid lists Superintendent of Cannabis Control, in consultation with the Director of Agriculture, shall establish four lists (see §7.7) and any additional container specificity; federal additions/changes/removals are automatically effected in the corresponding list, subject to superintendent amendment, and the superintendent shall immediately publish an updated list. "The superintendent of cannabis control, in consultation with the director of agriculture, shall establish the following lists for purposes of section 928.01 of the Revised Code: (1) Cannabinoids known to be capable of being naturally produced by a Cannabis sativa L. plant; (2) Tetrahydrocannabinol class cannabinoids known to the superintendent to be naturally occurring in the plant Cannabis sativa L.; (3) All other known cannabinoids with similar effects to, or marketed to have similar effects to, tetrahydrocannabinol class cannabinoids; (4) Any additional cannabinoids that have similar effects or are marketed to have similar effects on humans or animals as a tetrahydrocannabinol." SB 56, eff. 20 Mar 2026. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-928.031 — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index]

"no person shall cultivate hemp without a hemp cultivation license issued by the director of agriculture under this chapter, if the director implements a program to monitor and regulate hemp cultivation under division (A)(1) of section 928.02 of the Revised Code, or process hemp without a hemp processing license issued by the director of agriculture under this chapter." 7.3 Licence type 1 — USDA Hemp Producer License (cultivation) — CURRENT, federal

Licensor: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS), Domestic Hemp Production Program. Ohio state plan: NONE (withdrawn 31 December 2025; USDA plan list, updated 17 February 2026, lists Ohio as "USDA Hemp Producer License"). This is not an Ohio licence. Do not list it in an Ohio licence count alongside ODA processor licences.

Field Detail
What it allows Planting, growing, harvesting and storing hemp in Ohio, subject to the USDA plan: land/location registration, pre-harvest sampling by a USDA-authorised sampling agent, testing, and reporting/disposal/remediation of non-compliant lots. It does NOT authorise processing into a hemp product for sale — processing in Ohio still needs the ODA processing licence (§7.4) — and it does NOT authorise any product over the Ohio 0.4 mg/container threshold to be sold as hemp.
Who must hold it Any person growing hemp in Ohio, including a grower who also processes (that grower needs BOTH the USDA producer licence and the ODA processing licence, for the two different activities). Growing for personal use without a licence is prohibited.
How to apply Create an account on the USDA Hemp eManagement Platform (HeMP) — via Login.gov credentials — and submit a USDA Hemp Application through HeMP, or request a mailed/PDF application from AMS. Applications are accepted on a rolling basis throughout the year. Source: https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/information-for-hemp-growers — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index]; https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index].
Information required Applicant contact information; for a business entity, full business name, principal business address, full names/titles of key participants, email if available, and EIN; FBI criminal history report (Identity History Summary) for the individual applicant or for every key participant, dated within 60 days of submission; legal description / geospatial coordinates for each field, greenhouse or indoor facility; acreage reporting (planted, harvested, disposed/remediated); certification that the applicant will adhere to the USDA Domestic Hemp Production Plan. Sources: USDA grower page (above) [Search-index]; 7 CFR 990.21 summary in secondary sources: https://hempcbdbusinessplans.com/ohio-hemp-industry/ — accessed 29 October 2026 [Secondary]; https://sativauniversity.com/cannabis-laws/ohio/ — accessed 29 October 2026 [Secondary].
Fee No USDA application or licence fee was found in the USDA materials checked, and secondary sources consistently state "no fee" — "The grower pays for the FBI check, sampling agent and lab" (Sativa University, Ohio page, accessed 29 October 2026 [Secondary]); "There is no application fee" / "There is no renewal application fee" (Hemp CBD Business Plans, Ohio page, accessed 29 October 2026 [Secondary]). Flag: [Verify] — the absence of a fee in 7 CFR 990.21 was not confirmed by a direct open of the eCFR text in this run. Do not quote "USDA hemp licence is free" without that check; quote it as "no fee stated in the USDA grower materials checked; secondary sources say no fee". FBI fingerprinting/background-check costs (secondary range $25–$100 per person) and sampling/lab costs are the grower's costs, not a USDA licence fee.
Background / disqualification No licence if convicted of a felony related to a controlled substance in the last 10 years. Source: USDA grower page [Search-index]; 7 CFR 990.21 [Secondary summary].
Term / renewal Valid until 31 December of the third year after the year of issue (7 CFR 990.21); renewal requires the same information as the initial application and must be made before expiry — it does not renew itself. Source: secondary summaries citing 7 CFR 990.21 [Secondary — Verify against eCFR text].
Sampling / testing A USDA-authorised sampling agent samples each lot no more than 30 days before the anticipated harvest; the producer may not sample its own facility. Testing is for total THC after decarboxylation, limit 0.3% or less on a dry-weight basis, with measurement uncertainty applied under the USDA plan. Non-compliant lots must be remediated or destroyed/disposed of under the plan. Federal overlay: USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing is delayed to 31 December 2026 (federal baseline; confirmed on the USDA hemp page excerpt returned in this run). Sources: secondary summaries of 7 CFR 990.24 [Secondary]; USDA hemp page [Search-index].
Reporting Producers must report acreage and disposition to USDA (and, via USDA, to FSA crop-acreage reporting). Lot-level reporting and record retention follow 7 CFR Part 990 — detail [Verify] against the current Part 990 text, which was not opened directly in this run.
Info link USDA Information for Hemp Growers: https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/information-for-hemp-growers — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index]. USDA plan list: https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index]. USDA Hemp Public Search Tool / HeMP search: see §7.8 (interactive, no bulk download confirmed).
Ohio counts Run 1's latest count (secondary, via USDA search tool, June 2026) was 26 growers. No new Ohio USDA producer count was located in this run — do not update the 26 figure, and do not present it as a current USDA-published count. See Research Notes R-7.

7.4 Licence type 2 — ODA Hemp Processing License — CURRENT, Ohio state

Licensor: Ohio Department of Agriculture, Director of Agriculture, under ORC 928.02(A)(1) ("shall establish a program to monitor and regulate hemp processing") and 928.03 rules, OAC Chapter 901:14-2. This is the only Ohio hemp licence that remains in 2026. It is a processing licence, not a cultivation, retail, or product-registration licence.

Field Detail
What it allows Processing hemp in Ohio — converting hemp plant material into hemp products — at the licensed location(s), for the product types listed on the application. Processing includes extraction of cannabinoids and production of hemp products for food, dietary supplements, cosmetics/personal care, fibre/grain products, and wholesale/retail production, as categorised for fees below. A processor may NOT process marihuana, may NOT process in a personal residence or on residentially zoned land (ORC 928.03(Y)), and may NOT process hemp in a location within 500 feet of a school or public park except for approved research (proposed/original rule summary — current text [Verify], see §7.5).
Who must hold it Any person who processes hemp in Ohio. Employees under the licensee's instruction and control need not hold a separate licence; persons processing under a Department-approved university research programme need not obtain a processing licence (proposed-rule summary — current text [Verify]). A processor who also grows needs the USDA producer licence as well (§7.3).
How to apply Apply on the ODA form (OAC 901:14-2-03). The applicant must provide: for an individual, full legal name, physical and mailing address, email and phone; for a business entity, full business name, federal tax ID, mailing address, principal Ohio business location, authorised signatory, persons primarily responsible for hemp operations, every key participant (with the individual information for each), business phone and email; for each processing location, GPS coordinates, physical address, and maps for each building/storage facility; a list of the types of hemp products to be produced; if applicable, the extraction operational plan under OAC 901:14-2-11; and documentation of compliance with building, fire, safety and zoning statutes, local ordinances and rules for the property. Source: OAC 901:14-2-03 text returned by search: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-901:14-2-03 — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index]. Historic ODA portal route (OH
Application window Processing applications are open all year (secondary summary, OhioStateCannabis hemp page, accessed 29 October 2026 [Secondary]). This contrasts with the historic cultivation window (1 November–31 March), which is now moot. Confirm against the live ODA programme page before advising an applicant.
Fees — CURRENT filing vs HISTORIC schedule (conflict, see §7.9) Latest filing (August 2026 RSFA, OAC 901:14-2-04): $100 application fee; annual licence fee $3,000 for extraction of cannabinoids; $500 for wholesale or retail production. The RSFA states the amendment "remov[es] the annual license fee for processing the raw grain and the raw fiber component" and "chang[es] the annual license fee for processors to be five hundred dollars for wholesale or retail production. This change in fee eliminates a business from paying a fee for a wholesale license and for a retail license." Sources: RSFA for 901:14-2-04: https://www.registerofohio.state.oh.us/pdfs/901/14/2/901$14-2-04_PH_OF_A_RS_20260825_1400.pdf — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index / RSFA]; RSFA for 901:14-2-03: https://www.registerofohio.state.oh.us/pdfs/901/14/2/901$14-2-03_PH_OF_A_RS_20260825_1400.pdf — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index / RSFA]. Historic schedule (Run 1, secondary summary, pre-amendment): $100 application; $500 raw grain; $500 raw fibre; $3,000 raw floral (incl. extraction/smokable); $500 wholesale cannabinoid food/supplement/cosmetic; $250 retail in the same categories; a processor of more than one component paid each component fee. Adopted position: quote the August 2026 RSFA schedule as the latest filing, with the effective date flagged [Verify] — an RSFA filing date (25 August 2026) is not proof of the rule's effective date, and the current codified 901:14-2-04 text was not opened directly in this run. Do not quote the $250 retail fee or the separate grain/fibre fees as current without that check.
Background check Each applicant, and every person with a >10% interest in an applicant business entity, must submit to a criminal records check/investigation. Denial if any required person has pleaded guilty to or been convicted of a felony disqualifying offence in the preceding 10 years (ORC 928.03; OAC 901:14-2-03 RSFA). Cost of the background check varies by provider. Note: HB 96's executive proposal would have eliminated the 10-year felony bar and the general background-check law compliance for hemp — the LSC comparison document shows "No provision" for those eliminations in the House committee version. Do NOT state that the felony bar was repealed; the current RSFA still states it. Source: LSC HB 96 comparison document (above) [Search-index].
Financial responsibility / surety bond A licensed processor who purchases raw, unprocessed hemp plant material must maintain current assets, in the form of a surety bond, of at least 5% of total purchases of raw plant material made in the previous calendar year — or $10,000, whichever is greater. Secondary summaries of the bond premium (typically 1–3% per year for good credit) are non-official estimates and are not ODA figures. Sources: RSFAs for 901:14-2-03, -2-08, -2-15, -2-17 (above) [Search-index / RSFA].
Facility / inspection / sampling Facility inspection is a condition of licensing (proposed-rule summary). ODA may inspect and sample; samples collected by the Department are taken free of charge for Department testing and become Department property, non-returnable. Processing facilities must establish and implement a food safety system including hazard analysis and risk-based preventive controls, as applicable, and comply with OAC 901:3-17 food safety regulations. Processors extracting cannabinoids must have and follow an operational plan (OAC 901:14-2-11). Sources: RSFAs for 901:14-2-08 and -2-21 [Search-index / RSFA].
Testing (processor products) A representative sample of all hemp products manufactured by a hemp processor shall be tested prior to sale by a laboratory meeting OAC 901:14-2-14. The proposed-rule summary describes the panel as microbial contaminants, cannabinoid potency, mycotoxins, heavy metals, pesticide/fertilizer residue and residual solvents, with a certificate of analysis for each batch/lot, and exemptions for hemp used exclusively for fibre, derived exclusively from hemp seed, and hemp extracts — current panel [Verify] against the current 901:14-2-14/-2-15 text, which was not opened directly in this run. Sources: RSFAs for 901:14-2-14/-2-15 [Search-index / RSFA]; OSU Farm Office hemp-rules summary: https://farmoffice.osu.edu/blog-tags/hemp-industrial-hemp-hemp-regulations — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index].
Labelling Products must be labelled under OAC 901:3-1 and 901:14-2-17, mirroring FDA standards for food, dietary supplements and cosmetics. The August 2026 amended 901:14-2-17 requires, for hemp-derived cannabinoid products except those made exclusively from hemp fibres: labelling per OAC 901:3-1-11 (labelling), -1-12 (standard of identity), -1-13 (food colouring); total THC (TTHC) in milligrams per 901:14-2-01(M)(4)(c); milligrams per serving for all cannabinoids identified on the label if the product meets the food or dietary-supplement definition; total milligrams per unit for all cannabinoids if it meets the cosmetic definition; the cannabinoid profile matching laboratory reporting for each unique batch/lot (per 901:14-2-15(A)(9)) if it meets none of those definitions; and unique batch/lot coding permanently visible to the naked eye, identifying the establishment, to facilitate warnings/recalls. Source: RSFA / rule text for 901:14-2-17: https://www.registerofohio.state.oh.us/pdfs/901/14/2/901$14-2-17_PH_OF_A_RU_20260825_1400.pdf — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index / RSFA].
Term 3 years (licences valid 3 years unless suspended/revoked, ORC 928.02; proposed-rule summary confirms 3-year processing licence). Renewal procedure and any renewal fee beyond the annual licence fee were not located in current form in this run — [Verify] against current 901:14-2-03/-2-04.
Info link ODA hemp programme — cultivation page (now expected to carry the USDA-transition notice; direct-open failed in this window, live status [Verify]): https://agri.ohio.gov/divisions/hemp-program/cultivation — accessed 28 October 2026 in Run 1 as a URL printed in OSU material, not directly opened [Verify]. ODA hemp FAQs (same caveat): https://agri.ohio.gov/divisions/hemp-program/faqs. ODA Food Safety hemp-products resources: https://agri.ohio.gov/divisions/food-safety/resources/Hemp-Products [Verify — not opened in this run]. Current rule text: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-901:14-2-03 — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index].
Ohio counts Run 1's strongest ODA-sourced count is 2024: 33 registered and active processors (7 raw-flower, 4 extraction, 30 wholesale, 18 retail — overlapping categories, so they do not sum to 33), via OSU testimony citing ODA information. Run 1's June 2026 figure of "44 processors" attributed to the USDA search tool is unreliable attribution (processors are ODA-regulated, not USDA) and is NOT adopted. 7.6 What does NOT exist as a separate Ohio hemp licence or registration

This section is included because the absence is routinely mis-stated. Each "no" below was checked against ORC Chapter 928 and the OAC 901:14-2 material returned in this run; a "no" means no such licence/registration was located, not proof that no other Ohio law (e.g. general retail-food law) applies to the activity.

Supposed type Position
Hemp retailer licence None in ORC Chapter 928. ODA "does not explicitly license retailers selling hemp products" and "does not have authority over retailers because they are not licensed" (OSU Drug Enforcement and Policy Center testimony, 3 December 2024, summarised in search: https://search-prod.lis.state.oh.us/api/v2/general_assembly_135/committees/cmte_s_gen_govt_1/meetings/cmte_s_gen_govt_1_2024-12-03-0330_1496/testimony/14192/douglasberman_sb326_iptestimony.pdf — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index]). Secondary summaries agree: "No license is required to sell or purchase CBD in Ohio" (Weedmaps, Ohio CBD page — accessed 29 October 2026 [Secondary, dated material — the 0.3% wording in that page predates SB 56's total-THC / 0.4 mg rules and must not be quoted as current law]). Retailers must still sell only compliant hemp (≤0.4 mg/container, no synthetic/similar-effect excess after SB 56), must meet food-safety standards and be inspected by the appropriate state/local agency where the product is a food, and are subject to general consumer-protection / adulteration law. There is no hemp-specific age limit in Chapter 928 for compliant hemp; the 21+ rule applies to marijuana (Chapter 3796), not to compliant hemp.
Hemp-derived product registration (standalone) None located. There is no ODA "hemp product registration" number, fee or form in the Chapter 928 / 901:14-2 material checked. Product compliance is achieved through the processor licence + pre-sale testing + labelling (901:14-2-14/-2-17) + food-safety rules (901:3-17, 901:3-1), not through a separate product registration. If a product is a food, dietary supplement or cosmetic, the general FDA / Ohio food-safety labelling standards incorporated by 901:14-2-17 apply. Do not invent a product-registration fee.
Intoxicating-hemp licence / hemp-beverage licence None in force. The enrolled SB 56 Chapter 3779 drinkable-cannabinoid regime (manufacture/distribution/retail tiers, up to 5 mg beverages to 31 December 2026) was line-item vetoed in relevant part by Governor DeWine on signing (19 December 2025) — see Run 1 §1.5. SB 86's three-tier DCP framework (manufacturer registration, distributor, retailer — liquor-permit holders and dispensaries) was an introduced bill, not enacted law, per the LSC analysis of SB 86 as introduced: https://search-prod.lis.state.oh.us/api/v2/general_assembly_136/legislation/sb86/00_IN/attachments/analysis/ — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index]. Neither is a current licence type. Over-threshold products are marijuana under ORC 928.01/3719.01 and may only be sold through the Chapter 3796 dispensary channel (and then only if the product itself complies with Chapter 3796) — see Run 1 §1.5, point 4, with its DCC-guidance [Verify].
Hemp testing-laboratory licence (standalone ODA) None located as a separate licence type. OAC 901:14-2-14 sets requirements for laboratories that test processor products, and 901:14-2-15 sets laboratory reporting, but the material checked describes laboratory requirements, not a standalone ODA hemp-lab licence with its own fee. Do not list a hemp-lab licence alongside the DCC cannabis testing laboratories in Run 1 Part 4 — they are different regimes. Laboratory requirements [Verify] against current 901:14-2-14 text.
Hemp distributor / wholesaler licence (standalone) None located as a separate type. "Wholesale production" is a fee category within the ODA processing licence (§7.4), not a separate distributor licence. Transport/storage procedures are in ORC 928.03(AA) and OAC 901:14-2 rules — detail [Verify].
Seed dealer licence Related, not a hemp licence. Entities distributing hemp seeds for planting must obtain a seed dealer's licence under ORC 907.02 (secondary summary, LegalClarity Ohio hemp page — accessed 29 October 2026 [Secondary]). It is included here only to prevent it being counted as a hemp licence type. Fee and procedure [Verify] against ORC Chapter 907.
University / research cultivation or processing Exemption, not a licence type. ORC 928.02: the Department or a university may cultivate/process hemp for research without a licence as authorised. Whether that exemption, as written for an ODA programme, survives the USDA transfer for cultivation research in 2026 — i.e. whether a university researcher still needs a USDA producer licence — was not resolved in this run — [Verify] with ODA and USDA AMS before advising a university. Do not state that university hemp cultivation is licence-free in 2026 on the basis of the pre-transfer statute alone.

7.7 The 928.031 cannabinoid lists — status update (Run 1 R-8, partially advanced)

  • Statute: ORC 928.031 (SB 56, eff. 20 March 2026) requires the Superintendent of Cannabis Control, in consultation with the Director of Agriculture, to establish: (1) cannabinoids capable of being naturally produced by Cannabis sativa L.; (2) THC-class cannabinoids known to be naturally occurring in the plant; (3) all other known cannabinoids with similar effects to, or marketed to have similar effects to, THC-class cannabinoids; (4) any additional cannabinoids with similar effects or marketed to have similar effects on humans/animals as THC. It also requires additional container specificity, and provides that federal additions/changes/removals are automatically effected in the corresponding list, with the superintendent to immediately publish an updated list.
  • Rulemaking found: OAC 1301:18-11-01, "Ohio Revised Code 928.031 Cannabinoids", RSFA filed 21 July 2026, Department of Commerce, Division of Cannabis Control. The RSFA states its reason as: "To establish lists of cannabinoids as required by ORC 928.031, enacted by Senate Bill 56", and summarises the rule as establishing the same four lists. Source: https://www.registerofohio.state.oh.us/pdfs/1301/18/11/1301$18-11-01_PH_OF_N_RS_20260721_1235.pdf — accessed 29 October 2026 [Search-index / RSFA].
  • What is still missing: The actual list contents (which cannabinoids are on each list, and the container specificity) were not located in this run. The RSFA summarises the rule's purpose; it does not reproduce the lists. Status: [Verify] — check the current OAC 1301:18-11-01 text and any DCC-published list on the day of use. Until the lists are read, the "similar effects" test in ORC 928.01 cannot be applied cannabinoid-by-cannabinoid from this file alone, and no cannabinoid should be asserted to be on or off a list on the basis of this report. This partially resolves Run 1 R-8 (a rule to establish the lists exists and was filed) but does not close it (list contents still unverified).

PART 8: CANNABIS-ZONED PROPERTIES

8.1 How to read this part — and why the count is small

Ohio has no state "cannabis zoning" category. Zoning is local (municipal ordinance / township resolution, subject to ORC 3796.29 local-prohibition power and the state 500-ft buffer in ORC 3796.30 and the 1-mile dispensary separation in ORC 3796.05(B)(4) — see Run 1 §§1.6, 3). A listing that says "zoned for cannabis" is therefore a broker claim about local permission, not a state zoning code, and it must be checked against (a) the city/village zoning code, (b) any local prohibition/moratorium under 3796.29, (c) the 500-ft / 1-mile state buffers, and (d) whether a DCC licence is actually attached to the property or the business.

Status rule applied in this part, per the commission: a listing's status is marked [Verify] unless the listing itself shows it is active and recent. In this run, individual listing detail pages could not be opened directly (browser_open 429 in this window), so every listing below is [Verify], even where an index page shows "ACTIVE" — an index "ACTIVE" badge is not the listing itself, and several flyers/index entries are demonstrably old (see Willowick, §8.2, P-1). Prices are as stated in the listing excerpt; where the excerpt gives no price, the price is [Unavailable in excerpt], not $0 and not estimated.

Result: 5 Ohio properties that are marketed for cannabis use with a real-property address are listed as qualifying/marketed (§8.2, P-1 to P-5, with P-2 to P-5 carrying a zoning caveat), 3 business/investment offerings are listed as near-misses and NOT counted as real-property zoned listings (§8.3), and no Ohio hemp-specific zoned/permitted property listing was found (§8.4). Do not present this as a complete market census — it is a sweep of the public listing sources checked (420Property Ohio pages, Crexi, a broker flyer, a Matthews investment memorandum excerpt), not a sweep of every Ohio MLS, LoopNet or local broker site, which were not all opened in this window.

8.4 Hemp-specific properties — none found in Ohio

No Ohio property marketed as hemp-zoned, hemp-permitted, or hemp-suitable was found in the sources checked. The only "hemp permitted" listing returned in the searches checked was out of state (59.52 acres, Lodoga Road, Williams, California — "HEMP PERMITTED OFF GRID", $540,000), which is excluded as California, not Ohio. This is consistent with the licensing structure in Part 7: hemp cultivation in Ohio is a USDA licence tied to a registered growing location, not a local "hemp zone", and hemp processing is an ODA licence tied to a facility that must comply with general building/fire/safety/zoning law — there is no Ohio local zoning category called "hemp" to search for. A farm that is suitable for USDA hemp cultivation will therefore appear in general agricultural listings, not in cannabis-specific listings, and cannot be identified as a "hemp property" from a listing alone without the USDA location registration. Do not import the California "hemp permitted" concept into Ohio.

  • Columbus, Ohio (Franklin County) vs Columbus, Georgia / Indiana: all Columbus listings above are Ohio (43215, 43209).
  • East Liverpool, Ohio (Columbiana County) vs Liverpool, England (the city's namesake): Ohio only.
  • Willowick, Ohio (Lake County) vs Willoughby, Ohio (also Lake County, nearby, and a different city): the Euclid Avenue flyer is Willowick, not Willoughby.
  • Wauseon, Ohio (Fulton County) search page returning Michigan listings: see N-4. No Michigan listing was counted as Ohio.
  • Marietta, Ohio (Washington County) vs Marietta, Georgia / Oklahoma: no Marietta property was used in this part; the Oklahoma "Marietta, OK" grow listing returned in a general 420Property search was excluded as out of state.

Steve Huffman), signed 19 December 2025 with line-item vetoes, effective 20 March 2026, repealed ORC Chapter 3780 and consolidated medical + adult-use into a rewritten ORC Chapter 3796. Current adult-use rules are therefore SB 56 amendments, not original Issue 2 text, unless expressly carried over unchanged.
  • Possession: 2.5 oz plant material + 15 g extract, cumulative across homegrown + dispensary marijuana (ORC 3796.221(B)). Home grow: 6 plants per adult, 12 per residence (ORC 3796.04).
  • Adult-use excise tax: 10%, distribution 64% General Revenue Fund / 36% Host Community Cannabis Fund (ORC 3796.40(F), SB 56).
  • Dispensary cap 400; ownership cap 8 dispensaries / 1 cultivator / 1 processor. Social Equity and Jobs Programme and Level III cultivator tier deleted by SB 56.
  • Intoxicating hemp over 0.4 mg combined total THC (incl. THCA) per container is out of the definition of "hemp" from 20 March 2026 (ORC 928.01, SB 56). Executive Order 2025-05D is expired/superseded, not current law.
  • First adult-use sales 6 August 2024; dual-use conversion opened 7 June 2024.
  • Lawful possession in Ohio is in practice limited to Ohio-dispensary or lawfully homegrown marijuana; out-of-state purchases fall outside the ORC 3796.221 safe harbour. This Run 2 check found no primary source contradicting that rule (see §10.3 for one secondary marketing page that does contradict it, and why it is rejected).

Federal baseline applied (given, not re-researched)

  • Split scheduling: state-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). All adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I.
  • IRS 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to 280E.
  • Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026. After 11 December 2026, the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply.
  • USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026.
  • The federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026.
  • There is no federal cannabis banking law.
  • Ohio interaction, carried from Run 1 and not contradicted in this run: a single Ohio licence does not make adult-use product Schedule III. Dual licensees must split medical from adult-use activity for federal purposes. ORC 3796.01(C) as amended 20 March 2026 still calls marijuana Schedule II "for purposes of this chapter" — a state-law classification that has NOT been updated to Schedule III in the text read, and does not override the federal split. [VERIFY — see Research Note R-2, carried forward.]

9.1.2 What each regulator does NOT do (common errors corrected)

  • DCC does not certify physicians — that is the State Medical Board (CTR).
  • The Board of Pharmacy does not license dispensaries or register patients today — that transferred to DCC (HB 33, completed by 31 Dec 2023, with the patient-application handover date flagged in §9.2).
  • ODA does not license hemp cultivation in Ohio in 2026 — that is USDA DHPP (see §9.1.4). ODA retains processing.
  • ODT does not license cannabis businesses — it taxes them. A dispensary's tax account (OAC 5703-43-02) is not a licence.
  • No Ohio agency publishes a cannabis-specific tribal programme, because there is no Ohio tribal regulator (see Part 10).
