9.1.4 The hemp cultivation transfer — Run 1 gap R-9 RESOLVED

Run 1 (§1.5, Research Note R-9) said the USDA transfer was unverified: the statute only authorised a transfer and did not prove one, and secondary claims (USDA licences from 1 Jan 2026; 26 growers / 44 processors, June 2026) were unconfirmed.

Resolved in this run, from an official ODA rule filing (not a secondary summary):

"Effective September 30, 2025, House Bill 96 of the 136th General Assembly modified Ohio Revised Code Chapter 928 which made the state hemp cultivation regulatory program discretionary (it was previously mandatory). On December 31, 2025, the Ohio Department of Agriculture (ODA) withdrew its Approved State Plan and transferred regulatory authority over hemp cultivation to the USDA Domestic Hemp Production Program. Persons interested in growing hemp in Ohio must receive a production license through USDA DHPP."

Source: ODA, Register of Ohio, Rule Summary and Fiscal Analysis for OAC 901:14-1-99 (Enforcement, rescission) and OAC 901:14-1-17 (Cultivation research, rescission), filed 25 Aug 2026 — https://registerofohio.state.oh.us/pdfs/901/14/1/901$14-1-99_PH_OF_R_RS_20260825_1350.pdf and https://registerofohio.state.oh.us/pdfs/901/14/1/901$14-1-17_PH_OF_R_RS_20260825_1350.pdf — accessed 29 Oct 2026.

Adopted position: Ohio hemp cultivation is USDA-licensed from 1 January 2026; ODA retains hemp processing. This confirms Run 1 Part 4–6's statement ("Hemp cultivation authority after 1 January 2026 is USDA, not ODA") and upgrades Run 1 Part 0–1's R-9 from Verify to confirmed on the transfer date and mechanism. The June 2026 grower/processor counts (26 / 44) remain secondary-only and are not adopted here. The ODA cultivation rules (OAC 901:14-1-) are being rescinded in the five-year review for exactly this reason; processing rules (901:14-2-) are being amended to reference 7 CFR Part 990 instead of the former Chapter 901:14-1.

Election Measure What it would have done Result (votes as reported from SOS certified results) Effect
3 Nov 2015 Issue 3 — "Grants a Monopoly for the Commercial Production and Sale of Marijuana for Recreational and Medicinal Purposes" (ResponsibleOhio, constitutional amendment) Legalise personal + medical marijuana for 21+; commercial cultivation limited to 10 facilities with exclusive rights (up to 300,000 sq ft each, genetically marked crops, 1,100+ licensed outlets in proponent materials); 21+ with a licence (like a fishing licence) could use/possess/grow/share up to 8 oz homegrown + 4 flowering plants; 21+ without a licence could purchase/possess/transport/use/share up to 1 oz; certified medical patients could use medicinal marijuana. A separate state commission would have regulated it. FAILED. No: 2,042,902 (63.65%); Yes: 1,166,692 (36.35%); total 3,209,594. Secretary of State Jon Husted certified the results (reported 11 Dec 2015). No law enacted. The monopoly structure was the central objection (opponents: Ohioans Against Marijuana Monopolies, $2.1m spent vs ResponsibleOhio $20.2m, per campaign-finance reporting). The legislature then took up medical marijuana itself (HB 523, 2016).
3 Nov 2015 Issue 2 — Initiated Monopolies Amendment (legislature-referred constitutional amendment) Requires the Ohio Ballot Board to determine whether an initiative would create an economic monopoly or special privilege for a nonpublic entity; if so, a second question is put to voters, and if both the initiative and the anti-monopoly question pass, the initiative is invalidated. This was aimed directly at Issue 3. PASSED. Yes: 1,621,329 (51.33%); No: 1,537,261 (48.67%). Constitutional barrier to future monopoly initiatives. It did not itself legalise or prohibit marijuana. It is the reason the 2015 "Issue 2" must never be confused with the 2023 "Issue 2" — same number, different election, different subject.
7 Nov 2023 Issue 2 — "Regulate Marijuana Like Alcohol" (citizen-initiated statute, Coalition to Regulate Marijuana Like Alcohol) Legalise adult-use marijuana for 21+: cultivate, process, sell, purchase, possess, home-grow and use within limits (2.5 oz / 15 g as enacted); create the Division of Cannabis Control licensing system with priority for existing medical operators; levy a 10% excise tax (plus sales tax) with the original 36/36/25/3 distribution. PASSED. Yes: 2,226,399 (57.19%); No: 1,666,316 (42.81%); total 3,892,715. Margin: 560,083 votes. Ohio became the 24th state to legalise adult-use cannabis. Enacted as former ORC Chapter 3780, effective 7 Dec 2023. Later substantially rewritten by SB 56 (20 Mar 2026) — the voters' statute was a statute, not a constitutional amendment, so the Assembly could amend it. County pattern (secondary): Yes won in 25 of 88 counties, with Franklin County (Columbus) ~68% and Cuyahoga County (Cleveland) ~66.8% Yes, and Athens County ~70% Yes — [VERIFY county figures against the SOS county canvass before quoting a specific county].

PART 10: TRIBAL AND INTERSTATE

10.1 Tribal — federally recognised, state-recognised, and operations: NONE in Ohio

10.1.1 Plain answer

Ohio has no federally recognised tribe, no state-recognised tribe, no Indian reservation, and no tribal cannabis or hemp operation in Ohio. There is therefore no Ohio tribal cannabis licence, no Ohio tribal hemp plan, no tribal-state cannabis compact, and no tribal jurisdiction in Ohio under which cannabis or hemp could be produced, sold or possessed on a different legal basis from Ohio state law.

This is not a gap in the research — it is a positive finding, established on the official federal list below and corroborated by the state-recognition record. Do not list any tribe from another state (Oklahoma, Michigan, New York, North Carolina or elsewhere) as an "Ohio tribe," and do not treat a tribe's ancestral ties to Ohio land as present-day Ohio tribal jurisdiction.

10.1.2 Official basis — federal recognition

  • The Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA), U.S. Department of the Interior, publishes the official list of Indian entities recognised by and eligible to receive services from the BIA, under the Federally Recognized Indian Tribe List Act of 1994 (Pub. L. 103-454) and 25 CFR 83.6(a).
  • The current list in this run: 575 Tribal entities, Federal Register Vol. 91, No. 20, 30 January 2026, FR Doc. 2026-01899, pp. 4102–4106, updating the 11 December 2024 list (89 FR 99899). The notice adds the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina (Pub. L. 119-60, §8803, with conditions on service eligibility) and otherwise makes formatting/name changes.
  • Source opened directly: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-01-30/html/2026-01899.htm — accessed 29 Oct 2026. The list is alphabetical by tribal entity name, not by state, and its entries are identified by their present location (e.g. "…of Oklahoma", "…Michigan", "…California"). No entity in the list is identified as an Ohio entity, and a text search of the retrieved list for "Ohio" returned no Ohio-located entry. The entities with Ohio ancestral history appear under other states (for example, the Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma, the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma, the Delaware Tribe of Indians, and Michigan/Ottawa/Chippewa bands) — they are tribes of those states for jurisdictional purposes, not Ohio tribes.
  • Corroboration (secondary, by-state compilation of the same BIA list): "Ohio — No federally recognized tribes" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_federally_recognized_tribes_by_state — accessed 29 Oct 2026. This secondary line is adopted only as corroboration of the primary Federal Register check above, not as a substitute for it.

10.1.3 State recognition — none, and no recognition office

  • Ohio has no office to manage Indian affairs and no state-recognised tribes, per the state-recognition survey relied on in this run — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State-recognized_tribes_in_the_United_States — accessed 29 Oct 2026 (secondary; the underlying point — no Ohio statute creating a state-recognition process — was not contradicted by any Ohio statute located in this run, and no Ohio recognition statute was found).
  • The one historical episode sometimes miscited as "recognition": in 1979–1980 the General Assembly held hearings on the Shawnee Nation United Remnant Band (Bellefontaine, Logan County, Ohio), and the Senate adopted Am. Sub. H.J.R. No. 8 (113th GA, 1979–1980), a joint resolution to "recognise" that band. The Ohio Attorney General's office has stated that resolution "has no force of law in the state [of] Ohio… It was basically a ceremonial resolution" (spokesperson Leo Jennings, as quoted in the survey above). Adopted position: H.J.R. 8 is ceremonial only and does not create a state-recognised tribe, a tribal government, or any cannabis/hemp jurisdiction.
  • Groups in Ohio that describe themselves as tribal communities and/or seek federal recognition (named in secondary sources: the Shawnee Nation United Remnant Band; the Munsee Delaware Indian Nation of Ohio) are non-federally-recognised groups for legal purposes in this dossier. No cannabis or hemp operation by any such group in Ohio was located in this run. [VERIFY — if a group claims a hemp/cannabis operation, check for a USDA or ODA licence in its own name; none was found.]
  • No USDA tribal hemp plan for Ohio: USDA's hemp programme provides for tribal plans under 7 U.S.C. §1639p, but a tribal plan requires a federally recognised tribal government. With no such government in Ohio, there is no Ohio tribal hemp plan, and Ohio growers use the USDA state-territory DHPP route (see §9.1.4), not a tribal route.

10.1.4 Historical context — why "no Ohio tribe" does not mean "no Ohio Native history" (do not conflate)

  • The peoples historically present in Ohio — Shawnee, Miami (Myaamia), Wyandot, Delaware (Lenape), Ottawa, Seneca-Cayuga, Mingo and others — were largely removed westward in the early 1800s; the Wyandot ceded their last Ohio lands in the early 1850s (secondary histories). Their present-day federally recognised successors are in Oklahoma, Kansas, Michigan, Wisconsin, New York and elsewhere.
  • The U.S. Forest Service, Wayne National Forest (Ohio), maintains a list of "Federally Recognized Tribes with Ancestral Ties to Ohio" for consultation purposes, tracing descent from the twelve 1795 Treaty of Greenville signatory tribes (Chippewa, Delaware, Eel River, Kaskaskia, Kickapoo, Miami, Ottawa, Piankishaw, Potawatomi, Shawnee, Wea, Wyandot) to present-day tribes in other states — https://www.fs.usda.gov/r09/wayne/working-with-us/tribal-relations/federally-recognized-tribes-ancestral-ties-ohio — accessed 29 Oct 2026. That list is a consultation/ancestry list, not an Ohio jurisdiction list, and none of its entries is an Ohio cannabis/hemp operator. It is cited here only to prevent the error of copying its entries into an "Ohio tribes" table.
  • Consequence for individuals: a person who is an enrolled member of a federally recognised tribe based in another state, when present in Ohio, is subject to the same Ohio cannabis/hemp law as any other person in Ohio. No provision in ORC Chapter 3796 or Chapter 928 creating a tribal-member or tribal-land exception in Ohio was located in this run. (This states the absence of an Ohio exception; it does not address tribal law on that tribe's own land in its home state, which is out of scope.)

10.1.5 Tribal cannabis/hemp operations — none to list

Question Answer Basis
Federally recognised tribe in Ohio with a cannabis operation? No — no such tribe exists in Ohio. §10.1.2 (BIA list, Jan 2026).
State-recognised tribe in Ohio with a cannabis/hemp operation? No — no state-recognised tribe exists in Ohio. §10.1.3.
Tribal hemp plan covering Ohio land? No. §10.1.3 (no tribal government to submit a plan).
Tribal-state cannabis compact or agreement involving Ohio? None located. [UNAVAILABLE — no compact was found in ORC, DCC or Governor materials in this run; if one existed it would require a tribal counterparty that does not exist in Ohio.]
Tribal dispensary, cultivation or processing site in Ohio? None located; none can be licensed as "tribal" under Ohio law, which licenses persons/entities under ORC 3796.09–3796.21 without a tribal category. DCC licence framework (Run 1 Part 4). A business owned by a tribal member, licensed as an ordinary Ohio licensee, would be an Ohio licensee, not a tribal operation — no such tribal-member licensee was identified as such in this run, and licensee ownership by tribal membership is not a DCC licence category.

10.2 Interstate — hemp shipments

10.2.1 The federal transit rule (and its limit)

  • 2018 Farm Bill, §10114 (Pub. L. 115-334): (a) rule of construction — nothing in the Farm Bill title prohibits interstate commerce of hemp or hemp products; (b) "No State or Indian Tribe shall prohibit the transportation or shipment of hemp or hemp products produced in accordance with subtitle G of the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946 … through the State or the territory of the Indian Tribe, as applicable." Codified in the hemp definitions at 7 U.S.C. §1639o (definitions) and the programme at 7 U.S.C. §1639p.
  • Source for the text (secondary legal summary quoting the statute): https://legalclarity.org/is-hemp-legal-in-the-us-federal-and-state-rules/ and https://ritterspencer.com/hemp-and-cbd-lawyer-dallas-tx/ — accessed 29 Oct 2026. The statutory text itself is at 7 U.S.C. §§1639o–1639p; the Farm Bill section number (§10114) and the "produced in accordance with subtitle G" qualifier are the operative points and are adopted here.
  • The qualifier is the whole analysis for Ohio: 1. Transit vs delivery/sale: the federal rule bars a state from prohibiting transportation/shipment through the state of compliant hemp. It does not require a state to permit sale, possession for sale, or use in the state of a product the state lawfully regulates more stringently, and it does not protect a product that is not "hemp" under the applicable definition. 2. Ohio's definition is now stricter than the pre-Dec-2026 federal delta-9 definition, and aligned with the post-11-Dec-2026 federal total-THC definition: a product that is hemp under the old federal delta-9-only test but exceeds Ohio's total-THC (incl. THCA) ≤0.3% plant limit or Ohio's 0.4 mg/container final-product limit is not hemp in Ohio (ORC 928.01, SB 56). Such a product shipped into Ohio for sale, or held in Ohio for sale, is treated as marihuana in Ohio (ORC 928.01(J) → ORC 3719.01), not as protected hemp in transit. A product that is compliant hemp under both definitions and is merely passing through Ohio is within the federal transit protection on the statute's terms. 3. After 11 December 2026, the federal and Ohio thresholds converge (total THC + 0.4 mg/container), which narrows — but does not eliminate — the transit/sale distinction, because Ohio's channel consequence (over-threshold product may only be possessed as licensed dispensary/homegrown marijuana under Chapter 3796) is a state-law consequence that federal transit law alone does not impose.
  • Documentation practice (secondary, not Ohio law): shippers are advised in secondary guides to carry a manifest (origin/destination/quantity), the producer's licence, and a certificate of analysis showing compliant THC, because hemp and marijuana are indistinguishable by sight/smell at a roadside stop and seizure pending testing is a practical risk even for compliant loads. This is practice advice, not an Ohio statutory documentation requirement, and is labelled as such. Ohio's own hemp transport rule is ORC 928.04 (no transport in violation of ORC 928.03 rules) + ORC 928.03 transport/storage rulemaking — the current OAC 901:14 transport text after the SB 56/HB 96 changes was not opened line-by-line in this run [VERIFY — OAC 901:14-2 transport/storage rules, Part 7/11 follow-up].
  • Mail: USPS treats hemp as mailable only when compliant with federal/state/local law and USDA-approved plans (USPS Publication 52, §453, as summarised in secondary guides) — secondary only, and the federal baseline in this dossier does not include a USPS rule, so no USPS proposition is adopted as an Ohio rule here. [VERIFY — USPS Publication 52 current hemp section, if mail is to be covered in Part 11/12.]

10.2.2 Ohio hemp shipments — direction by direction

Ohio-grown hemp (USDA-licensed grower, from 2026) shipped out of Ohio Lawful as hemp if it meets the destination state's hemp definition and the federal definition in force at shipment; Ohio's own export is not separately licensed as "export" in Chapter 928 as read. The grower's USDA licence and test results are the compliance documents. ORC 928.02/928.04 (licence/transport framework); USDA DHPP (see §9.1.4); 7 U.S.C. §1639o transit rule (§10.2.1).
Hemp shipped through Ohio to another state Federal transit protection applies to hemp "produced in accordance with subtitle G" — Ohio may not prohibit mere through-shipment of such hemp on the statute's terms. Practical roadside risk (seizure pending testing) remains, per secondary practice guides. 7 U.S.C. §1639o / Farm Bill §10114(b) (§10.2.1).
Hemp shipped into Ohio for sale in Ohio Must meet Ohio's hemp definition (total THC incl. THCA ≤0.3% plant; final product ≤0.4 mg/container; no synthetic/non-naturally-producible or synthesised-outside-plant cannabinoids, ORC 928.01) and Ohio processing/sale rules. A product that fails Ohio's definition is marihuana in Ohio, even if it was hemp where it was made. No Ohio "import licence" for hemp products was located as a separate category. ORC 928.01 (SB 56) — Run 1 §1.5, confirmed in this run.

Ohio plaintiff-specific injunctions (Titan Logistics et al., §9.2) do not create a general import right — they bar enforcement against the named plaintiffs on the reporting. General import for retail sale outside a licensed dispensary has no lawful channel in the statute read. ORC 928.01; Run 1 §1.5; §9.2 litigation note.

10.3 Interstate — marijuana: who can buy in Ohio, and what can (and cannot) cross a state line

10.3.1 The governing Ohio rule — confirmed, not contradicted

ORC 3796.221(A) (SB 56) safe-harours an adult-use consumer who obtains adult-use marijuana from a licensed [Ohio] dispensary (plus homegrown marijuana under ORC 3796.04). Run 1's reading — lawful possession in Ohio is in practice limited to Ohio-dispensary or lawfully homegrown marijuana, and out-of-state purchases fall outside the safe harbour, with over-limit/out-of-channel possession falling back to ORC 2925.11 / 2925.03 via ORC 3796.99 — was confirmed, not contradicted, by the sources in this run:

  • LSC analysis paraphrase (via secondary legal analysis): "marijuana acquired elsewhere (like an out-of-state dispensary) cannot be legally possessed under the bill" — https://www.brianjsmithesq.com/blog/2025/12/12/ohios-new-marijuana-rules-under-sb-56-what-everyday-users-need-to-know — accessed 29 Oct 2026 (secondary summary of LSC analysis; the LSC analysis itself was not opened in this run — [VERIFY against the LSC SB 56 final analysis]).
  • Multiple Ohio practitioner/consumer guides agree: "Since March 20, 2026, it has been illegal in Ohio to have cannabis that was not bought at an Ohio store" (visitor guide, Oct 2026) — https://markets.financialcontent.com/stocks/article/marketersmedia-2026-10-25-alexis-420-publishes-a-50-state-guide-to-where-tourists-can-legally-buy-weed-ahead-of-holiday-travel — accessed 29 Oct 2026; "Out-of-state marijuana is contraband. Only cannabis from an Ohio-licensed dispensary or a legal home grow is lawful to possess" — https://www.briansmithlaw.com/ohio-recreational-marijuana-uses-and-penalties — accessed 29 Oct 2026.

Conflict flagged and rejected: one Michigan dispensary marketing page ("Visiting a Michigan Dispensary From Ohio", Pure Cannabis Outlet) states: "You can drive cannabis from Michigan into Ohio for personal use … The drive home? Totally normal" — https://shoppure.com/blog/🌿-what-to-know-when-visiting-a-michigan-dispensary-from-ohio — accessed 29 Oct 2026. This is rejected. It contradicts ORC 3796.221 as read in Run 1, the LSC paraphrase above, and every practitioner guide in this run; it is a retail marketing page, not a legal source, and it predates or ignores the SB 56 source restriction. Adopted position: Michigan-bought marijuana brought into Ohio is outside the Ohio safe harbour. Do not quote the marketing page as law.

10.3.2 Buying in Ohio as a non-Ohioan

Buyer Can they buy adult-use in Ohio? Can they buy medical in Ohio? What happens to the product at the state line?
Any adult 21+ with a valid government-issued photo ID, including a resident of KY, IN, WV, PA or MI (or any other state) Yes — Ohio's adult-use purchase rule (ORC 3796.20(C), SB 56) requires proof of 21+ by government ID and a daily purchase no greater than the possession amount; no Ohio-residency requirement for adult-use purchase was located in the statute read. Secondary visitor guides agree Ohio is among the states that "sell to any visitor 21 or older" with a valid ID from any state. No, on an out-of-state card. Ohio has no medical reciprocity: an out-of-state medical card does not register the holder as an Ohio patient/caregiver, does not give access to medical-only products or the medical excise-tax exemption, and does not substitute for an Ohio CTR + Ohio registration. The visitor's route to lawful purchase in Ohio is the adult-use route (21+), not the medical route. The product must stay in Ohio for lawful possession under Ohio law, and must not be carried into the buyer's home state unless that state's law independently permits it (see neighbour table). Federal law independently prohibits interstate transport of marijuana (Schedule I adult-use; Schedule III medical does not create an interstate-transport right for a consumer).
Ohio resident, 21+ Yes, from an Ohio licensed dispensary (or homegrown, ORC 3796.04). Yes, if registered as an Ohio patient/caregiver. Same: Ohio-bought product must stay in Ohio. Taking it to another state is an interstate-transport act governed by federal law and the destination state's law, not by Ohio law.
Ohio resident, under 21 (medical patient only) No adult-use purchase. Only as a registered Ohio patient (with caregiver/parent-guardian rules — Run 1 §1.4, minor-patient detail Verify). Out-of-state purchase does not cure an Ohio age bar. As above.
Non-Ohioan under 21 No. No (Ohio medical registration requires Ohio residency in practice — Run 1 §1.4 secondary guides state Ohio ID/residency for registration; the residency rule itself is [VERIFY against OAC 1301:18-10]). —

Sources for the visitor-purchase row (accessed 29 Oct 2026): ORC 3796.20(C) (Run 1 §1.1/§1.3); visitor guide, Oct 2026 — https://markets.financialcontent.com/stocks/article/marketersmedia-2026-10-25-alexis-420-publishes-a-50-state-guide-to-where-tourists-can-legally-buy-weed-ahead-of-holiday-travel ("23 states sell to any visitor 21 or older … Ohio"; "Since March 20, 2026, it has been illegal in Ohio to have cannabis that was not bought at an Ohio store, so visitors cannot bring any in"); Bloom guide — https://bloommarijuana.com/oh/learn/cannabis-laws ("Adults 21+ from any state can buy at a licensed Ohio dispensary with a valid government-issued photo ID. Visitors can't bring cannabis into Ohio from another state, and anything bought in Ohio must stay in Ohio"). The visitor guides are secondary; the statute (no residency bar for adult-use) is the primary basis, and the guides are consistent with it.

10.3.3 Neighbour-by-neighbour table (Ohio law + destination law in outline; destination-law detail is secondary and must be re-checked against that state's current code before advising a traveller)

Neighbour That state's position (outline, secondary — see note) Ohioan / visitor consequence
Michigan (north; border counties in Ohio: Lucas, Fulton, Williams) Adult-use and medical legal (Marijuana Herald 50-state table, 2026: Michigan Legal / Legal). Michigan adults 21+ may possess up to 2.5 oz in public / 10 oz at home, 15 g concentrates, 12 plants (Michigan MRTMA summaries). Michigan dispensaries sell to visitors 21+. But Michigan law does not legalise the interstate act: transporting cannabis across the Michigan–Ohio line is a federal offence on the secondary guides' uniform statement, and Michigan possession law alone does not authorise import into Ohio or export from Ohio. Ohio → Michigan: Ohio-bought product carried to Michigan is an interstate transport under federal law, even though possession in Michigan (within Michigan limits) would otherwise be lawful. Do not describe it as "legal because Michigan is legal." Michigan → Ohio: Michigan-bought product possessed in Ohio is outside ORC 3796.221 (see §10.3.1) — the SB 56 rule, not Michigan's price advantage, controls in Ohio. West Virginia → Ohio: a West Virginian 21+ may buy adult-use in Ohio; a WV medical card gives no Ohio medical right; WV product brought into Ohio is outside ORC 3796.221.

It is not an Ohio source and must not be quoted for Ohio law. Each neighbour's detailed visitor, possession and penalty rules must be checked against that state's current code before any traveller advice — this dossier's scope is Ohio law, and the neighbour column is context, not a neighbour-state dossier.

10.3.4 What can legally be taken across a state line — summary rules

  1. Marijuana (adult-use or medical, any amount): NO. There is no Ohio-law right to export marijuana, no federal consumer right to transport marijuana interstate, and no interstate compact or reciprocity agreement located that would create one. The fact that both states at either end have legalised possession does not legalise the transport between them. This applies Michigan↔Ohio as much as Ohio↔Indiana.
  2. Compliant hemp (both definitions met, in transit): YES, in transit — federal transit protection (§10.2.1), subject to documentation/practical seizure risk and to the destination state's sale/possession rules once the shipment stops being "in transit."
  3. Compliant hemp for sale in Ohio: only if it meets Ohio's definition (§10.2.2). A shipment that is hemp at origin but not hemp in Ohio is not protected as hemp in Ohio.
  4. Homegrown marijuana: NO interstate movement. Homegrown marijuana is lawful only as Ohio homegrown marijuana possessed in Ohio under ORC 3796.04/3796.221; taking it across a state line is the same interstate act as taking dispensary marijuana, with the same federal/destination-law consequences.
  5. No "personal-use exception" to the interstate ban was located in Ohio law, federal law as given in the baseline, or any Ohio agreement. Small amounts, medical need, and a valid card in the home state do not create one in the sources read. [VERIFY — if a federal medical-transport exception is ever asserted, it must be sourced to a federal statute/regulation, not to a state guide.]

Where a fact could only be read through a search-result excerpt or a secondary summary, it is labelled as such and flagged Verify; it is not presented as a verbatim quotation of current official text.
  • Sourcing rule applied: Laws are stated only from current official text where that text was opened. Secondary sources (news, law-firm blogs, industry pages, university news) are used only for non-law facts — market/intelligence counts, recall examples, programme descriptions, pending-bill status — and are labelled secondary with a publication/crawl date where known. Nothing in this file is legal advice.

  • Verify = the proposition could not be confirmed in current official text opened in this session; check the named source before republication.

Columbus in this file is Columbus, Franklin County, Ohio; Jackson is Jackson, Jackson County, Ohio; Athens is Athens, Athens County, Ohio; Wilberforce is in Greene County, Ohio; West Chester is in Butler County, Ohio; Streetsboro is in Portage County, Ohio; Piqua is in Miami County, Ohio; Zanesville is in Muskingum County, Ohio; Lorain is in Lorain County, Ohio; Findlay is in Hancock County, Ohio; Cincinnati is in Hamilton County, Ohio. Federal baseline — fixed, not re-researched

As fixed in the commission, and applied throughout Parts 11–12:

  • Split scheduling: State-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). All adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. The broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is not final.
  • 280E: Generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use activity remains fully subject to 26 U.S.C. § 280E.
  • Hemp dates: PL 119-37 § 781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 § 2019 limits it until 11 December 2026. After 11 December 2026 the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026. The federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026. There is no federal cannabis banking law.
  • Ohio application: Ohio has both medical and adult-use, and most licensees hold both. Schedule III and the 280E change apply to medical activity only; dual (medical and adult-use) licensees must split their activity for federal purposes; all adult-use activity remains Schedule I and fully subject to 280E. Ohio's own intoxicating-hemp rules (ORC Chapter 928 as rewritten by SB 56, effective 20 March 2026) already remove products over 0.4 mg total THC per container from the Ohio hemp definition from 20 March 2026 — ahead of the federal 11 December 2026 date — so Ohio licensees cannot wait for the federal date to treat such products as hemp. See Run 1 Part 1.5; this point is carried, not re-proved, here.
  • Guns: Federal 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) issues for marijuana users are explained in §12.7. Schedule III medical status alone does not resolve § 922(g)(3) on the evidence found; that point is flagged Verify against current ATF guidance and the Hemani opinion itself (see §12.7).

Run 1 baseline preserved unless primary evidence contradicts it

From the Run 1 commission and report (accessed 28 October 2026):

  • Possession: 2.5 oz plant material + 15 g extract, cumulative. Home grow: 6 plants per adult, 12 per residence. Public smoking/vaping: only on privately owned residential/agricultural property. See §11.3 and §12.4 for the statutory text.
  • Adult-use product limits: Edibles 10 mg/serving, 100 mg/package; beverages 10 mg/container (OAC 1301:18-4-06, effective 5 October 2026). Carried from Run 1; the rule was not re-opened in this session — Verify the current OAC 1301:18-4-06 text before republication.
  • State buffer: 500 ft (ORC 3796.30; OAC 1301:18-3-01). See §12.9.
  • Seed-to-sale database: Under ORC 3796.07; the vendor name Metrc is flagged Verify in Run 1 and remains Verify here — no Division of Cannabis Control (DCC) page naming Metrc as vendor was opened in this session (see Research Note R-9).
  • Employment: No protection; ORC 3796.28 preserves zero-tolerance and drug-testing. See §11.8.

That is an Ohio chapter definition, not federal law, and no Ohio conforming amendment to Schedule III was located in this session. Do not publish a claim that Ohio law now calls medical marijuana Schedule III.

PART 11 — OPERATIONS RULES

11.1 Testing: required tests, sampling, failed tests and recalls, licensed labs

11.1.1 Statutory basis

  • ORC 3796.21 (as rewritten by SB 56, effective 20 March 2026) provides that licensed laboratories test for potency, homogeneity and contamination and prepare a report of test results. Source: ORC Chapter 3796, https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/chapter-3796 — accessed 29 October 2026. The full ORC 3796.21 text was not re-opened in this session; the proposition above is carried from Run 1 — Verify the current section text before quoting it verbatim.
  • ORC 3796.09(C)(2) (Run 1): a cultivator/processor applicant must show that no owner, officer, board member, administrator, employee, agent or affiliate who may significantly influence or control it has an ownership/investment interest in, or a compensation arrangement with, a licensed laboratory or laboratory applicant. This is the statutory independence bar; the rule-level version is in §11.1.9. Source: ORC Chapter 3796 — accessed 29 October 2026 (carried from Run 1; Verify current text).

11.1.2 Codified laboratory rules directly opened

The following OAC Chapter 1301:18, division 7 rules were opened on codes.ohio.gov on 29 October 2026:

  • OAC 1301:18-7-01 — Testing laboratory certificate of operation, effective 20 December 2024. No laboratory activity until a certificate of operation issues; 12 months from provisional licence issuance to obtain the certificate; the certificate is valid only for the designated business entity, owners and licensed premises in the initial application under OAC 1301:18-2-02; on receipt, a laboratory may obtain cannabis from a licensed cultivator, processor or dispensary for testing only and conduct laboratory testing, research and development under division 1301:18. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-7-01 — accessed 29 October 2026.
  • OAC 1301:18-7-04 — Accreditation, effective 28 August 2025. ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation within two calendar years of provisional licence issuance, by a non-profit accreditation body that is a signatory to the ILAC Mutual Recognition Agreement and operates under ISO/IEC 17011; the accrediting agency must provide inspection/accreditation reports directly to DCC; tolling is by written petition with facts and a detailed plan/timeline, with a DCC stay order stating the lift date. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-7-04 — accessed 29 October 2026.
  • OAC 1301:18-7-05 — Proficiency testing, effective date shown in search results as 28 August 2025 / last updated 16 September 2025. DCC may require third-party proficiency testing; at least once every 24 months each laboratory must successfully participate for all test analytes in division 1301:18; the proficiency provider must be accredited to ISO/IEC 17043 and report directly to the laboratory and DCC with statistical evaluation; failure to report a required analyte counts as unacceptable; a failed laboratory must notify DCC in writing within 24 hours, repeat the failed proficiency testing within 30 calendar days unless otherwise authorised, and may be required to cease testing for those analytes after two consecutive failures or two out of three failures until DCC is satisfied nonconformances are corrected and will not recur; before certificate renewal, proficiency testing must include each matrix within the ISO accreditation scope; laboratories must not communicate with another laboratory about proficiency samples until after the submission deadline, nor refer or accept proficiency samples to or from another laboratory. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-7-05 — accessed 29 October 2026. Verify the effective date against the codified PDF before citing it as 28 August 2025.
  • OAC 1301:18-7-06 — Testing laboratory minimum security and surveillance. Content is security; it is summarised in §11.4.3. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-7-06 — accessed 29 October 2026.

11.1.4 Required test panels — Package 7 material and secondary summaries, NOT all confirmed in codified text

Flag the whole of this subsection Verify against the current codified division 1301:18 testing rules before republication. The panels below are as stated in DCC Package 7 material and secondary summaries:

Panel Analytes / measures stated
Microbial contaminants As specified in Package 7 / DCC standards; Salmonella and Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) are treated as immediate-destruction failures (see §11.1.7).
Mycotoxins As specified in Package 7 / DCC standards.
Moisture content; water activity Both required; failure may be remediable by further drying under the old protocol (see §11.1.7) — current remediation rule Verify.
Foreign matter contamination Required.
Heavy metals At minimum arsenic, cadmium, lead and mercury.
Pesticide and fertilizer residue Approved pesticides at numeric thresholds; unapproved pesticides at limit of detection (LOD) — see §11.1.5.
Cannabinoid potency At minimum delta-8-THC, delta-8-THCA, delta-9-THCA, delta-9-THC, CBD, CBN, CBDA, THC as defined in the rule, and any other cannabinoid determined by the department.
Voluntary in-process testing (Package 7 material) Residual solvents, pH and terpenes, in addition to the above. Voluntary testing is not a substitute for state-required testing.

11.1.6 Sampling — Package 7 / rule summaries; Package 7 status flagged

The following is from Package 7 material and rule summaries, not from codified text confirmed on codes.ohio.gov in this session. Flag Verify before quoting as rule text:

  • Prior to any transfer or sale, each licensee must submit all cannabis in final form to a licensed testing laboratory; all cannabis is subjected to all applicable test panels/analytes; all cannabis must meet or exceed DCC testing standards.
  • Prior to sample collection, the licensee submits a written request in the DCC-prescribed form/manner; the batch/lot must not exceed the allowable weight/size/amount under division 1301:18; the entire batch/lot is presented to the collector; if stored in multiple containers/trays, the sample must comprise increments from each container/tray as equally as possible; each sample must be statistically representative and documented in the state inventory tracking system contemporaneously with collection, with the amount recorded as provided by the collector, the batch/lot accurately recorded, and the certificate of analysis (CoA) uploaded for each batch/lot.
  • All test samples are collected at the originating licensee and transported solely by the test sample collector to the testing laboratory.
  • Under the OAC 1301:18-7-09 procedure material, the collector must review container identifying information against the originating licensee's information under OAC 1301:18-4-10; must not collect if a container/tray is unidentified, if batch/lot size or appearance appears inaccurate, if the licensee does not provide batch/lot size, or if batch/lot size exceeds the allowable weight/number under OAC 1301:18-1-01, 1301:18-4-13 and 1301:18-4-14; and must determine the minimum sample size/number of increments from Appendix A to division 1301:18.
  • Transfer manifests for test samples (OAC 1301:18-4-11 in Package 7 material) must include sending/receiving entity names and facility addresses, departure time and estimated arrival, and for each package: description of each test sample, total number of test samples, unique tracking-system identifying number, and units of measure (net weight or quantity of units). Source for Package 7 material: DCC Rule Package 7 PDF (above) — accessed 29 October 2026.

11.1.7 Failed tests, remediation and retesting — version conflict, do not resolve silently

Two incompatible versions are in the record. Do not quote the old protocol as current.

  • Old MMCP retesting protocol (Constant Contact PDF, undated in search results, pre-dates current rules): A cultivator/processor may request reanalysis of the same sample package within 10 days of the initial test; potency is not eligible for reanalysis unless total THC exceeds 35% for plant material or 70% for manufactured products accounting for the allowable range; on second failure, further drying for moisture/water activity failure, designation for hydrocarbon or carbon dioxide extraction for microbial failure (citing former OAC 3796:4-2-04(F)(1)), and immediate destruction for any other contaminant; on reanalysis pass, the licensee may request analysis by a second laboratory of a new sample within 7 days of the reanalysis, with notice to MMCP, and a second-laboratory pass clears the product. Source: secondary/legacy MMCP document via search — accessed 29 October 2026. Status: legacy; Verify against current rules before any use.
  • Package 7 material (current-rule direction, codified text not confirmed): Any cannabis failing standards for analytes in paragraphs (F) or (G) of that rule "shall adhere to all procedural requirements and shall not be re-tested by the testing laboratory"; any cannabis failing all state-required testing may be remediated and re-tested solely in accordance with paragraph (H). Paragraph (F), "Immediate Destruction Required," requires immediate destruction under OAC 1301:18-3-12 for failures including microbial contaminants, including Salmonella. The full (F)/(G) lists were not fully retrieved — Verify.
  • DCC guidance, "Testing Required Prior to Tech Solution" (secondary summary of DCC guidance): If Salmonella and/or STEC are detected, the cultivator shall not submit the batch to any technological solution or any other retesting/remediation and the failed batch must be immediately destroyed under OAC 1301:18-3-12; if both are negative, the technological solution may be used, with full compliance testing after the solution before any transfer/sale/distribution, and failure to comply may result in revocation of approval for the technology solution and/or further enforcement. Source: DCC guidance as summarised in search results — accessed 29 October 2026. Verify against the DCC guidance document itself.

11.1.8 Recalls

Rule directly opened — OAC 1301:18-9-04, effective 28 August 2025. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-9-04 — accessed 29 October 2026. Operative requirements:

  • Each licensee must establish, maintain and comply with written product alert/recall policies and procedures; designate a trained recall coordinator responsible for timely and accurate communication to DCC and for maintaining up-to-date recall-team contact lists; and include product name, unique product identification, description and batch/lot number; reports/complaints; inventory/sales review including inventory, transfers, dispensaries transferred to, and products sold; adequate quarantine steps; and notification templates. Policies must address alerts/recalls whether licensee- or DCC-initiated.
  • Immediately quarantine all affected product from viable inventory in a secure location.
  • Notify all associated licensees that cultivated, processed or dispensed the affected cannabis, all patients who have or likely have obtained it, and all customers who have or may have obtained it via conspicuous posting at each dispensary where sold.
  • Notice must include the business name and licence number of all licensed entities that received the product, product identity, description, net contents and batch/lot number, and, if applicable, that the customer must return the product within 30 calendar days of notice to receive a refund and revision of days' supply.
  • If a dispensary is directed to accept returns, it must accept unused affected product returned within 30 days (or within a more expansive policy under OAC 1301:18-8-12), refund contemporaneously, revise days' supply if applicable, and, unless otherwise authorised by DCC, destroy/dispose of returned cannabis under OAC 1301:18-3-12.

DCC recall authority — OAC 1301:18-9-05(A)(20)–(21), effective 28 August 2025. DCC may initiate or require a product advisory or recall when there is a reasonable probability cannabis violates Chapters 3780/3796, and may implement or mandate a recall when use or exposure constitutes a risk to public health or safety. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-9-05 — accessed 29 October 2026. (Note: the rule text still cites Chapter 3780, repealed by SB 56 — see C-7.)

11.2 Licence rules: transfers, ownership changes, renewals, caps, relocation, surrender/revocation, insurance and bonding

11.2.1 Licence types and ownership caps

  • The four licence types remain cultivator, processor, retail dispensary and testing laboratory (ORC 3796.02, as rewritten by SB 56). There is no separate consumption-lounge, research or smoke-shop licence in Chapter 3796 (see §§11.9, 12.4). Source: ORC Chapter 3796 — accessed 29 October 2026.
  • Ownership caps — adopt Run 1: ORC 3796.05(C): no person shall own or operate more than 8 licensed dispensaries, more than 1 licensed cultivator, or more than 1 licensed processor at any time. The older medical "5 dispensaries per owner" figure is superseded — do not repeat it as current. Plus the laboratory-specific bar in §11.1.9 (no more than 1 laboratory; no laboratory + any other cannabis entity; no shared officers/employees with another cannabis entity). Source: ORC Chapter 3796 — accessed 29 October 2026 (carried from Run 1; Verify current ORC 3796.05 text).
  • Dispensary cap: 400 (Run 1). 1-mile separation between dispensaries (see relocation, §11.2.5). Carried from Run 1.

11.2.2 Enforcement and discipline — statute (search-result text, Verify verbatim) and rule (directly opened)

  • ORC 3796.14 (Authority of Department of Commerce), effective 20 March 2026 (SB 56) — search-result text, flag direct open for the final report: DCC may, for any reason specified in rules under ORC 3796.03, suspend, suspend without prior hearing, revoke, or refuse to renew a licence issued under Chapter 3796 or a licence/registration issued by the State Board of Pharmacy before transfer; and refuse to issue. Summary suspension without prior hearing requires clear and convincing evidence of danger of immediate and serious harm; suspension remains unless lifted until a final adjudication order, and if DCC does not issue the order within 90 days after the adjudication hearing, suspension is lifted on the 91st day following the hearing. The 90/91-day passage was in search-result text only — Verify against the codified ORC 3796.14 text.
  • ORC 3796.15 (Enforcement), effective 20 March 2026 (SB 56) — search-result text: DCC and the Ohio Investigative Unit shall enforce Chapter 3796 or cause it to be enforced; subject to ORC 3796.14(E), if DCC or the Unit has information of a violation, it shall investigate and take any action it considers appropriate; if DCC suspends/revokes/refuses to renew and determines clear and convincing evidence of danger of immediate and serious harm, DCC may place under seal all medical/adult-use/homegrown marijuana owned by or in the possession, custody or control of the affected holder/registrant; except as provided, DCC shall not dispose of sealed marijuana until the holder/registrant exhausts all Chapter 119 appeal rights; the court in an appeal may order DCC, during pendency, to sell perishable marijuana and deposit proceeds with the court. Verify against codified text.
  • OAC 1301:18-9-05, effective 28 August 2025 — directly opened. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-9-05 — accessed 29 October 2026. DCC authority includes:
  • Inspection at any time with or without notice; inspection/examination/investigation of any premises or motor vehicle where cannabis is grown, stored, cultivated, harvested, transported, processed, extracted, manufactured, tested, distributed, transferred or dispensed, and related inventory, equipment, instruments and records; requests for information; obtaining samples of cannabis, grow media, chemicals/ingredients, labels/containers and raw packaged cannabis; investigating suspected prohibited activities.
  • Refusing to issue or renew provisional licences/certificates and provisional/badge certificates; suspending or revoking licences/registrations; suspending without prior hearing on clear and convincing evidence that continued distribution presents danger of immediate and serious harm; cease-and-desist orders; summonses/subpoenas including administrative subpoenas ad testificandum/duces tecum by personal service or certified mail return receipt requested, with ordinary-mail fallback rules; placing conditions on applicants/licensees/registrants; issuing guidance; ordering administrative holds to prevent destruction of evidence, diversion or threats to public safety; initiating/requiring/mandating product advisories/recalls; mandating destruction on violation; assessing investigation costs including travel and employee time.
  • Civil penalty not to exceed $50,000 for each violation. Sanctions are not mutually exclusive and may be combined. Adjudicatory hearings are under ORC Chapter 119.
  • Tax deficiency: On Taxation deficiency notice for failure to comply with all applicable taxes, DCC shall suspend without prior hearing; lift on notice of compliance; revoke if deficiencies are not alleviated within 30 calendar days of suspension.
  • On suspension/revocation/refusal to renew or clear and convincing danger of immediate and serious harm, DCC may seal all cannabis owned, possessed or controlled by the entity.
  • If a licence is voluntarily surrendered or not renewed, DCC may impose other penalties permitted by Chapter 3796/rules.
  • A suspended certificate holder shall not sell, offer for sale, transport, or conduct operations outside the facility related to cannabis; employees may enter for necessary care/maintenance of premises and cannabis/products; removal of cannabis from a cultivator/processor/testing laboratory is strictly prohibited during active suspension; during suspension, at DCC direction/discretion, the licensee may update the state inventory tracking system.
  • A revoked holder must adhere to OAC 1301:18-3-15, close the facility and prohibit entry except DCC employees, law enforcement, or persons carrying out official duties related to revocation; revocation of a provisional licence/certificate immediately terminates employee identification cards of that licensee's employees.
  • On revocation/suspension, DCC will notify local law enforcement and the county sheriff with jurisdiction.
  • DCC employees will not serve as expert witnesses in private litigation; DCC may move to quash subpoenas seeking fact testimony, but may certify licence/employee status, admissible as prima-facie evidence.

11.2.6 Relocation — rule directly opened

OAC 1301:18-3-02. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-3-02 — accessed 29 October 2026.

  • A licensee shall not change licensed premises location without prior DCC approval.
  • Application on a DCC-prescribed form evidencing: the proposed location (for dispensaries: same dispensary district as the existing location and, unless otherwise authorised by DCC, not within 1 mile of another licensed dispensary); plans/specifications; evidence the proposed location meets OAC 1301:18-5-02, 1301:18-6-02, 1301:18-7-02 and 1301:18-8-02; evidence of continued compliance with division 1301:18; supporting documentation; and the non-refundable change-of-location fee under OAC 1301:18-2-09.
  • DCC may approve, deny, or advise in writing that the applicant failed to meet requirements. On written approval, the licensee may construct/prepare the new location.
  • Once fully constructed/prepared, the licensee must submit a proposed transition plan for safe/secure transfer of all inventory/materials from the original location within 90 calendar days, confirmation of security/surveillance at both locations mitigating theft/loss/diversion, and assurance of ongoing compliance. DCC reviews the plan, advises modifications, and conducts a change-of-location inspection under OAC 1301:18-9-01.
  • Unless otherwise authorised, the licensee has 90 calendar days from passing the change-of-location inspection to transfer all inventory; no inventory may transfer before the approved transition period begins; any cannabis remaining at the original location past 90 days shall be destroyed under OAC 1301:18-3-12; the licensee must notify DCC once transfer is complete and business may commence at the new location; DCC may inspect both locations.
  • On verification of full compliance, DCC issues a modified certificate reflecting the new location with the same expiration date as the previous licence. The licensee shall not operate at the new location until DCC approves/issues the amended certificate, and shall not operate in two locations under the same certificate.
  • Note: The rule cites OAC 1301:18-7-02, which returned "Number Not Found" on codes.ohio.gov in this session — flag that cross-reference as Verify (see C-7).

11.3.1 Licensed canopy — statute

ORC 3796.18(E): Expansions on DCC approval so long as the total including expansions does not exceed the applicable maximum. A cultivator's actual authorised area is the area specified by DCC in its licence, up to the maximum — the statute does not grant every Level I holder 100,000 sq ft. Source: ORC Chapter 3796 — accessed 29 October 2026 (carried from Run 1; Verify current ORC 3796.18 text).

11.3.4 Home grow — statute directly opened

ORC 3796.04, effective 20 March 2026 (SB 56). Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.04 — accessed 29 October 2026. Verbatim operative provisions (paragraph (A)(1)):

"(A) Notwithstanding any conflicting provision of the Revised Code, an adult-use consumer may do all of the following: (1) Cultivate, grow, and possess homegrown marijuana plants at the adult-use consumer's primary residence, if all of the following apply: (a) Not more than six homegrown marijuana plants are cultivated or grown by each adult-use consumer; (b) Not more than twelve homegrown marijuana plants are cultivated or grown at a single residence; (c) Cultivation or growing of homegrown marijuana takes place only within a secured closet, room, greenhouse, or other enclosed area in or on the grounds of the residence that prevents access by individuals under twenty-one years of age, and which is not visible by normal unaided vision from a public space; (d) Cultivation or growing of homegrown marijuana does not take place at a residence that is any of the following: (i) A type A family child care home or type B family child care home, as those terms are defined in section 5104.01 of the Revised Code; (ii) A halfway house, community transitional housing facility, community residential center, or other similar facility licensed by the division of parole and community services under section 2967.14 of the Revised Code; (iii) A residential premises occupied pursuant to a rental agreement that prohibits the activities otherwise authorized by this section."

  • Also authorised at the primary residence: process homegrown marijuana by manual or mechanical means (not hydrocarbon extraction); store homegrown + adult-use marijuana at the primary residence; use homegrown grown/cultivated/processed at the primary residence; possess paraphernalia/accessories for administration of adult-use or homegrown marijuana.
  • Not authorised: Cultivate/grow/process except at the primary residence; any use/cultivation/processing/transfer/transport before age 21; hydrocarbon extraction; sale or profit; growing on behalf of another. Source: ORC 3796.04 — accessed 29 October 2026.
  • Penalty route (Run 1, flag carried forward): Knowing violation of ORC 3796.04(C) → illegal cultivation under ORC 2925.04 via ORC 3796.99(E). Run 1 flagged a secondary LSC-analysis claim that SB 56 lowered the criminal threshold versus Issue 2 (formerly criminal only at double the plant limit; now any excess) as Verify — carry that flag forward; do not resolve it here. Note also that a secondary home-grow guide's claim of a "3 flowering / 3 vegetative" split within the 6-plant limit was not found in ORC 3796.04 text opened and must not be stated as current law without a rule citation.

11.4 Security: cameras, alarms, storage, transport

11.4.1 General facility visitors

OAC 1301:18-3-11, effective 31 October 2024. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/chapter-1301:18-3 — accessed 29 October 2026. On entering licensed premises, every visitor must provide valid government-issued photographic ID evidencing 21+ years of age, obtain a visitor badge visibly displayed at all times and returned on departure, and be escorted/monitored by an assigned registered employee at all times; the licensee must maintain a visitor log with full legal name, arrival/departure date/time, assigned escort employee, and purpose of visit.

11.4.2 Cultivator security — rule directly opened

OAC 1301:18-5-05. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-5-05 — accessed 29 October 2026. Each cultivator shall establish, maintain and comply with written policies/procedures ensuring adequate security, surveillance and control preventing diversion, theft or loss and meeting the rule's minimum requirements. Prior to commencement of business, each cultivator shall: (1) designate a secure, limited-access area for all equipment maintained under the rule, accessible only by authorised registered cultivator employees with foundational training in security and surveillance; (2) maintain or construct fencing to prevent unauthorised entry or access to waste disposal containers, disposal areas or compost areas located outside the facility; (3) install a security alarm system with commercial-grade equipment including (a) an access alarm on all entry points and windows, (b) motion detectors identifying unauthorised access, and (c) a silent duress alarm sending a pre-recorded voice message to designated security personnel and law enforcement/public safety/emergency services requesting dispatch, including capability to enter a designated code at an arming station signalling the user is being forced to turn off the system; (4) install a video surveillance system capable of electronic monitoring and real-time DCC access, collecting 24-hour live video feed (remainder of the video specifications was truncated in the search excerpt — Verify the full OAC 1301:18-5-05 video paragraph, including frame rate, retention and monitor size, before quoting those figures for cultivators; do not copy the dispensary/laboratory figures in §11.4.3–11.4.4 across to cultivators). Pursuant to OAC 1301:18-5-02, each cultivator shall petition DCC prior to implementing any major modification to security procedures, systems or equipment.

OAC 1301:18-7-06 (Chapter 1301:18-7 page). Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-7-06 — accessed 29 October 2026. Written security/surveillance/control policies/procedures preventing diversion/theft/loss; petition DCC before any major modification to security procedures/systems/equipment under OAC 1301:18-7-02 (note: 7-02 returned "Number Not Found" — flag cross-reference); on notice of pending criminal/civil/administrative investigations or legal proceedings for which a recording may be relevant, retain an unaltered copy until the investigation/proceeding closes or the conducting entity notifies retention is no longer necessary.

OAC 1301:18-8-05 (search-result text, last crawl 33 days before 29 October 2026). Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-8-05 — accessed 29 October 2026. Verify the full rule before quoting verbatim. As stated in the excerpt: install a video surveillance system capable of electronic monitoring and real-time access by DCC; 24-hour live video feed with motion-activated recording for all cameras recording at at least 15 frames per second; archive/retain recordings at least 45 calendar days; display monitor minimum 19 inches; export still images in an industry-standard format guaranteeing authentication and preventing alteration; produce clear colour still photographs minimum 600 x 600 dpi from any camera image, live or recorded; embed date/time stamp on all recordings; include a failure notification system providing audible and visual notification of any failure; install unobstructed cameras preventing tampering, capturing the entirety of licensed premises, clearly identifying all individuals/activities in the surveilled area; camera placement at all points of ingress/egress, all secure limited-access areas, any area storing cannabis/facility inventory, the destruction/disposal area, all areas where sales proceeds are stored/transferred, and each point of sale; daily records of all registered employees' access to secure limited-access areas; emergency policies/procedures for securing inventory/currency on diversion/theft/loss; any other DCC-required security/surveillance/public-safety requirements. Each dispensary shall inspect/test all security/surveillance equipment at least once per month; record/maintain tests under OAC 1301:18-3-16; notify DCC of any failure; repair/replacement within 24 hours of identification.

11.4.5 Storage generally

  • Secure, limited-access storage areas accessible only by authorised registered employees (cultivator OAC 1301:18-5-06; dispensary/laboratory security rules above).
  • Cannabis intended for destruction separated from viable inventory and maintained in a secure location (OAC 1301:18-3-12(B) — see §11.5).
  • Recalled product quarantined from viable inventory in a secure location (OAC 1301:18-9-04(A)(4) — see §11.1.8).

11.4.6 Transport to another licensed entity — rule directly found

OAC 1301:18-3-13, last updated 20 December 2024. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-3-13 — accessed 29 October 2026.

  • Each licensee shall establish, maintain and comply with written transportation policies/procedures ensuring proper security protocols mitigating diversion/theft/loss and safety measures for emergency scenarios; real-time knowledge of the location of all motor vehicles while in transit; the originating licensee creates a transfer manifest in the state inventory tracking system and ensures all manifest information is transmitted to the recipient entity and DCC.
  • All individuals transporting cannabis shall be registered under OAC 1301:18-3-09 and issued a badge certificate; maintain/display their badge during transportation; ensure the vehicle is attended by at least one badged employee; ensure delivery times vary and routes are randomised; maintain a physical copy of the transfer manifest for the duration of transportation; notify the originating entity when delivery reaches the recipient and is completed; and report (i) any vehicle accident to a person designated by the transporting entity within 2 hours after the accident, (ii) any loss/theft during transportation under OAC 1301:18-9-02, and (iii) in an emergency, immediately notify law enforcement through 911 and the cannabis entities, which will immediately notify DCC, unless notification is impractical under the circumstances.
  • The vehicle shall be Ohio-registered and insured as required by law; store cannabis in a locked, safe, secure storage compartment affixed to the motor vehicle, or in a locked storage container with a separate key or combination pad; ensure product is not visible from outside the vehicle; have access to a secure form of communication with entity personnel and ability to contact law enforcement through 911 at all times the vehicle contains cannabis, unless impractical; and contain no marks/logos/brands/illustrations on the exterior other than those affixed by the vehicle manufacturer/dealership.
  • Consumer transport is different and must not be conflated: ORC 3796.062 (original unopened packaging or trunk/behind-last-seat) and ORC 3796.06(H) (edibles in original packaging when not actively in use) govern consumers (Run 1). Licence transport is OAC 1301:18-3-13; consumer transport is ORC 3796.062/3796.06(H).

11.5 Waste disposal

OAC 1301:18-3-12, effective 31 October 2024 (Chapter 1301:18-3 page text). Sources: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/chapter-1301:18-3 and https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-3-12 — accessed 29 October 2026.

  • (A) All licensees shall destroy/dispose of all excess, unwanted, outdated, deteriorated, adulterated or misbranded cannabis under video surveillance and in a manner rendering it unusable and non-retrievable.
  • (B) All cannabis intended for destruction shall be weighed and recorded into the state inventory tracking system, separated from other viable inventory intended for distribution, and maintained in a secure location.
  • (C) Cannabis intended for disposal shall be weighed and recorded into the statewide inventory tracking system.
  • (D) Cannabis shall be rendered unusable/non-retrievable by grinding and incorporating the waste with one or more of: paper waste; cardboard waste; food waste; yard or garden waste; grease or other compostable oil waste; bokashi or other compost activators; or any other waste approved by DCC, such that the resulting mixture is at least 51% non-cannabis waste.
  • (E) Destruction/disposal shall be conducted in a secure, limited-access area that is surveilled and accessible only to registered employees.
  • (F) Licensees shall maintain records of all destruction/disposal under OAC 1301:18-3-14, memorialising for each occurrence: manner of destruction; rationale for destruction; date and time of disposal; (item (4) was omitted in the search-result excerpt — flag the full (F) list as Verify); volume or weight of associated waste; and, if applicable, further item(s) truncated in the excerpt.
  • Related destruction duties: Failed batches requiring immediate destruction (§11.1.7); recalled product returned to a dispensary destroyed/disposed of under OAC 1301:18-3-12 unless otherwise authorised by DCC (OAC 1301:18-9-04(A)(7)(e)); cannabis remaining at an original location past the 90-day relocation transition destroyed under OAC 1301:18-3-12 (OAC 1301:18-3-02(E)(2)); sealed cannabis on suspension/revocation not disposed of until Chapter 119 appeal rights are exhausted, except a court may order sale of perishable marijuana during appeal with proceeds deposited with the court (ORC 3796.15 search-result text — flag direct verification).
  • No separate cannabis-waste hauler licence or landfill/composting destination rule was located in this session — Unavailable. Do not claim rendered waste may go to any particular municipal waste stream without a DCC/Ohio EPA source.

11.6 Environmental: water, pesticide limits, energy

11.6.1 Pesticides — approved-list system (secondary + DCC pages; full current list Verify)

  • Secondary analysis (Cannabis Business Times, publication date in search results as 147 days before 29 October 2026): Ohio requires cultivators to use pesticides from an approved list; Ohio approves pesticides that are (1) already registered with the Ohio Department of Agriculture and (2) registered with the U.S. EPA or exempt from registration under the minimum-risk exception; even minimum-risk pesticides must be approved by DCC before use to cultivate medical or adult-use marijuana; Ohio prohibits application of pesticides after a specified point in the flowering stage (the secondary summary does not give the day in the excerpt — the DCC list itself shows a column "AFTER 21ST DAY OF FLOWERING" with APPROVED / NOT APPROVED entries). Source: secondary analysis — accessed 29 October 2026. Verify against the current DCC list.
  • A September 2025 DCC list copy hosted by a dispensary (https://roamdispensary.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/5/DCC_Approved%2BPesticides%2Bfor%2BUse%2Bin%2Bthe%2BCultivation%2Bof%2BMedical%2BMarijuana.pdf — accessed 29 October 2026) shows, in the excerpt, e.g. Oxiphos as APPROVED and Organocide Bee Safe 3-in-1, Anatis Bioceres WP, Azasol, Eco-1 40, Athena IPM, Serenade Garden, AzaGuard, GreenClean and Oxidate 2.0 as NOT APPROVED after the 21st day of flowering. Do not reproduce the full product list from a dispensary-hosted copy as the current DCC list; the current DCC-approved list must be opened on a DCC page and dated in the final report.
  • Pesticide residue testing: see §11.1.5 (approved pesticides at numeric thresholds; unapproved at LOD). The old rule citation OAC 3796:4-2-04(I) on the DCC thresholds page must be updated/verified to the current division 1301:18 citation.
  • Facility pest control — OAC 1301:18-4-01 (search-result text, last crawl 32 days before 29 October 2026). Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-4-01 — accessed 29 October 2026. Verify full text. Pests are not allowed in any area of a cannabis facility; guard/guide/pest-detecting dogs may be allowed in some areas if presence is unlikely to result in contamination of cannabis/contact surfaces/packaging; effective measures must exclude pests from cultivation/production/manufacturing/processing/testing/packing/holding areas and protect against contamination by pests; pesticide use to control pests in the facility is permitted only under precautions/restrictions protecting against contamination of cannabis, cannabis-contact surfaces and cannabis-packaging materials. Also from the same rule excerpt: only toxic materials necessary for clean/sanitary conditions, facility operations, laboratory testing, or facility/equipment maintenance/operation may be used/stored where cannabis is processed/exposed; toxic cleaning compounds, sanitising agents and pesticide chemicals must be identified/held/stored protecting against contamination; processors must use food-safe sanitisers for utensils/contact surfaces.
  • Processor ingredient bans — Run 1 secondary only, flag Verify: OAC 1301:18-6-07 bans nicotine, melatonin, alcoholic beverages, dietary supplements and vitamins in cannabis products; caffeine only in narrow approved cases; bars MCT oil, squalene, squalane, vitamin E acetate and propylene glycol from smoked/vaped products; DCC fiscal analysis for OAC 1301:18-6-07 states hemp-derived ingredients must be tested by a DCC-licensed laboratory or another accredited laboratory, at an average testing cost of $380 per sample (Register of Ohio RSFA, 21 July 2026 filing). Do not quote the ingredient bans as rule text until OAC 1301:18-6-07 is opened directly.

11.6.4 Hemp cannabinoid lists — cross-reference to Part 7

  • ORC 928.031, effective 20 March 2026 (SB 56), requires the Superintendent of Cannabis Control, in consultation with the Director of Agriculture, to establish lists of (1) cannabinoids capable of being naturally produced by Cannabis sativa L., (2) THC-class cannabinoids naturally occurring in the plant, (3) all other known cannabinoids with similar effects to, or marketed to have similar effects to, THC-class cannabinoids, and (4) any additional cannabinoids with similar/marketed-similar effects on humans/animals; plus additional specificity about "container" under ORC 928.01; federal additions/changes/removals are automatically effected subject to superintendent amendment under ORC 928.031(D) and immediate publication of an updated list.
