11.7 Sampling, giveaways, discounts, promotions

11.7.1 Consumer sampling and giveaways — what the rules do and do not say

  • Test samples are laboratory samples, not consumer samples. Test samples in division 1301:18 are collected by a test sample collector and transported solely to a testing laboratory (see §11.1.6). They are not consumer samples.
  • Dispensary free samples — prohibition in the former rulebook, current-rule status Verify: Former OAC 3796:6-3-01(E) (still visible on codes.ohio.gov as a legacy division) states: "No person at a dispensary shall provide free medical marijuana samples or engage in compounding as defined under section 4729.01 of the Revised Code." Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-3796:6-3-01 — accessed 29 October 2026. Flag: This is the former Board of Pharmacy division (3796:6), not current division 1301:18. The DCC Package 7 definitions document likewise states: "No person at a dispensary shall provide cannabis samples or engage in compounding as defined under section 4729.01 of the Revised Code." Source: DCC Rule Package 7, https://dam.assets.ohio.gov/image/upload/com.ohio.gov/DCC/Guidance/Rules/Package%207/DCC_Rule_Package_7_-_All.pdf — accessed 29 October 2026. Verify the current codified division 1301:18 dispensary rule before stating the prohibition as current law.
  • Smell jars — legacy provision, do not state as current without verification: Former OAC 3796:2-2-02(E) (legacy division) provided that a cultivator may provide a dispensary free samples of plant material sold at the dispensary, packaged in a sample jar protected by a plastic or metal mesh screen to allow patients/caregivers to smell the plant material before purchase; a sample jar may not contain more than three grams of a particular strain; the sample jar and plant material within may not be sold and shall be destroyed by the dispensary after use, with destruction documented under Chapter 3796 rules. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-3796:2-2-02 — accessed 29 October 2026. This is legacy text. Whether a smell-jar provision survives in current division 1301:18 was not confirmed in this session — Verify; do not present smell jars as a current consumer right.
  • Bottom line for this subsection: No rule authorising free consumer samples, "tasting" or giveaways of cannabis to consumers was located in current division 1301:18 in this session. State this as Unavailable/Verify, not as "samples are allowed" or "samples are banned" without a current rule citation. A dispensary may sell paraphernalia (ORC 3796.20(A)(1)(d)) and may offer discounts under OAC 1301:18-8-11 (§11.7.3), but neither provision authorises giving cannabis away.

11.7.2 Promotions — prohibited; advertising — prior approval and placement bans

OAC 1301:18-4-22, effective 5 October 2026; statutory authority ORC 3796.03 and 3796.32; five-year review 15 January 2031 (RSFA, 24 August 2026 filing). Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/assets/laws/administrative-code/authenticated/1301/18/4/1301$18-4-22_20261005.pdf — accessed 29 October 2026.

  • Promotions prohibited — OAC 1301:18-4-22(F): "Promotion" means a drawing, contest, raffle, game, or other similar activity granting a person the chance to win a gift, prize, or item from a licensee; the use of promotions is prohibited.
  • Prior approval: All advertising must be submitted by each licensee for DCC review and written approval before use. Run 1 flagged the tension with ORC 3796.32(G) deemed approval for names/logos/signs/materials within 21 business days — carry that flag; do not resolve it without DCC guidance.
  • Content bans (rule excerpt): Advertisements must not be false/misleading; obscene/indecent; attractive to children; including an image/text referencing/resembling a cartoon/fictional/pop-culture icon whose target audience is children/youth; encouraging consumption leading to excessive use/intoxication/overconsumption or in combination/conjunction with other intoxicants/illegal substances or in an unauthorised method; containing a depiction of cannabis consumption/administration; departing from the registered cannabis name including slang/similar references; disparaging to a competitor's products; containing a health-related statement; suggesting DCC/State of Ohio or any person/entity endorsement/approval without consent; violating Ohio/federal trademark/copyright law; or otherwise violating Chapters 3780/3796 or their rules.
  • Placement bans (rule excerpt): On a billboard; on radio/television broadcast or internet programming; left on private property without the property owner's consent; on/in a public transit vehicle or public transit shelter; on/in a stadium or arena; on/in publicly owned/operated property; at any scheduled event including conferences/trade shows/similar events the licensee plans to attend/participate in/sponsor, educational or otherwise, unless the licensee provides written notification to DCC of intent to attend at least 10 business days before the event; plus an earlier excerpt line covering placement in a location not restricted to persons 21+ or any location where placement targets or is attractive to children, as determined by DCC, excluding signage on the licensee's facility.
  • Merchandise/paraphernalia: No licensee shall market/distribute/offer/sell/license, or cause to be marketed/distributed/offered/sold/licensed, any merchandise related to a licensed entity, cannabis, or cannabis paraphernalia to an individual under 21; and no licensee shall market/distribute/offer/sell/license any cannabis paraphernalia to a patient under 18 or to an individual under 21.
  • Universal THC symbol: Each licensee must ensure the symbol, as prescribed by DCC and outlined in OAC 1301:18-4-04(C), appears on any advertisement that is on, or is a depiction of, any item required to contain the symbol under OAC 1301:18-4-04 and 1301:18-6-06, and on any advertisement on/depicting any other medium capable of storing cannabis, accurately depicting the symbol and DCC seal in the precise location/display as on the respective item.
  • Website/web presence: OAC 1301:18-4-22(H) begins "A licensee may develop a website or otherwise establish a web presence advertising…" — the remainder was truncated in search results; flag the full (H) text (including any age-affirmation requirement) as Verify before quoting it.

11.7.3 Discounts — rule directly opened

OAC 1301:18-8-11, effective 28 August 2025. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-8-11 — accessed 29 October 2026.

  • A dispensary may offer discounts only under written discount policies/procedures ensuring, among other things: any discount offered to all patients registered as indigent or veteran (paragraph (A)(1)(a) in the rule as opened — the opening excerpt truncates the exact indigent/veteran discount formulation, so quote the operative parity rules carefully); any discount offered to an adult-use consumer is also offered to all registered patients and caregivers; for a patient who is also a registered employee of a licensed entity, the discount requires presentation of the employee identification card in addition to identification required under OAC 1301:18-10-01 and must not exceed the discount offered under paragraph (A)(1)(a); any discount offered to a veteran must not exceed the discount offered under paragraph (A)(1)(a).
  • Dispensary employees shall not receive rebates or discounts on cannabis offered by a cultivator, processor, or third-party entity.
  • Receipts must show a complete description of any discounts applied (OAC 1301:18-8-08(A)(7)(f) for adult-use; OAC 1301:18-8-09(H)(6) for medical).

11.7.4 Returns and dispensing errors — cited, not opened

  • OAC 1301:18-8-12 (Dispensary Returns) is cited in OAC 1301:18-9-04(A)(7)(b) for a more expansive return policy, and listed in the JCARR agenda, but its full text was not opened in this session — Verify. Recall returns are governed by OAC 1301:18-9-04(A)(7) (§11.1.8): 30 days, contemporaneous refund, days'-supply revision.
  • OAC 1301:18-8-10 (Dispensing Errors) is listed in the JCARR agenda; its text was not opened — Verify; do not invent an error-correction procedure.

11.8 Drug testing and background checks for licence holders and employees

11.8.1 General employment — statute (Run 1, SB 56)

ORC 3796.28, effective 20 March 2026 (SB 56). Source: ORC Chapter 3796 — accessed 29 October 2026 (carried from Run 1; Verify current text). Nothing in Chapter 3796 requires an employer to permit/accommodate use/possession/distribution; prohibits nothing in refusing to hire, discharging, disciplining or taking adverse action for use/possession/distribution; does not prohibit drug-testing, drug-free-workplace or zero-tolerance policies; does not interfere with federal employment restrictions including U.S. DOT Title 49 CFR; does not permit a cause of action against an employer for such action; does not affect workers' compensation drug-free-workplace premium rebates/discounts under ORC Chapter 4123. Discharge for use in violation of a drug-free-workplace/zero-tolerance/formal marijuana policy is discharge for just cause for ORC 4141.29(D) unemployment purposes and ineligibility for waiting period/benefits for the duration described in ORC 4141.29(D)(2). Such action is not a violation of ORC 4112.02(A)/(D)/(E) if for use in violation of such a policy.

11.8.2 Licence-applicant and employee background checks — statute (search-result text / Run 1 summary, Verify)

  • ORC 3796.12 — search-result text, flag direct open: As part of the licence application, DCC shall require a criminal records check for each administrator/other person responsible for daily operation, owner/prospective owner, officer/prospective officer, and board member/prospective board member, via the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation (BCI) and, where 5-year Ohio residency proof is not shown, the FBI; DCC must deny a licence if a subject person fails to complete/forward the check or instruct BCI to submit the report to DCC. ORC 3796.12 uses the ORC 109.572 meaning of "criminal records check." Source: ORC Chapter 3796 — accessed 29 October 2026.
  • ORC 3796.13 — Run 1 summary, flag direct text: Each person seeking employment with a licensed entity shall comply with ORC 4776.01–4776.04; except as provided in ORC 3796.13(B), the entity shall not employ the person unless the person has submitted a criminal records check under those sections and the report demonstrates the person has not been convicted of or pleaded guilty to a disqualifying offence; provisional employment regime (max 3 months, renewable once for 3 months) for exigent circumstances under ORC 3796.13(B) as summarised in Run 1 — flag the exact (B) conditions as Verify.

11.8.3 Employee badges — rule directly found

OAC 1301:18-3-09. Sources: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-3-09 and Cornell LII mirror — accessed 29 October 2026.

  • (A) Each licensee shall ensure all of the following obtain an employee badge from DCC before commencement of business: any administrator/individual responsible for daily operation; all owners, officers and board members; and all employees/agents.
  • Designations: Responsible party — at least 1 but not more than 3 individuals designated before issuance/renewal of a certificate; manages daily operations and ensures compliance with standard operating procedures; physically present at licensed premises at least 20 hours per week and immediately available to communicate with facility staff or DCC during operating hours when not physically present. Owner or officer — any/all owners, officers, board members. Employee — all other employees/agents.
  • (B) Before petitioning DCC for a badge, each licensee shall complete a thorough background evaluation confirming the applicant does not have a disqualifying offence as defined by OAC 1301:18-1-01, and submit a receipt/transaction number confirming the applicant submitted to Ohio BCI, as required by ORC 3780.08 and 3796.12 (note: the rule text still cites former Chapter 3780 — flag the post-SB 56 citation update as Verify), a complete/accurate application for an Ohio BCI records check and a federal FBI records check, two fingerprint impressions, and clearly indicated both checks be sent directly to DCC.
  • (C) Badge application, submitted by the licensee on the applicant's behalf on a DCC-prescribed form, evidencing: full legal name; intended employee designation; telephone number usable during normal business hours; email address; mailing address (all in working order and readily available for voice/electronic communication); fingerprint submission to BCI for Ohio + federal checks; no disqualifying offence under OAC 1301:18-1-01; copy of valid, unexpired government-issued photographic ID evidencing at least 21 years of age; clear, recognisable headshot captured within the past 6 months; business name and licence number for each associated cultivator/processor/testing laboratory/dispensary where employment is sought; individuals resident in Ohio continuously for the past 5 years may apply for expedited renewal if the applicant consents to enrolment in the Ohio Attorney General's Retained Applicant Fingerprint Database ("Rapback") — the excerpt truncated at that point; flag the full (C) remainder and renewal terms as Verify.
  • Badge fees: $100 initial and $100 renewal for each designation under OAC 1301:18-2-09(A)(4), effective 8 October 2026 — this resolves Run 1's badge-fee flag in favour of $100 surviving (see C-2).
  • Provisional badges — secondary, flag Verify: Package 5 stakeholder summary (2024) states a provisional employee badge valid for 90 days, available on submission of a complete/accurate application, attestations of no disqualifying offences, and evidence of BCI + FBI fingerprint submission, with the facility responsible for the thorough background evaluation; and that an employee may maintain one badge for each licence in a family of companies rather than a badge per individual licence. The current codified provisional-badge paragraph was not confirmed in the truncated OAC 1301:18-3-09 excerpt — Verify.
  • Badge revocation preclusion — excerpt, flag rule paragraph: A search-result excerpt (Register of Ohio compilation, rule action 644057) states: "An individual whose employee badge was revoked, and any individual whose actions directly caused a license entity's license revocation, is precluded from applying for an employee identification for at least five years from the date of revocation or final judicial decision upon an order of revocation." Flag the exact rule number/paragraph as Verify; do not cite it as OAC 1301:18-3-09 without confirmation.

11.8.4 Employee drug testing — gap, do not invent

  • No rule in division 1301:18 located in this session imposes a routine drug test on licence employees as a condition of badging. The applicable drug-testing authority for employers generally is ORC 3796.28 (§11.8.1) and, for safety-sensitive/DOT roles, federal DOT rules. Flag any claim of a DCC-mandated employee drug test as Unavailable on the evidence found.

11.8.5 Employee training and records

  • OAC 1301:18-3-10 (Employee Training and Qualification Requirements) — rule summary, flag full text: Each licensee shall establish/oversee an employee training programme. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/chapter-1301:18-3 — accessed 29 October 2026.
  • OAC 1301:18-3-14(A)–(B) — records (Chapter 1301:18-3 search text): Maintain all books/records/policies/procedures/documentation evidencing daily operations/business transactions at licensed premises, in auditable format, immediately available for DCC inspection/duplication, with electronic storage safeguards (confidentiality, anti-erasure/unauthorised-change safeguards, administrative hold capability, reconstructability); retain for the current calendar year and preceding calendar year, including standard operating procedures, cleaning/sanitisation procedures, waste disposal records, inventory records, security/surveillance records, production records, packaging/labelling records, and records of all test samples sent to a licensed testing laboratory (list truncated in search results — flag the full (B) list). OAC 1301:18-3-14(D) requires documenting all training with names/qualifications of the person responsible for training content, a set of training materials provided to each participant, and date(s) of training.

11.9 Research and university cannabis/hemp licences

11.9.1 No DCC research licence

  • ORC 3796.032, effective 20 March 2026 (SB 56), is a carve-out, not a licence type. Chapter 3796 does not authorise DCC to oversee or limit research at a state university, academic medical center, or private research and development organisation approved by a listed federal agency/body. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/assets/laws/revised-code/authenticated/37/3796/3796.032/3-20-2026/3796.032-3-20-2026.pdf — accessed 29 October 2026. The four licence types remain cultivator, processor, retail dispensary and testing laboratory (ORC 3796.02). A testing laboratory's certificate under OAC 1301:18-7-01(D)(2) includes "laboratory testing, research, and development" in accordance with division 1301:18 — that is laboratory R&D within a testing licence, not a university research licence.
  • IRB-approved research exemptions in Chapter 3796 (Run 1 + search results): ORC 3796.24(H)(6) (chapter does not restrict IRB-approved research at a state university, academic medical center, or private R&D organisation); ORC 3796.29 (localities may not prohibit/limit IRB-approved research); ORC 3796.30(B) (500-ft buffer does not apply to IRB-approved research). Also OAC 1301:18-3-01 (Run 1): the 500-ft rule does not apply to entities already holding a certificate for the same premises, nor to IRB-approved university/medical-centre/private R&D research. Sources: ORC 3796.24, https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.24 — accessed 29 October 2026; ORC Chapter 3796 — accessed 29 October 2026.

11.9.2 Central State University, Wilberforce, Greene County, Ohio — secondary, dated

  • Farm Progress article (undated in search results, crawl 4 days before 29 October 2026) describes Central State University launching a hemp research initiative led by Craig Schluttenhofer (from University of Kentucky, hemp research since 2014), focusing on hemp for grain, reducing yield losses from shattering, germplasm adapted to Ohio growing conditions, how cannabis plants regulate compounds, fibre uses, and CBD production. Source: secondary — accessed 29 October 2026.
  • Central State University Combined Research and Extension Plan of Work 2022–2026 (NIFA portal PDF) states CSU will conduct research/extension on plant systems including alternative crops, with hemp defined as Cannabis sativa with THC content less than 0.3%, plus amaranth, sweet potato, high-amylose corn, tree fruit/nut crops, medicinal plants and hops; ARDP (Agricultural Research and Development Program) proposes advanced technologies, IPM/pesticide use, and small/medium farm assistance. Source: secondary (NIFA portal PDF) — accessed 29 October 2026.

PART 12 — CONSUMER AND SOCIAL RULES

12.1 Paraphernalia and smoke shops

12.1.1 Licensed-dispensary paraphernalia sales — statute (Run 1)

  • ORC 3796.20(A)(1)(d) allows a licensed dispensary to sell paraphernalia that may be used in administration of adult-use/medical marijuana as specified in rules under ORC 3796.03. Adult-use consumers may possess paraphernalia under ORC 3796.221 (Run 1 §1.1 table). Source: ORC Chapter 3796 — accessed 29 October 2026 (carried from Run 1; Verify current ORC 3796.20 text).
  • Dispensary advertising of paraphernalia: OAC 1301:18-4-22(D)–(E) (§11.7.2) — no merchandise/paraphernalia marketing to under-21; no paraphernalia marketing to a patient under 18 or individual under 21. Source: OAC 1301:18-4-22 PDF (above) — accessed 29 October 2026.

12.1.2 General paraphernalia offences — ORC 2925.14 / 2925.141 (secondary summaries with statute citations; Verify direct text for penalty bands)

Provision Offence as summarised Penalty as summarised
ORC 2925.14(C)(1) Knowingly use, or possess with purpose to use, drug paraphernalia Fourth-degree misdemeanor, up to 30 days' jail and/or up to $250 fine
ORC 2925.14(C)(2) Knowingly sell, or possess/manufacture with purpose to sell, drug paraphernalia, if the person knows or reasonably should know it will be used as drug paraphernalia Second-degree misdemeanor, up to 90 days and/or up to $750; if the offender also sold drug paraphernalia to juveniles, first-degree misdemeanor, up to 180 days and/or up to $1,000
ORC 2925.14(C)(3) Placing an advertisement in a newspaper/magazine/handbill/other publication published/printed and circulating primarily in Ohio, knowing its purpose is to promote illegal sale in Ohio of equipment/product/material intended/designed for use as drug paraphernalia Second-degree misdemeanor
ORC 2925.141 Knowingly use, or possess with purpose to use, drug paraphernalia that is equipment/product/material used/intended/designed for storing/containing/concealing/injecting/ingesting/inhaling/otherwise introducing marijuana ("marihuana" in state law) into the body Minor misdemeanor, up to $100 fine

Sources: secondary summaries — Dayton lawyer summary (crawl 148 days before 29 October 2026) and NORML Ohio penalties page (sale offence as misdemeanor up to 90 days/$750, consistent on the base offence) — accessed 29 October 2026. Flag direct ORC 2925.14 / 2925.141 text as Verify, including whether ORC 2925.141 is limited to marijuana paraphernalia versus all drug paraphernalia, and the full penalty bands.

  • ORC 2925.14 factors for determining paraphernalia status (secondary summary listing statute factors): oral/written instructions concerning use; descriptive material accompanying the item explaining/depicting use; national/local advertising concerning use; manner/circumstances of display for sale; direct/circumstantial evidence of ratio of sales of the item to total business sales; existence/scope of legitimate uses in the community; expert testimony concerning use. Source: secondary summary — accessed 29 October 2026. Verify against ORC 2925.14 text.
  • A separate secondary summary (Find US Lawyers, crawl 246 days before 29 October 2026) adds that a paraphernalia conviction can trigger a CDL suspension of at least 6 months up to 5 years and professional-licence consequences — flag as secondary; do not quote as statute without ORC 2925.14 / 4506 verification.

12.1.3 Smoke shops — no statewide smoke-shop licence located

  • No Ohio statute/rule creating a "smoke shop licence" was located in this session. General retail sale of pipes/bongs/rolling papers etc. remains subject to the ORC 2925.14 intent test above.
  • Secondary LegalClarity summary (crawl 5 days before 29 October 2026) states a glass pipe in a smoke-shop display case is a legal retail product, but the same pipe with residue in a car with a baggie of powder becomes paraphernalia; retailers often label products "for tobacco use only," but that label is not a legal shield if surrounding evidence suggests drug-related intent; combinations (e.g. digital scale + small baggies + cutting agent) strengthen a prosecution case. Source: secondary — accessed 29 October 2026. Treat these as secondary illustrations of the intent test, not as statutory safe harbours.
  • Local zoning/business-licence requirements for smoke shops are outside the evidence gathered — flag as Unavailable/local, not statewide.

12.2 THC driving limits and impairment testing — CORRECTION: Ohio DOES have per se limits

12.2.1 The correction

The assignment asked to "confirm Ohio has no per se THC limit or cite one if it exists." Ohio does have per se THC limits. This section states them plainly and must not be summarised as "no per se limit."

12.2.2 Per se limits — ORC 4511.19(A)(1)(j) (multiple secondary summaries converging; Verify verbatim text)

What is measured Urine Whole blood, blood serum or plasma
Marijuana (THC) At least 10 ng/mL At least 2 ng/mL
Marijuana metabolite, standalone At least 35 ng/mL At least 50 ng/mL
Marijuana metabolite, when the offender is under the influence of alcohol or a drug of abuse, as measured by gas chromatography mass spectrometry At least 15 ng/mL At least 5 ng/mL

Sources: Brian Smith Law, https://www.briansmithlaw.com/ohio-marijuana-thc-ovi — accessed 29 October 2026 (citing ORC 4511.19(A)(1)(j)(vii)–(viii)); Strauss Troy, https://www.strausstroy.com/articles/proposed-ohio-legislation-could-change-how-marijuana-impairment-is-evaluated-in-ovi-cases — accessed 29 October 2026; Yonas & Phillabaum and Dearie Fischer & Martinson summaries — accessed 29 October 2026. Before republication, open ORC 4511.19 directly on codes.ohio.gov and quote (A)(1)(a), (A)(1)(j)(vii)–(viii) and (K) verbatim, with last-amended date — that direct open was not completed in this session and is the single most important remaining verification for Part 12.

  • A result at or above a limit can support a per se charge whether or not actual impairment is proven at the time of driving. Metabolites, especially carboxy-THC (THC-COOH), can remain detectable in blood for days and urine for weeks after use, so a per se result may reflect use days/weeks earlier rather than impairment at driving — secondary explanation, consistent across the summaries above. Source: secondary — accessed 29 October 2026.

12.2.3 Impairment theory — ORC 4511.19(A)(1)(a)

  • No person shall operate a vehicle, streetcar or trackless trolley in Ohio if, at the time of operation, the person is under the influence of alcohol, a drug of abuse, or a combination of them. This is distinct from the per se theory. Officer observations (slurred speech, lethargy, eye appearance in secondary summaries), field sobriety tests, and Drug Recognition Expert (DRE) 12-step evaluations are used as impairment evidence — secondary; flag DRE protocol details as secondary. Source: ORC 4511.19 via secondary summaries — accessed 29 October 2026.

12.2.4 Medical-patient limits on testing — statute directly opened

ORC 3796.24(E), effective 20 March 2026 (SB 56). Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.24 — accessed 29 October 2026. A person's status as a registered patient/caregiver is not a sufficient basis for conducting a field sobriety test or suspending a driver's licence; to conduct a field sobriety test, an officer must have an independent, factual basis giving reasonable suspicion the person is operating a vehicle under the influence of marijuana or with a prohibited concentration of marijuana in whole blood, blood serum, plasma, breath or urine.

12.2.5 Prescription defence does not cover a medical marijuana recommendation — secondary, Verify (K) text

  • Multiple secondary summaries state ORC 4511.19(K)(1)–(2) provides a statutory defence when a substance was taken pursuant to a valid prescription from a licensed health professional, but that defence does not apply to medical marijuana recommendations because a recommendation is not a prescription under Ohio law; lawful medical use therefore does not serve as a defence to a per se OVI charge. Source: secondary (Brian Smith Law and others) — accessed 29 October 2026. Flag the exact (K) text as Verify before quoting it verbatim.

12.2.6 Implied consent / refusal — secondary, conflicting framings, Verify

  • A driver lawfully arrested for OVI is deemed to have consented to chemical testing. Secondary framings differ: Billak Law summary — first refusal triggers a 1-year administrative licence suspension, second refusal 2 years, third refusal 3 years; another secondary summary — refusal triggers immediate suspension at least until the initial court appearance (typically within 5 days) and a reinstatement fee, and failure to submit within 2 hours of the alleged violation is treated as automatic refusal. Flag the exact ORC 4511.192 consequences as Verify; do not merge the two framings. Sources: secondary — accessed 29 October 2026.

12.2.7 First-offence OVI penalties — secondary, Verify full table

  • First conviction in 10 years: 72 hours' jail or court-ordered driver intervention programme; fine $375 to $1,075; licence suspension 1–3 years (Dearie Fischer & Martinson / CannabisOH summaries, with CannabisOH stating 3 days' jail minimum and 1–3 year suspension). Source: secondary — accessed 29 October 2026. Flag the full penalty table (including second/third offences, vehicle forfeiture and ignition-interlock provisions) as Verify against ORC 4511.19(G); do not present the first-offence figures as the complete penalty scheme.

12.2.8 Vehicle conduct rules — adopt Run 1

  • Operator OVI law (ORC 4511.19 etc.) applies; passenger smoking/vaping while the operator is operating or in physical control is a third-degree misdemeanor (ORC 3796.99(A)(2) per Run 1); operating while under the influence is never authorised (ORC 3796.04(E), 3796.221(E), 3796.22(D) per Run 1); transport in original unopened packaging or trunk/behind-last-seat (ORC 3796.062 per Run 1). Sources: Run 1 report — accessed 28 October 2026.
  • Watercraft/aircraft — Run 1 related statutes, not re-verified here: ORC 1547.11 (watercraft), ORC 4511.194, ORC 4561.15 (aircraft) impaired-operation offences incorporated by ORC 3796.99(A)(1) per Run 1 §1.2(G) — flag as carried from Run 1, not re-opened in this session.

12.2.9 Pending bill — SB 55, NOT law

  • Senate Bill 55 (136th GA), as described by secondary sources, would: raise the whole-blood THC limit from 2 ng/mL to 5 ng/mL; move away from automatic metabolite testing, letting a test result support a rebuttable inference of impairment rather than an automatic violation; reduce the four current marijuana OVI prohibitions to two (operating under the influence of THC; operating with a prohibited concentration of THC in blood); and give defendants tools to challenge testing methods, equipment and reliability before and during trial. As of mid-2026 it had passed the Ohio Senate (unanimously, per multiple secondary accounts) and was under consideration in the Ohio House (House Judiciary Committee hearing, March 2026, per EIN Presswire 6 March 2026 and Scioto Valley Guardian 6 March 2026). It is not yet law, so the limits in §12.2.2 remain in effect. Sources: Brian Smith Law (above); Strauss Troy (above); EIN Presswire, https://www.einpresswire.com/article-pdf/897659292/ohio-senate-bill-55-operating-under-the-influence-of-marijuana-advances-in-house — accessed 29 October 2026; Scioto Valley Guardian, https://sciotovalleyguardian.com/2026/03/06/ohio-lawmakers-weigh-major-overhaul-of-marijuana-ovi-laws-as-bill-moves-to-house/ — accessed 29 October 2026. Flag SB 55 status as Verify on legislature.ohio.gov before republication; do not present it as enacted.

12.3 Expungement and sealing for marijuana offences

12.3.1 New marijuana-specific expungement — statute directly opened

ORC 2953.321, effective 20 March 2026, latest legislation SB 56 (136th GA); codes page last updated 2 February 2026. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-2953.321 — accessed 29 October 2026.

  • (A) "Expunge" means to destroy, delete and erase a record as appropriate for its physical/electronic form/characteristic so it is permanently irretrievable; "official records" and "prosecutor" have the ORC 2953.31 meanings.
  • (B) Eligibility, only if before the effective date of the section the person was the defendant named in a dismissed complaint/indictment/information for, or was convicted of, or pleaded guilty to: (1) a violation of ORC 2925.11(C)(3)(a) or (C)(7)(a) or (b); or (2) a violation of ORC 2925.11(C)(7)(c) or (d) involving possession of not more than 15 grams of hashish.
  • (C) Eligible persons may apply to the sentencing court at any time on or after the effective date; the application must identify the applicant, the offence, the date of conviction/plea/dismissal, and the court; include evidence the offence was one of the (B) offences and the conviction/plea/dismissal occurred before the effective date; and request expungement of the record of conviction or official records.
  • (D) On filing and payment of the fee in (G) if applicable, the court shall set a hearing date and notify the prosecutor; the prosecutor may object before the hearing date, specifying reasons denial is justified; the court shall direct its regular probation officer, a state probation officer, or the county department of probation where the applicant resides to make inquiries/written reports as the court requires; the court shall hold the hearing; the hearing shall be held not less than 45 days and not more than 90 days after filing.
  • (E) At the hearing, the court shall determine whether the applicant was, before the effective date, a defendant in a dismissed case or convicted/pleaded guilty to a (B) offence; consider any prosecutor objection reasons; and weigh the applicant's interests in expungement against the legitimate needs, if any, of the government to maintain the records.
  • (F) If the court finds the (B) predicate and that the applicant's interests in having the record of conviction/official records sealed are not substantially outweighed by legitimate governmental needs to maintain the records, the court shall order expungement of all official records pertaining to the case and deletion of all index references, send notice to each public office/agency the court has reason to believe may hold an official record, and the proceedings shall be considered not to have occurred; the records shall not be used for any purpose including a criminal records check under ORC 109.572; the applicant may, and the court shall, reply that no record exists on any inquiry.
  • (G) Fee: $50 on filing, unless indigent; the court shall pay $30 into the state treasury (half credited to the Attorney General reimbursement fund under ORC 109.11) and $20 into the county general revenue fund.

Limits to state plainly: This is a petition route, not automatic expungement; it is limited to the pre-20 March 2026 offences/amounts above; it requires a hearing and a balancing test; it does not cover all marijuana offences (e.g. trafficking, cultivation, larger-amount possession, or post-effective-date offences are outside (B) on the text read). Do not describe ORC 2953.321 as "automatic" or as covering all Ohio marijuana records.

  • Note on the codes page: ORC 2953.321 is listed as "Enacted by Senate Bill 56" with a March 20, 2026 version available — the section did not exist as a prior version in the versions list shown. Flag whether any pre-SB 56 marijuana expungement provision existed under a different number as Verify if the final report makes a historical claim.

12.3.2 General sealing/expungement — ORC 2953.32 (secondary summaries; Verify direct text)

  • ORC 2953.32 is the general sealing/expungement framework, unified by SB 288 effective April 2023 (secondary Medium summary; SB 288 date from secondary, flag direct verification). "Expunge" under ORC 2953.31(B)(2)(b) means destroy/delete/erase so the record is permanently irretrievable (Ohio Court of Appeals, Tenth District, In re E.H., 2025, 24AP-718, concurring discussion, Justia). Source: secondary — accessed 29 October 2026.
  • Sealing/expungement in Ohio is not automatic and is described in secondary law-firm summaries as a privilege / "act of grace created by the state," not a right; even if eligible, a judge/magistrate holds a hearing, determines eligibility, evaluates rehabilitation, and weighs the applicant's interest against the government's interest; denial is reviewed for abuse of discretion. Source: secondary — accessed 29 October 2026.
  • Waiting periods vary by offence (secondary ExpungeMap table: Ohio, petition, 1–5 years by offence, many convictions and arrests after a wait, ORC 2953.32). Example, secondary (LegalClarity, F5 drug possession): if the defendant completes intervention in lieu of conviction (ILC), the charge is dismissed and the record can be sealed immediately; for a conviction followed by community control, the defendant can apply to seal 1 year after final discharge from supervision; F5 drug possession is not among offences excluded from sealing eligibility on that secondary account. Flag both the general waiting-period table and the F5 example as secondary/Verify against ORC 2953.32 and ORC 2953.36.
  • Filing fees: secondary summaries state no filing fee for nonconvictions, and for convictions a fee typically $0–$400 depending on county (LegalClarity F5 summary) — flag as secondary/county-variable; do not quote a single statewide fee except the ORC 2953.321 $50 fee above.
  • Juvenile records: secondary attorney summary states records can be sealed 2 years after the case is closed and expungement is automatic once the person turns 23 or 5 years after the incident, whichever comes first (citing ORC 2953.32 and 2953.36) — flag as secondary/Verify; do not present juvenile automatic expungement as the adult rule.
  • No Ohio "Clean Slate" automatic sealing programme for adult marijuana convictions was located in this session — flag as Unavailable/Verify against ORC 2953.32–2953.36 and any 2025–2026 clean-slate bill; do not claim Ohio has automatic adult expungement.
  • Related collateral point — badge/licence eligibility after expungement: ORC 2953.321(F)(2) states expunged records shall not be used for any purpose including an ORC 109.572 criminal records check. The report may note this consequence but must not advise that expungement guarantees DCC licensure/badging, which also turns on disqualifying-offence definitions in OAC 1301:18-1-01 and DCC suitability review — flag that interaction as Verify.

12.4 Consumption lounges and events

12.4.1 No consumption-lounge licence

  • Chapter 3796 licenses only cultivators, processors, retail dispensaries and testing laboratories (ORC 3796.02). No lounge, café or on-site consumption licence type exists in the statute/rule text read. Secondary summaries agree: MedicateOH (crawl 16 hours before 29 October 2026) states state regulators have not established rules for public consumption lounges and legal consumption is restricted almost entirely to private property with owner permission; Cannabis Industry Lawyer SB 56 guide states "A licensed consumption lounge? Not yet — Ohio doesn't have those licensed establishments (yet)." Sources: secondary — accessed 29 October 2026.

12.4.2 Public consumption is prohibited

  • ORC 3796.04(C)(2) (knowing consumption in a public place prohibited) and ORC 3796.04(C)(3) (operator must not knowingly permit it), plus ORC 3796.06(C)(2) (smoking/combustion/vaporisation only on privately owned real property used primarily for residential or agricultural purposes) and ORC 3796.06(C)(3) (also banned in child-care homes, halfway-house-type facilities, lease-prohibited rentals, public places/places of employment as defined in ORC 3794.01) — all Run 1, SB 56. Source: ORC Chapter 3796 — accessed 29 October 2026 (carried from Run 1).
  • Moritz College of Law summary (updated 26 March 2026, secondary): smoking/combustion/vaping in public spaces is a minor misdemeanor, prohibited at any time in private homes operating as childcare centres, prohibited in rental housing if the lease prohibits it, and prohibited as a passenger in a motor vehicle (third-degree misdemeanor, consistent with Run 1). Source: https://dev-moritz-college-of-law-v2.pantheonsite.io/sites/default/files/2026-07/Ohio%20reforms_SB56%20and%20Issue%202_January%208%202026_final.pdf — accessed 29 October 2026.

12.4.3 Events

  • OAC 1301:18-4-22 placement rules require written DCC notification at least 10 business days before a scheduled event (conferences, trade shows, similar events) the licensee plans to attend/participate in/sponsor, educational or otherwise (§11.7.2). That is an advertising-placement notice rule, not permission to consume at the event. Trade-show/conference attendance with advertising is therefore regulated, but on-site consumption at a public event remains barred by the public-consumption rules above.
  • Private events on private residential/agricultural property with owner permission are the only smoking/vaping locus stated in the statute; whether a ticketed private event on private property counts as a "public place" was not resolved in the sources found — flag as Unavailable/Verify (case law, not statute, would decide it).
  • Smoking in bars/restaurants/venues: Ohio's indoor smoking law (ORC Chapter 3794, referenced via ORC 3796.06(C)(3) "place of employment" definition) plus the private-property-only smoking/vaping rule together bar smoking/vaping in bars, restaurants, sports venues, etc. — secondary Moritz summary states this expressly for bars/restaurants/sports venues. Flag the ORC 3794 interaction as carried from Run 1/secondary, not re-opened here.

12.5 Cannabis tourism and visitor purchase rules

12.5.1 Adult-use visitors may purchase

  • Secondary Marijuana Herald Ohio laws page (crawl 3 days before 29 October 2026) states adults 21+ visiting Ohio may purchase recreational marijuana from licensed dispensaries; Ohio does not require adult-use customers to be state residents; a customer must present valid government-issued photo ID showing 21+; visitors are subject to the same 2.5 oz plant-material and 15 g extract possession limits as Ohio residents; marijuana purchased in Ohio cannot legally be transported across state lines. Source: secondary — accessed 29 October 2026. The residency point is consistent with ORC 3796.20(C) as summarised in Run 1 (government-issued ID proving 21+, no residency element stated in the statute excerpt) — flag the "no residency requirement" as statute-consistent but secondary-confirmed, not as a verbatim statutory sentence, until ORC 3796.20(C) is quoted in full in the final report.

12.5.2 Daily purchase limits for visitors (same as residents)

  • Adult-use per day, OAC 1301:18-8-08(A)(2), effective 28 August 2025: 2.5 oz plant material + cannabis products with total THC content of no more than 15,000 mg; plant-material calculation includes cannabis plant material and raw-single serving units; all other products count toward the 15,000 mg total-THC limit. Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-1301:18-8-08 — accessed 29 October 2026. This is a purchase/dispensing limit, distinct from the statutory possession limit (2.5 oz + 15 g extract, cumulative) — the 15,000 mg THC figure must not be quoted as the possession limit for extracts.
  • Medical per-day dispensing limits are in §11.2 / C-3 (OAC 1301:18-8-09: patient 10 oz / 60,000 mg; caregiver 2.5 oz / 15,000 mg).

12.5.3 Medical visitors — no reciprocity on evidence found

  • Run 1: no reciprocity right exists unless DCC has entered an agreement under ORC 3796.16 (substantially comparable eligibility + mutual recognition); no such agreement was located in Run 1. Carry that flag forward; an out-of-state cardholder may purchase as an adult-use consumer (21+) subject to adult-use caps/taxes, but that is not medical recognition. Re-check the DCC reciprocity list before republication — Verify.

12.5.4 Interstate transport warning

  • Buying in Ohio does not authorise taking marijuana into Kentucky, Indiana, West Virginia, Pennsylvania or Michigan; each destination state's law and federal law govern transport, and Run 1 states Ohio's safe harbour is limited to Ohio-dispensary or lawfully homegrown marijuana (ORC 3796.221(A)). Do not soften this to "visitors may take it home." Source: Run 1 report — accessed 28 October 2026.

12.5.5 Hotels / short-term rentals and federal land

  • Hotels: No hotel exception exists in Chapter 3796. Secondary summaries describe hotels as "legally questionable" (CannabisOH) because a hotel room is not the visitor's privately owned residential property and may be a public place/place of employment. Flag hotel-room consumption as Unavailable/Verify (no statute or DCC guidance located); do not state hotels are lawful consumption sites. Source: secondary — accessed 29 October 2026.
  • Federal land: ORC 3796.24(H)(3) — Chapter 3796 does not permit use/possession/administration on federal land in Ohio (Run 1). Relevant to tourists visiting national parks, VA hospitals, military installations and federal courthouses in Ohio — secondary LegalClarity summary lists these examples; flag the examples as secondary illustrations of the federal-land rule. Source: ORC 3796.24, https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.24 — accessed 29 October 2026.

12.6 Landlord and tenant rules

12.6.1 Statute directly opened — ORC 3796.24 (SB 56, effective 20 March 2026)

Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.24 — accessed 29 October 2026. Verbatim operative provisions:

  • (F) Tenant rejection and lease prohibitions: "A person's status as a registered patient or caregiver shall not be used as the sole or primary basis for rejecting the person as a tenant unless the rejection is required by federal law. This division does not prohibit a landlord from prohibiting, as long as such prohibition is included in the applicable lease agreement: (1) consumption of marijuana in a residential premises or common areas by smoking, combustion, or vaporisation; (2) cultivation or growth of homegrown marijuana."
  • (G) Public benefits: Except for unemployment compensation benefits under ORC Chapter 4141, including as prescribed under ORC 3796.28(B), the use/possession of medical/adult-use/homegrown marijuana in accordance with Chapter 3796 shall not be used as a reason for disqualifying an individual from a public benefit programme administered by any state/local authority, or otherwise denying a state/local public benefit.
  • (A) Professional licences: A professional/occupational licence holder is not subject to professional disciplinary action solely for engaging in professional/occupational activities related to medical marijuana.
  • (B) Children: Unless there is clear and convincing evidence a child is unsafe, medical marijuana use/possession/administration in accordance with Chapter 3796 shall not be the sole/primary basis for (1) an abused/neglected/dependent child adjudication under ORC 2151.28, (2) allocation of parental rights/responsibilities under ORC 3109.04, or (3) a parenting-time order under ORC 3109.051 or 3109.12.
  • (C) Medical care: Medical marijuana use/possession in accordance with Chapter 3796 shall not be used as a reason for disqualifying a patient from medical care or from a transplant waiting list.
  • (D) Forfeiture: Medical marijuana use/possession/administration/cultivation/processing/testing/dispensing in accordance with Chapter 3796 shall not be used as the sole/primary reason for action under any criminal/civil statute in forfeiture/seizure of property/assets.
  • (H)(4)–(5) Public places: Chapter 3796 does not require any public place to accommodate a registered patient's/adult-use consumer's use, and does not prohibit any public place from accommodating a registered patient's medical use, except no public place shall accommodate consumption of medical marijuana by smoking, combustion, or vaporisation. (H)(1)–(3) and (6) and (I) (no requirement for a physician to recommend; no permission beyond Chapter 3796; no permission on federal land; no restriction on IRB-approved research; contracts related to licence holders are enforceable as Ohio public policy) are also in the section text opened.

12.6.2 Home-grow lease bar — statute (Run 1)

  • ORC 3796.04(A)(1)(d) prohibits home grow at residential premises occupied under a rental agreement that prohibits the activities otherwise authorised by ORC 3796.04 (see §11.3.4). Source: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.04 — accessed 29 October 2026.
  • Ohio Judges 2026 Marijuana Facts PDF (secondary/official-judicial-education summary, crawl 14 days before 29 October 2026) summarises: landlord may prohibit, as part of the lease, (a) consumption by smoking/combustion/vaping and (b) growing at the rental premises; the smoking/vaping prohibition is limited to smoking/vaping and does not include other forms of consumption; use of medical marijuana may not be used as the sole/primary reason to reject a tenant unless prohibited under federal law; all marijuana including medical is strictly prohibited in HUD-assisted (Section 8) housing properties. Source: https://www.ohiojudges.org/cdn/2026-marijuana-facts.pdf — accessed 29 October 2026. Treat the "does not include other forms" gloss and the HUD statement as secondary summaries of ORC 3796.24(F) and federal housing law respectively — flag HUD's current multifamily guidance as Verify before quoting it as a HUD rule.

12.6.3 Adult-use tenant rejection — gap

  • ORC 3796.24(F) by its terms protects registered patients/caregivers. Whether an adult-use consumer (non-patient) has the same tenant-rejection protection was not resolved in the statute text read; secondary LegalClarity summaries extend a similar "cannot reject solely/primarily because applicant is an adult-use consumer, unless federal law requires rejection" claim to adult-use consumers, citing former Chapter 3780 — that citation is now repealed, so flag the adult-use tenant-rejection point as Verify against current ORC 3796.24/3796.04 text, not as settled law.

12.6.4 Local government and home grow; eviction mechanics

  • Ohio Judges summary states "Local government may not prohibit or limit homegrown marijuana," citing ORC 3796.29 — carry as secondary, flag direct ORC 3796.29 text in the final report. This is distinct from a landlord's lease-based prohibition, which is expressly preserved.
  • Eviction / lease enforcement mechanics: No Ohio landlord-tenant eviction procedure specific to marijuana was located (ORC Chapter 5321 general landlord-tenant law was not opened in this session). Flag eviction procedure, notice periods, and damages for lease violations as Unavailable in this session; do not import general 5321 procedure without opening it.

12.7 Gun ownership conflicts

12.7.1 Federal prohibition — baseline + secondary, Verify ATF / Supreme Court

  • 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) bars persons who are unlawful users of, or addicted to, a controlled substance from possessing firearms/ammunition. Secondary summaries agree FFLs may not sell to verified marijuana users and ATF Form 4473 carries a warning that medical marijuana is federally illegal; Ohio's medical registry information is confidential and not a public record and, per OhioStateCannabis secondary summary, is not accessible in a NICS check — flag the NICS/registry-confidentiality interaction as secondary/Verify. Sources: secondary — accessed 29 October 2026.
  • Schedule III point, as instructed: Schedule III medical status alone does not resolve § 922(g)(3) on the evidence found. Secondary Leafwell article, published/updated 23 October 2026, states the issue is unresolved in 2026: § 922(g)(3) still bars unlawful users, ATF narrowed its definition of unlawful user, and the Supreme Court ruled in United States v. Hemani that one marijuana user's prosecution was unconstitutional while calling that ruling narrow, and the ATF's new gun-purchase form is not final. Source: secondary, 23 October 2026 — accessed 29 October 2026.
  • Secondary Brad Wolfe Law summary states Hemani involved a federal statute, not Ohio law; Hemani did not affect the federal government's ability to ban "addicts… or those presently intoxicated" from possessing a firearm; and ORC 2923.13(A)(4) remains in effect and will likely continue to be enforced as before. Source: secondary — accessed 29 October 2026. Do not cite Hemani's holding, citation, or scope beyond this narrow secondary framing without opening the slip opinion — flag Verify.
  • Conflicting secondary claim, rejected: A secondary U.S. LawShield summary (crawl 3 days before 29 October 2026) contains a stale premise (May 2024 DOJ proposed rule, "anticipated… in 2024 or 2025") and a claim that Schedule III prescription use would allow lawful firearm possession. This conflicts with the fixed baseline (Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 for state-licensed medical marijuana, not a federal prescription) and with Leafwell/Brad Wolfe's "unresolved" framing. Do not adopt the LawShield prescription-use claim; list it in research notes as a conflicting secondary claim, rejected for the reasons above.

12.7.2 Ohio state gun law — secondary, with official-code search confirmation for the operative text

  • ORC 2923.13(A)(4) — Having weapons while under disability. Official-code search text confirms the operative structure: "Unless relieved from disability as provided in section 2923.14 of the Revised Code, no person shall knowingly acquire, have, carry, or use any firearm or dangerous ordnance, if any of the following apply: … (4) The person is drug dependent, in danger of drug dependence, or a chronic alcoholic." Secondary summaries add that violation may be charged as a third-degree felony (Cincinnati criminal-defence summary) and that the disability covers persons under indictment for or convicted of a felony drug offence, among other categories (NRA-ILA Ohio summary). Sources: codes.ohio.gov search, https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/search?pageSize=25&sort=BestMatch&keywords=firearm&start=101 — accessed 29 October 2026; Ohio Supreme Court opinion State v. Bushong, 2003-Ohio-2296, http://www.supremecourt.ohio.gov/rod/docs/pdf/5/2003/2003-Ohio-2296.pdf — accessed 29 October 2026 (quoting the (A)(4) text). Flag the exact current (A)(4) text, penalty class, and whether lawful medical-marijuana use alone constitutes "drug dependence" as Verify — no Ohio case holding that lawful medical use alone triggers (A)(4) was located in this session, and this report does not state that it does.
  • ORC 2923.15 — Using weapons while intoxicated. "(A) No person, while under the influence of alcohol or any drug of abuse, shall carry or use any firearm or dangerous ordnance. (B) Whoever violates this section is guilty of using weapons while intoxicated, a misdemeanor of the first degree." Source: codes.ohio.gov search (above) — accessed 29 October 2026.
  • Ohio permitless carry: Secondary OhioStateCannabis summary states following SB 215, Ohioans are no longer required to obtain gun permits if they fulfil other requirements, so medical patients "may be able to carry firearms without permits" under state law, but possessing guns while a medical marijuana user is illegal under federal law and may attract severe penalties. Montgomery County Sheriff's Office (Montgomery County, Ohio) concealed-carry page (secondary county source, crawl 4 days before 29 October 2026) warns there are no exceptions in federal law for medical use even if sanctioned by state law, and a person legally using medical marijuana under the programme may be denied an Ohio Concealed Handgun License and may be prohibited from carrying a concealed handgun under federal law. Flag both as secondary/county-level; do not present permitless carry as resolving the federal conflict.
  • Federal penalties (secondary, Verify against 18 U.S.C. § 924): Elevate Holistics (crawl 2 days before 29 October 2026) states up to 10 years' imprisonment and up to $250,000 fines for possession as a § 922(g)(3) person; falsifying Form 4473 is a separate crime punishable by 5 years. Flag as secondary; do not quote as the current federal penalty table without § 924 verification.
  • Practical advice in secondary sources ("get rid of your card and stop using, then you may purchase again, but you must no longer be a user; lying on the form is perjury") must not be reproduced as legal advice in this report; the report states only the legal conflict and that persons should seek firearms counsel, as Leafwell does.

12.8 Pet and veterinary products

12.8.1 No Ohio-specific veterinary cannabis statute/rule located — Unavailable

  • No Ohio-specific veterinary cannabis statute or rule was located in this session — state this as Unavailable; do not fill it with other states' law.
  • Stale Ohio summary, do not rely on it: PawsAndClawsCBD (crawl 209 days before 29 October 2026) states Ohio CBD/cannabis products are "technically legal for medical use" but there is "gray area caused by a state regulation from the Ohio Board of Pharmacy that makes sales of CBD products illegal," and that "state veterinary leaders say the Ohio Veterinary Medical Association defers [to] federal regulations." That Board of Pharmacy framing predates the current DCC/hemp framework and the SB 56 hemp definition — do not rely on it; flag the current Ohio Veterinary Medical Association position as Verify/Unavailable.

12.8.2 Federal / professional position — secondary, general (not Ohio-specific)

  • JD Supra summary "Six Things You Need to Know About CBD and Other Hemp-containing Pet Products" states: FDA has not approved cannabis-derived products for animals, so veterinarians are unable to prescribe a CBD product for a pet; products for animals with therapeutic claims not evaluated/approved by FDA are unapproved animal drugs, considered "unsafe" under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act because safety/efficacy have not been shown; there are currently no approved cannabis-derived drugs for animals; use of unapproved drugs can put pets at risk and create legal risks for veterinarians who administer/prescribe/dispense/recommend them; marketing unapproved treatments may lead owners to choose them instead of approved therapies. The National Animal Supplement Council (NASC) and Association of American Feed Control Officers (AAFCO) are working with members, FDA and manufacturers on self-regulation/GMP/quality assurance for CBD/hemp animal products. Source: secondary — accessed 29 October 2026.
  • Bluegrass Hemp Oil guidance (secondary, crawl 144 days before 29 October 2026) adds: pet CBD products are not FDA-approved animal drugs; pet CBD should not be marketed for anxiety/pain/seizures/inflammation/arthritis/mobility/behaviour/skin/appetite/urinary conditions; full-spectrum pet CBD may contain trace THC; THC exposure can be dangerous for dogs/cats; use pet-specific products only; avoid human CBD gummies, THC products, xylitol, chocolate, essential oils, vague flavour blends; review label and batch-specific CoA. Source: secondary — accessed 29 October 2026. Treat all of this as general secondary guidance, not Ohio law.

12.8.3 What can be stated from Ohio law — by inference only, flagged as such

  • Dispensary products under ORC 3796.20 are dispensed/sold to registered patients/caregivers and adult-use consumers (humans, 18+/21+ as applicable); no provision in Chapter 3796 authorises dispensing medical/adult-use marijuana for animal use.
  • Hemp products within the ORC 928.01 definition (≤0.3% total THC plant; ≤0.4 mg total THC per container final product; no synthetic/non-naturally-producible cannabinoids) remain hemp, not marijuana — but that definition does not create a veterinary approval, dose, or labelling regime. The report must not state a pet dose, a pet product approval, or that hemp CBD is "legal for pets in Ohio" as a statutory conclusion without an Ohio veterinary/ODA source.

12.9 Medical cannabis in schools

12.9.1 No Ohio statute authorising school administration located — Unavailable

  • No Ohio statute authorising school administration of medical marijuana was located in this session — state this as Unavailable; do not fill it with other districts' policies.
  • Non-Ohio school policies found in searches must be excluded: District medical-marijuana policies from Bradford Schools, Pennsboro/PSDSchools, Twin Rivers R-X (Missouri) and Nassau County, Florida, appeared in school searches; they are not Ohio law and must not be cited for Ohio schools or pets.

12.9.2 Ohio law that does bear on schools (directly found or Run 1)

  • 500-ft buffer: ORC 3796.30(A) (version effective 3 October 2023, HB 33, shown in search results; SB 56 version must be quoted in the final report) — no medical marijuana cultivator/processor/retail dispensary/laboratory shall be located within 500 ft of parcel boundaries of a school, church, public library, public playground or public park; relocation into the buffer requires licence revocation under that version; "school" means a child care centre under ORC 5104.01, a preschool under ORC 2950.034, or a public/nonpublic primary/secondary school; research exemption in ORC 3796.30(B) for IRB-approved research (see §11.9.1). Run 1 states the current 500-ft rule as ORC 3796.30(A) + OAC 1301:18-3-01 (measured linearly, shortest parcel-line-to-structure distance, same-premises certificate exception, later-arriving protected facility rule with written notice + security modifications) — adopt Run 1 for the current rule; flag the 3 October 2023 version shown in search results as superseded. Source: ORC Chapter 3796 — accessed 29 October 2026.
  • Public-place accommodation: ORC 3796.24(H)(4)–(5) (§12.6.1) — Chapter 3796 does not require any public place to accommodate a patient's/adult-use consumer's use, and does not prohibit a public place from accommodating a patient's medical use, except no public place shall accommodate consumption by smoking, combustion, or vaporisation. A school is not stated to be required to accommodate administration, and no school-nurse administration duty was located.
  • Child-care / school premises as prohibited home-grow and smoking locations: ORC 3796.04(A)(1)(d) (Type A/B family child care homes) and ORC 3796.06(C)(3) (child-care homes, halfway-house-type facilities, lease-prohibited rentals, public places/places of employment) — Run 1. Sources: ORC 3796.04, https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-3796.04 — accessed 29 October 2026; ORC Chapter 3796 — accessed 29 October 2026.
  • Minor patients: OAC 1301:18-8-09(A)(1)(a) requires a patient to be at least 18 or a caregiver at least 21 for dispensary review of ID; minor-patient consent/caregiver rules were flagged Verify in Run 1 (OAC 1301:18-10 not opened) — carry that flag; do not state a K-12 administration procedure for minor patients.

12.9.3 University (not K-12) federal overlay — secondary/university policy, not statute

  • Ohio University (Athens, Athens County, Ohio) news reminder, August 2024, on the federal Drug-Free Schools and Communities Act: while Issue 2 (November 2023) and medical cannabis (2016) are legal under Ohio law, they remain illegal under federal law; the Act requires Ohio University to maintain policies on unlawful possession/use/distribution; therefore use/storage of medical and/or recreational cannabis by students, faculty, staff and visitors remains prohibited on all property/buildings including residence halls owned/leased/operated/controlled/managed by Ohio University including regional/extension campuses regardless of location, and during all University-sponsored activities/programmes on- and off-campus; student reports go to the Office of Community Standards and Student Responsibility under the Student Code of Conduct; employee reports are handled under Policy 41.133. Source: secondary (Ohio University news, August 2024) — accessed 29 October 2026. This is a university policy under federal funding conditions, not an Ohio K-12 statute, and must be labelled as such.

12.9.4 K-12 conclusion

  • On the evidence found, Ohio has no statewide K-12 medical-cannabis administration statute located; administration, storage and staff-volunteer questions, if addressed at all, would be district-policy matters and federal-funding matters, and must be flagged as Unavailable — check the individual Ohio school district's board policy and the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce guidance before stating any district practice as Ohio law. Do not cite the Florida/Missouri district policies found in searches.
